He believed that people should be allowed to accumulate property within limits, forbidding any citizen, as I have already noted, to possess more than five times the minimum qualification. Those who make laws of this kind should remember something they often overlook: a legislator who fixes the amount of property must also fix the number of children. If there are too many children for the property available, the law will have to be broken. Apart from that breach, it is itself harmful for many people to fall from wealth into poverty, since people whose fortunes have collapsed are certain to promote revolution. Even some early legislators clearly understood the influence that equalizing property has on political society. Solon and others passed laws preventing an individual from acquiring as much land as he wished. Other states have laws forbidding property sales. Among the Locrians, for example, a man may not sell his property unless he can give unmistakable proof that some misfortune has struck him. Laws have also required the original allotments to be preserved. The island of Leucas had such a law; abolishing it made the constitution excessively democratic, because the rulers no longer possessed the required property qualification. Moreover, even where property is equal, the amount may be too great or too small, leaving its owners in luxury or poverty. The legislator must therefore aim not simply at equality of possessions, but at a moderate amount. Yet assigning the same moderate amount to everyone still does not bring him nearer his goal. What needs equalizing is human desire, not possessions; and this cannot be achieved unless the state provides an adequate education. Phaleas will probably answer that this is exactly his point: he thinks states should have equality of education as well as of property. But he must explain what kind of education he intends. Giving everyone the same education is useless if it encourages greed, ambition, or both. Furthermore, civil conflict arises from inequality of honour as well as inequality of property, though in opposite ways. Ordinary people resent unequal property, whereas those of higher standing resent equal honours. As the poet puts it—

'The bad receive the same honour as the good.' Some crimes are driven by need. Phaleas expects equal property to remedy these, by removing the hunger or cold that tempts a man to become a highway robber. Yet need is not the only inducement to crime. People also want to satisfy a passion that torments them; or they seek pleasures that are not accompanied by the pain of desire. These motives, too, lead people to commit crimes.

What remedies, then, are there for these three disorders? For the first, a moderate amount of property and employment; for the second, habits of self-restraint. For the third, if people seek pleasures that depend on themselves, they can satisfy that desire only through philosophy, since every other pleasure depends on other people. The greatest crimes, in fact, arise from excess rather than need. No one becomes a tyrant merely to keep himself warm. That is why great honour goes to the man who kills a tyrant, not to the man who kills a thief. We can therefore see that Phaleas' institutions are effective only against minor crimes.

There is a further objection to these institutions. Their chief purpose is to secure the state's internal well-being, but the legislator must also consider its relations with neighbouring nations and everyone outside it. Government must be organized with military strength in view, a subject on which Phaleas says nothing. Property presents the same issue. There must be enough not only to meet needs within the state, but also to face dangers from abroad. The state's wealth should not be so great that it attracts more powerful neighbours while its owners lack the strength to repel them. Nor should it be so small that the state cannot sustain a war even against other states of equal strength and similar character. Phaleas gives no rule here. We should remember that a certain amount of wealth is advantageous. The best limit is probably an amount too small to tempt a stronger neighbour or make war against you profitable. A story is told of Eubulus when Autophradates was preparing to besiege Atarneus. Eubulus asked him to consider how long the siege would last and calculate the expense for that period. 'For less than that sum,' he said, 'I am ready to leave Atarneus immediately.' His words impressed Autophradates, who abandoned the siege.

Equalizing property has the advantage of preventing disputes among citizens, though its benefit even here is not very great. The nobles will resent being denied the honours they believe they deserve, and such resentment often produces rebellion and revolution. Human greed, moreover, knows no satisfaction. Once, two obols were sufficient pay; now that this payment is customary, people endlessly demand more. Desire is by nature unsatisfied, and most people live only to gratify it. Reform should therefore begin less with equalizing property than with teaching nobler natures not to want more, and preventing baser natures from obtaining more. The latter must be restrained, but not mistreated. Besides, Phaleas' equalization is incomplete. He equalizes land alone, yet someone can also be rich in slaves, livestock, money, and a great quantity of what are called movable possessions. Either all these must be equalized too, or limits must be set on them, or they must all be left unrestricted. It would also appear that Phaleas is drafting legislation only for a city with a small population, since he assumes that every artisan will be a public slave and excluded from its citizen population. If a law requires artisans to be public slaves, however, it should apply only to those engaged in public works, as at Epidamnus, or under the arrangement Diophantus once introduced at Athens.

These observations enable anyone to judge where Phaleas' ideas are right and where they are wrong. Hippodamus, a man from Miletus and the son of Euryphon, was the—[Alternative reading, following Bernays: 'the remedy for such evils.']

very man who devised the art of planning cities and laid out the Piraeus. [Textual note: place a comma after itvtu and remove the following comma.] He was an unusual man. His desire to stand out made his whole way of life eccentric, and some thought him affected: he wore his hair long and flowing, and adorned himself with expensive ornaments, yet wore the same inexpensive, warm garment in both summer and winter. Besides aspiring to mastery in the study of nature, he was the first person who was not a statesman to investigate the best kind of government.

Hippodamus' city contained ten thousand citizens divided into three groups: artisans, farmers, and armed defenders of the state. He likewise divided the land into three portions, sacred, public, and private. The sacred portion supported the customary worship of the gods; the public portion maintained the warriors; and the private portion belonged to the farmers. His laws, too, fell into exactly three categories, because he held that lawsuits concerned three things: insult, injury, and homicide. He also established a single court to serve as the final court of appeal, to which any case thought to have been wrongly decided could be referred. This court consisted of elders selected for that purpose. He also thought that judges should deliver their decisions on tablets rather than by casting voting pebbles. A judge could write an unqualified condemnation, or leave his tablet blank to acquit outright; if he acquitted in part and condemned in part, he would set down the distinction. Hippodamus objected that the existing law forced judges into perjury whichever vote they cast. He further prescribed rewards for anyone who discovered something beneficial to the state, and provided that

the children of citizens killed in battle should be supported at public expense. He treated this provision as though no one had heard of such a law before, although it already exists at Athens and elsewhere. He proposed that all magistrates should be elected by the people, meaning the three classes just described. Once elected, they would protect the interests of the public, foreigners, and orphans. These are the principal features of Hippodamus' constitution; beyond them there is little to mention.

The first proposal open to objection is the division of citizens into three groups. Artisans, farmers, and warriors all participate in government. But the farmers have no weapons, while the artisans have neither weapons nor land, so both become virtually slaves of the warriors. They cannot possibly share every office. Generals, guardians of the citizens, and almost all the leading magistrates must come from the armed class. Yet if the other two classes have no role in government, how can they remain loyal citizens? One might reply that those with weapons must inevitably control both other classes. But that control is difficult to establish unless the warriors are numerous. If they are numerous, why should the other classes participate in government at all, or have the authority to appoint magistrates? Artisans are indispensable in every city and can support themselves through their trades, as they do elsewhere. Farmers, too, could reasonably claim a share in government if they supplied the warriors with food. But in Hippodamus' republic the farmers own land which they cultivate for their own benefit. [Compare Thucydides II, chapter 46.]

Then consider the common land intended to maintain the soldiers. If the soldiers themselves cultivate it, warriors and farmers become the same class, despite the legislator's intention to keep them distinct. If other people cultivate it, separate both from the warriors and from the farmers who own private land, these people constitute a fourth class, with no place in the state and no share in anything. Alternatively, if the same people cultivate their private land and the public land, they will struggle to produce enough to support two households. Why, on that arrangement, divide the land at all? The same allotments could supply food for their own households and also provide the food they give to the warriors. All of this is surely deeply confused.

Nor can we approve the law requiring judges to qualify their verdict when the issue put to them is a simple one. It turns a judge into an arbitrator. In arbitration, several arbitrators can confer about their decision, and can therefore make distinctions. A law court does not permit this; indeed, most legislators take care to prevent any communication between judges. Further confusion follows if a judge believes that compensation is due, but less than the claimant demands. Suppose the claim is for twenty minae, and the judge awards ten. Or one judge awards more and another less: five minae from one, four from another. They will continue dividing the damages in this fashion, while some award the entire sum and others nothing. How can a final amount be calculated? Moreover, a judge who votes simply to acquit or condemn is not forced into perjury, provided the charge is straightforward and properly framed. A judge who acquits does not decide that the defendant owes nothing; he decides that the defendant does not owe twenty minae. Perjury occurs only when a judge believes the defendant should not pay twenty minae and nevertheless condemns him to do so.

Rewarding anyone who discovers something useful to the state sounds attractive, but it cannot safely be made law. It may encourage informers and perhaps even provoke political disturbances. This raises a further question. People dispute whether changing a country's laws is advisable at all, even when the proposed law is better. If every change is inadvisable, we can hardly endorse Hippodamus' proposal: someone might claim to serve the public while introducing measures that actually destroy the laws or constitution. Since we have reached this subject, we should perhaps examine it more closely. As I said, opinions differ, and change can sometimes seem desirable. Changes in other arts and sciences have certainly brought benefits. Medicine, physical training, and every other art and science have moved away from inherited practices. If politics is an art, it too must need change, like the others. The extreme simplicity and barbarity of ancient customs show the need for improvement. The early Hellenes carried weapons everywhere and purchased their wives from one another. The surviving remnants of ancient law are quite absurd. At Cumae, for example, a law on murder declares the accused guilty if the accuser supplies a prescribed number of witnesses from among his own relatives. [Compare Thucydides I, chapters 5 and 6.] Furthermore, people generally seek what is good, not merely what their fathers possessed. The earliest inhabitants, whether born from the earth or survivors of some catastrophe, can be assumed to have been no better than ordinary foolish people today. This, at any rate, is what tradition says of those born from the earth. It would be ridiculous to remain satisfied with their ideas. Even written laws should not always be left unchanged. As in other arts, so in framing a constitution, not everything can be stated precisely in writing. Laws necessarily speak in general terms, whereas actions concern particular circumstances. We may therefore conclude that laws can sometimes be altered in particular cases. Viewed from another angle, however, the matter calls for great caution. Readily changing laws is itself a harmful habit. When the benefit is slight, it is better to leave some mistakes of legislators and rulers uncorrected: the citizen gains less from the improvement than he loses through acquiring the habit of disobedience. The comparison with the arts is misleading. Altering a law is very different from altering an art. Law has no source of obedience except habit, and habit develops only over time. A readiness to exchange old laws for new ones therefore weakens the authority of law itself. Even if we agree that laws should change, should every law change, and in every state? And may changes be made by anyone who

wishes to make them, or only by specified people? [Alternative interpretation of the preceding passage, relating ofxoiovs to yrpffvus: whether the earliest people were born from the earth or survived a catastrophe and were no better than earth-born men, they may be assumed to have been ordinary foolish people.] These questions are extremely important, so we should postpone them until a more appropriate occasion. In examining the governments of Lacedaemon and Crete, as indeed any government, we must consider two questions. First, is a particular law good or bad when measured against the best state? Second, does it agree with the conception and character of life that the legislator has placed before the citizens? It is generally accepted that citizens in a well-ordered state should have leisure, free from the task of supplying their daily necessities. The difficulty is how to secure that leisure. Slaves, if employed, are liable to revolt. The Thessalian Penestae have often risen against their masters, as have the Helots against the Lacedaemonians, whose misfortunes they are always waiting to exploit. Nothing similar has yet occurred among the Cretans. Probably this is because neighbouring cities, even when they fight one another, never ally themselves with rebellious serfs. They have no interest in encouraging revolt, since they too have dependent populations. By contrast, all the Lacedaemonians' neighbours, whether Argives, Messenians, or Arcadians, are their enemies, and the Helots continually revolt and go over to them. In Thessaly, likewise, the slaves' first rebellion came while the Thessalians were still fighting their neighbours, the Achaeans, Perrhaebians, and Magnesians.

Even if none of these other difficulties existed, dealing with and managing slaves is troublesome. If they are not controlled, they grow insolent and regard themselves as their masters' equals. If they are treated harshly, they hate their masters and plot against them. Clearly, citizens who produce these results have not discovered how to manage a subject population successfully.

The freedom from restraint enjoyed by Lacedaemonian women also frustrates the purpose of the Spartan constitution and damages the state's good order. Every household contains a husband and a wife, so we may regard the state as divided roughly equally between men and women. Where women's condition is badly regulated, therefore, half the city can be considered to live without laws. This is exactly what has happened at Sparta. The legislator intended the entire state to be disciplined and self-controlled. He accomplished this for men but neglected women, who live in every kind of luxury and self-indulgence. As a result, wealth receives excessive honour in such a state, especially when husbands fall under their wives' control. This is characteristic of warlike peoples, apart from the Celts and a few others who openly approve of love between males. The ancient storyteller seems to have been right to join Ares with Aphrodite, since all warlike peoples are inclined towards love either of men or of women. Sparta displayed this tendency in the days of its greatness, when women directed many affairs. What difference does it make whether women govern or the governors themselves are governed by women? The outcome is identical. Even regarding courage, which is needed in war rather than ordinary daily life, Lacedaemonian women's influence has been extremely harmful. The Theban invasion exposed the harm: unlike the women of other cities, they were wholly useless and created more confusion than the enemy. This lack of restraint among Lacedaemonian

women goes back to the earliest times and is readily explained. During the Lacedaemonians' wars, first against the Argives and later against the Arcadians and Messenians, the men spent long periods away from home. When peace returned, they placed themselves in the legislator's hands. Military discipline, which contains many elements of virtue, had already prepared them to accept his laws. But tradition says that when Lycurgus tried to subject the women to his laws, they resisted, and he abandoned the attempt. They, rather than he, bear responsibility for what followed, and this constitutional defect must plainly be attributed to them. Our concern, however, is not what deserves an excuse, but what is right and wrong. As I have already said, the women's disorderliness not only makes the state appear indecorous in itself, but also contributes to the encouragement of greed.

Mentioning greed leads naturally to a criticism of unequal property. Some Spartan citizens own very little, while others own a great deal, and the land has consequently fallen into a few hands. This reveals another defect in the laws. The legislator rightly makes buying or selling an inherited estate disgraceful, but permits anyone to give it away or leave it by will as he wishes. Both practices lead to the same result. Moreover, women own nearly two-fifths of the entire country because there are so many heiresses and because large dowries are customary. Surely it would have been better to allow no dowries, or only small or moderate ones. Under the present law, a man can marry his heiress to anyone he chooses. If he dies without a will, his heir receives the right to give her in marriage. Consequently, although the

country can support fifteen hundred cavalry and thirty thousand hoplites, the total number of Spartan citizens fell below one thousand at the time of the Theban invasion. The outcome demonstrates the defects in their property laws. A single defeat brought the city down; a shortage of men destroyed it. According to tradition, under their ancient kings they used to grant citizenship to foreigners. Consequently they did not lack people despite their long wars. Sparta is even said to have had at least ten thousand citizens at one time. Whether that report is true or false, equalizing property would certainly have been a better way of maintaining their numbers. The law concerning childbirth, moreover, works against correcting this inequality. Wanting as many Spartans as possible, the legislator encouraged large families. A Spartan law exempts a father of three sons from military service, and a father of four from every public burden. Yet with land distributed as it is, an increase in children plainly means that many of them must fall into poverty. The constitution has another defect, namely the Ephoralty. This office has authority over matters of the highest importance, but all Ephors are selected from the people. It therefore often falls to very poor men whose need makes them susceptible to bribery. Sparta has experienced many examples of this evil in the past. Quite recently, in the affair of the Andrians, some Ephors accepted bribes and did everything they could to ruin the state. Their power is so great and so tyrannical that even the kings have had to court their favour. Through

their influence the constitution has deteriorated from aristocracy into democracy. Still, the Ephoralty does hold the state together. People are satisfied when they share in the highest office, and this result has been beneficial, whether the legislator intended it or it happened by chance. For a constitution to last, every section of the state must want it to exist and be preserved. This condition is met at Sparta. The kings want it preserved because their own persons receive the honour due to them. The nobles have their place in the council of elders, since membership rewards virtue. The people have theirs in the Ephoralty, for everyone is eligible. It is entirely right to elect Ephors from the whole population, but the existing electoral method is excessively childish and should be changed. These quite ordinary men also decide cases of great importance. They should therefore follow written rules and laws instead of relying merely on their own judgment. Their manner of living is likewise at odds with the constitution's spirit: they enjoy far too much licence. Other citizens, meanwhile, face such intolerably severe restrictions that they evade the law by secretly indulging in sensual pleasures.

The council of elders also has defects. One may argue that elders are good men, thoroughly trained in manly virtue, and that their presence therefore benefits the state. Yet giving lifelong office to judges of important cases is undesirable, since the mind ages as the body does. There is real danger when their education is such that even the legislator cannot trust them. [Compare IV.9, section 10, and section 5.] Many elders are known to have accepted bribes and shown favouritism in public business. They ought therefore to be answerable for their conduct, whereas at Sparta they are not. Someone may reply, 'Every magistracy is answerable to the Ephors.' True, but that gives the Ephors too great a privilege; we maintain that oversight should be arranged differently. Furthermore, the Spartans' way of electing elders is childish. A candidate ought not to campaign for the position. The worthiest man should be appointed whether he seeks it or not. Here the legislator plainly displays the same intention found elsewhere in his constitution. He wants citizens to be ambitious and relies on that ambition in electing elders, since no one would seek election without it. Yet ambition and greed are, more than almost any other passions, incentives to crime.

I shall consider on another occasion whether kings benefit states at all. In any event, they should be selected with regard to their personal lives and conduct, rather than by the present method. The legislator plainly did not believe he could make them truly good; at least, he shows profound mistrust of their virtue. For this reason the Spartans used to send enemies together on the same embassy, and regarded disputes between the kings as a means of preserving the state.

The person who first established the common meals, called 'phiditia', also regulated them badly. They should have been paid for publicly, as they are in Crete. Among the Lacedaemonians, however, everyone must contribute, and some are too poor to meet the cost. The legislator's purpose is therefore defeated. The common meals were intended as an institution for the people, but their present organization has the opposite effect. The very poor can hardly participate, and ancient custom denies continued citizenship to anyone unable to make the required contribution.

The law governing Spartan admirals has often been criticized, and rightly so. It creates conflict: the kings already hold permanent commands as generals, so establishing the admiral's office amounts to establishing another king.

Plato's criticism in the Laws of the legislator's purpose is also justified. The entire constitution attends to only one aspect of virtue: a soldier's excellence, which secures victory in war. While they remained at war, the Spartans retained their strength; once they gained an empire, they declined. They knew nothing of the arts of peace and had never pursued any activity higher than warfare. They have made another, equally serious mistake. They rightly believe that the goods they struggle for are won through virtue rather than vice. But they wrongly value those goods above the virtue by which they are acquired.

Furthermore, the state's revenues are badly administered. Although they have major wars to fight, the treasury is empty, and they are unwilling to pay taxes. Since most of the land belongs to Spartans, they do not examine one another's contributions very closely.

The legislator's achievement has thus been harmful rather than beneficial: he has impoverished his city and made its citizens greedy. These are the chief defects of the Spartan constitution; let this be enough about it.

The constitutions of the Cretan cities closely resemble Sparta's. In a few respects they are equally good, but in most their arrangements are less developed. Older constitutions are generally less elaborate than newer ones, and the Lacedaemonian constitution is said, probably correctly, to copy the Cretan ones to a very considerable extent. Tradition relates that Lycurgus went abroad after ceasing to be King Charilaus' guardian and spent a long time in Crete. The two countries are closely connected. The Lyctians are a Lacedaemonian colony, and when their settlers arrived in Crete they adopted the inhabitants' existing constitution. Even today the Perioeci, Crete's subject population, live under the original laws enacted by Minos. Nature seems to have fitted the island for ruling Hellas by giving it an advantageous position. It stretches across the sea around which nearly all the Hellenes live. One end lies near the Peloponnese, while the other reaches almost to the Asian region around Triopium and Rhodes. Minos consequently established control of the sea, conquering some islands and settling colonies on others. Finally he invaded Sicily, where he died near Camicus. Cretan institutions resemble those of Lacedaemon. Helots cultivate the land in the one, Perioeci in the other, and both Cretans and Lacedaemonians have common meals. The Lacedaemonians formerly called these meals 'andria', rather than 'phiditia'. The Cretans use the same word, proving that common meals, or syssitia, originated in Crete. The two constitutions also correspond in many details. The Ephors' office matches that of the Cretan Cosmi, except that there are five Ephors and ten Cosmi. The elders likewise correspond to the Cretan elders, whom the Cretans call the council. Crete once also had kings, but abolished the office; the Cosmi now lead its people in war. Every class participates in the ecclesia, although that assembly can only ratify decisions made by the elders and Cosmi.

Crete's common meals are certainly organized better than the Lacedaemonian ones. At Lacedaemon, each person must pay a fixed contribution; as I have already explained, anyone who fails to pay is forbidden by law to exercise the rights of citizenship.

In Crete they have a more popular character. A portion of everything available—the produce of the land, livestock, public revenues, and tribute paid by the Perioeci—is allocated to the gods and the service of the state. Another portion goes to the common meals, so that men, women, and children all receive support from a common fund. The legislator uses many ingenious devices to keep eating moderate, which he regards as beneficial. He also encourages men to remain apart from women, so that they do not have too many children, and promotes companionship between men. I shall have occasion elsewhere to examine whether this is good or bad. There can be no doubt, however, that Crete's common meals are better arranged than those of Lacedaemon.

The Cosmi, by contrast, are an even worse institution than the Ephors: they possess all the faults of the Ephoralty without its benefit. [Compare VII.10, section 10, and VII.16 (?).] Like the Ephors, they may be people of no particular distinction, but Crete gains no corresponding political advantage to offset this. At Sparta everyone is eligible, so the people, sharing in the highest office, want the state to endure. Crete chooses its Cosmi from particular families instead of from the entire population, and chooses its elders from former Cosmi.

The criticism already made of the Lacedaemonian elders applies equally to those in Crete. Lifelong office without accountability gives them excessive privilege. Their unchecked freedom to decide matters according to their own judgment instead of written law is dangerous. The absence of popular resentment at exclusion does not prove that the institution is good. There is no money to be made from holding the office; and, unlike the Ephors, the Cosmi are insulated from temptation by living on an island.

Their remedy for the institution's defects is extraordinary, more appropriate to an exclusive oligarchy than to a constitutional state. Conspiracies among fellow officeholders or private individuals often drive the Cosmi out of office. They may also resign before their term ends. Surely law should regulate all such matters, rather than human will, which is a thoroughly unsafe authority. Worst of all is the suspension of the Cosmi's office. The nobles frequently resort to this device when they refuse to submit to justice. It reveals that, despite certain features of constitutional government, Crete is actually an exclusive oligarchy. They also habitually set up a leader, organize a following among the common people, assemble their friends, and then quarrel and fight with one another.

What is this except a temporary destruction of the state and a dissolution of the community? A city is in danger when people who want to attack it have the means to do so. As I have said, however, Crete's location protects it. Remoteness serves the same purpose as the Lacedaemonian exclusion of foreigners, and the Cretans possess no foreign dependencies. This explains why the Perioeci remain content in Crete while the Helots continually revolt. Yet when foreign invaders recently entered the island, they exposed the Cretan constitution's weakness. Let this suffice concerning Crete's government. The Carthaginians, too, are thought to have an excellent constitution. It differs in several ways from every other state's, though in certain respects it closely resembles the Lacedaemonian. Indeed, all three constitutions—Lacedaemonian, Cretan, and Carthaginian—are much alike and differ greatly from all others. Many Carthaginian institutions are excellent. Evidence of their constitution's superiority is its durability despite the democratic element it contains. Carthage has never experienced any rebellion worth mentioning and has never been ruled by a tyrant.

The Carthaginian constitution resembles the Lacedaemonian in several ways. Its clubs' common dining tables correspond to the Spartan phiditia, and its magistracy of one hundred and four to the Ephors. Here Carthage improves on Sparta: whereas the Ephors may be undistinguished people, Carthaginian magistrates are selected for merit.

Carthage also has kings and a gerusia, or council of elders, corresponding to Sparta's kings and elders. Unlike Spartan kings, theirs are not invariably drawn from a single, unexceptional family. When a distinguished family exists, they choose kings from it, rather than appointing them by seniority. This is a much better arrangement. Such officials possess great power, and if they lack worth they can inflict great harm. They have already done so at Lacedaemon.

Most defects or departures from the best state that one might criticize in Carthage's constitution are shared by all the constitutions we have discussed. Among its departures from aristocracy and constitutional government, however, some tend towards democracy and others towards oligarchy. If the kings and elders agree, they may decide whether to submit a question to the people. If they disagree, the people may decide whether it should be brought forward. Whatever the kings and elders do submit is not merely heard by the people but decided by them, and anyone may speak against it. Sparta and Crete do not allow this. The boards of five oversee many important matters, fill their own vacancies by co-option, choose the supreme council of one hundred, and exercise power for longer than other magistrates, effectively ruling both before and after their actual term. These are oligarchical features. Other features are aristocratic: officeholders receive no salary and are not chosen by lot; similarly, magistrates try every lawsuit, instead of different classes of judges or jurors hearing different kinds of cases, as at Lacedaemon. [Compare III.1, sections 10 and 11, and the note at the end.] The chief point at which the Carthaginian constitution departs from aristocracy towards oligarchy is one on which public opinion supports it. People generally believe that magistrates should be chosen for wealth as well as merit. A poor man, they say, cannot govern well because he lacks leisure. If selection by wealth defines oligarchy and selection by merit defines aristocracy, Carthage must belong to a third form combining them. The Carthaginians consider both wealth and merit when choosing magistrates, especially their highest officials, the kings and generals.

We must nevertheless recognize that the legislator has made a mistake in departing from aristocracy in this way. Nothing is more essential than ensuring that the highest class has leisure and need not engage in anything degrading, both while holding office and while out of it. This should receive his first attention. Even if wealth must be considered as a means of securing leisure, it is surely wrong to allow the greatest offices, including kingships and generalships, to be purchased. A law permitting this abuse places wealth above virtue and makes the whole state greedy. Whenever the state's leaders honour something, the other citizens inevitably follow their example. Where virtue does not hold first place, aristocracy cannot take firm root. People who have spent money purchasing office will habitually seek to recover that expense. It is absurd to suppose that an honest poor man would want to make money from office, but that a less worthy man who paid heavily for it would not. Those most capable of governing should therefore govern. Even if the legislator does not concern himself with protecting good people against poverty, he must at least ensure that those holding office have leisure.

It also seems wrong for one person to hold several offices, a practice particularly favoured by the Carthaginians. One task is performed better by one person. The legislator should attend to this and should not assign the same man the work of both a flute-player and a shoemaker. In a large state, distributing public offices among many people therefore accords better with both constitutional and democratic principles. As I have said, it gives more people a share; moreover, repeated practice makes any activity easier to perform well and quickly. Military and naval organization provide evidence: in both services, the duties of commanding and obeying extend to everyone.

The Carthaginians have an oligarchical government, but their wealth enables them to avoid oligarchy's evils successfully. From time to time they send part of their population to their colonies. This is their cure for every difficulty and their means of stabilizing the state. Circumstances favour them, but a legislator ought to prevent revolution without depending on favourable circumstances. Under the present arrangement, if misfortune struck and the people rebelled against their rulers, there would be no legal means of restoring peace.

Such is the character of the rightly celebrated constitutions of Lacedaemon, Crete, and Carthage. Among writers on government, some have never participated in public affairs, spending their whole lives as private individuals. For most of these writers, we have already given all the information about them that is worth recounting here. Others have administered their own cities or foreign cities as lawgivers. Some of these have merely made laws, while others have also designed constitutions. Lycurgus and Solon, for example, did both. I have already discussed the Lacedaemonian constitution. Some consider Solon a good legislator because he ended oligarchic exclusiveness, freed the people, established the ancient Athenian democracy, and reconciled the state's different elements. On this account the Areopagus council supplied oligarchy, elected magistrates supplied aristocracy, and the law courts supplied democracy. The truth appears to be that the council and elected magistracies preceded Solon, and he retained them. By forming the courts from all the citizens, however, he created democracy, and this is precisely what some people criticize. By giving supreme authority to courts selected by lot, they think he

destroyed the constitution's non-democratic element. Once the courts became powerful, the old constitution was transformed into the present democracy to satisfy the people, who were now acting as a tyrant. Ephialtes and Pericles reduced the Areopagus' authority and introduced jury pay. Thereafter each successive demagogue strengthened democracy until it reached its present form. This account is true, but the outcome seems to have arisen from circumstances rather than from Solon's intentions. The people had helped secure naval supremacy in the Persian War, and consequently developed a high opinion of themselves. They followed worthless demagogues opposed by the better class. Solon himself seems to have given the Athenians only the indispensable powers of electing officials and holding magistrates to account. Without those powers they would have been enslaved and hostile to the government. He drew all magistrates from notable and wealthy men: the pentacosio-medimni, the class called zeugitae because they owned a yoke of oxen, and the third class known as knights or cavalry. The fourth class consisted of labourers, who were excluded from every magistracy.

Among those who supplied laws without constitutions were Zaleucus, legislator for the Epizephyrian Locrians, and Charondas, who legislated for his own city, Catana, and for the other Chalcidian cities in Italy and Sicily. Some try to establish that Onomacritus was the first expert in legislation. They say that, although born a Locrian, he received his training in Crete, where he lived practising prophecy; that Thales was his companion; that Lycurgus and Zaleucus studied under Thales; and that Charondas studied under Zaleucus. But this account is entirely incompatible with the dates.

Thebes also had a legislator named Philolaus, a Corinthian. This Philolaus was a member of the Bacchiadae family and a lover of Diodes, the Olympic victor. Diodes left Corinth, horrified by the incestuous passion

his mother Halcyone felt for him, and withdrew to Thebes, where the two friends lived out their lives together. [Alternative reading, following Bernays, of the earlier account: 'to establish an unbroken succession of great legislators, with Onomacritus regarded as the first.'] The inhabitants still show visitors their tombs. Each is plainly visible from the other, but only one faces Corinth. Tradition says the friends deliberately arranged this: Diodes, horrified by his misfortunes, wanted the land of Corinth hidden from his tomb, whereas Philolaus wanted it visible. These events explain their settlement at Thebes. Philolaus consequently legislated for the Thebans and, among his other measures, gave them rules about having children, called the 'Laws of Adoption'. These distinctive laws were his own contribution, intended to keep the number of allotments unchanged.

Nothing in Charondas' legislation is especially distinctive except his provisions concerning false witnesses: he was the first to introduce prosecutions for perjury. His laws are more exact and more precisely worded even than those of legislators in our own day.

Equalizing property is Phaleas’ distinctive proposal. Plato's are the sharing of women, children, and property; common meals for women; and the drinking rule that sober people should direct the feast. He also prescribes military practice that makes soldiers equally skilled with both hands, so that either hand serves them as well as the other.

Draco left a body of laws, but adapted them to an existing constitution. They contain nothing particularly worth mentioning except the extraordinary severity of their punishments. Pittacus likewise supplied laws rather than designing a constitution. His distinctive rule imposes a heavier punishment on someone who strikes another person while drunk than on someone who does so while sober. He considered expediency, not the excuse that might be made for drunkenness, because drunken people commit violence more frequently than sober ones. [Compare Laws II, 671 D–673 A, and Laws VII, 794 D.]

Androdamas of Rhegium legislated for the Chalcidians in Thrace. Some of his laws concern homicide and heiresses, but none has anything distinctive to mention. Let us end here our examination of the different constitutions, both those that actually exist and those devised by theorists.

paragraphs: Anyone investigating the nature and different kinds of government must first establish what a state is. The answer is currently disputed. Some people attribute a particular action to the state; others say that the oligarchy or tyrant acted, not the state. The legislator or statesman is concerned entirely with the state, since a constitution or government is an arrangement of its inhabitants. Yet a state is a composite thing, a whole consisting of many parts, namely the citizens who constitute it. We must therefore begin by asking who counts as a citizen and what the word means. Here too opinions differ: someone who is a citizen in a democracy will often not be one in an oligarchy. Setting aside people who have been specially admitted to citizenship or have acquired the title through some other exceptional circumstance, we can first say that residence alone does not make a citizen. Resident foreigners and slaves live in the same place as citizens. Nor does the mere right to bring or defend a lawsuit make someone a citizen, since a treaty may grant this right. Resident foreigners in many places possess such legal rights, though incompletely, because they must have a patron.

Their participation in citizenship is therefore incomplete. We call them citizens only with a qualification, just as we might apply the word to children too young to enter the register, or to elderly men released from public duties. We do not simply call these people citizens: we add that the children are under age and the elderly are past the required age, or use some similar expression. The exact wording does not matter, since the meaning is plain. Similar difficulties arise concerning people deprived of citizenship and those in exile, and can be answered in the same way. But we seek to define the citizen in the fullest sense, without any such qualification. His distinguishing feature is participation in administering justice and holding office. Some offices have fixed terms, and their holders may not serve twice, or must wait a specified interval before serving again. Others, such as those of dicast and ecclesiast, have no fixed term. Someone might argue that these are not magistracies at all, and that their functions give no share in government. Yet it would be absurd to say that those who wield supreme authority do not govern. We need not dwell on this verbal dispute. What we require is a term covering both dicast and ecclesiast. To distinguish it, let us call their role 'indeterminate office', and regard those who participate in it as citizens. This is the broadest definition of a citizen and the one that best fits those generally given that name.

We must remember, however, that when the underlying conceptions of things differ in kind, with one ranked first, another second, and another third, those things, considered in that relation, have little or nothing significant in common. Now we

observe that constitutions differ in kind and that some are prior to others. Defective or distorted constitutions necessarily come after the sound ones. We shall explain later what we mean by distortion. Citizenship must therefore differ according to the constitution. Our definition best describes a democratic citizen and need not fit citizens of other states. Some states do not recognize the people as a body and have no regular popular assembly, only assemblies called on special occasions. Lawsuits are allocated among the magistrates. At Lacedaemon, for example, the Ephors divide contract disputes among themselves, the elders judge homicides, and other magistrates decide other cases. Carthage follows a similar arrangement, with particular magistrates deciding all lawsuits. We can, however, adjust our definition to include these states. Strictly understood, it applies only to democracies. Elsewhere, the person who legislates and judges holds a determinate rather than an indeterminate office. Some or all holders of these determinate offices have the exclusive right to deliberate or judge on some matters or on every matter. The meaning of citizenship is now becoming clearer.

We call a person a citizen of a state when he is entitled to participate in its deliberative or judicial administration. Generally speaking, a state is a body of citizens numerous enough to provide for the purposes of life. In practice, however, people define a citizen as someone whose parents are both citizens. Others trace descent further back, requiring two, three, or more citizen ancestors. This definition is brief and practical, but some then ask how the ancestor in the third or fourth generation became a citizen. [Compare section 11 and II.11, section 7.] Gorgias of Leontini, partly puzzled and partly ironic, said: 'Mortars are produced by mortar-makers; the citizens of Larissa, like the kettles named after it, are manufactured by the magistrates.' Yet the answer is straightforward. Under the definition just given, those ancestors were citizens if they participated in government. This definition is better than the other, since being 'born of a citizen father or mother' cannot possibly describe the first inhabitants or founders of a state.

A harder problem concerns people admitted to citizenship after a revolution. Cleisthenes did this at Athens after the tyrants were expelled, enrolling many strangers, slaves, and resident foreigners in the tribes. Here the question is not who is a citizen, but whether someone who is a citizen ought to be one. A further doubt follows: is someone who ought not to be a citizen nevertheless really a citizen, since what ought not to be may be considered false and nonexistent? Yet people sometimes hold office who ought not to hold it, and we still call them rulers, even when they govern unjustly. We defined a citizen by participation in a certain kind of authority or office: someone occupying a judicial or legislative office meets our definition. Clearly, therefore, the people whose status is disputed must

be called citizens. Whether they ought to possess that status is a question connected with our preceding inquiry. [The earlier saying contains an untranslatable play on the Greek word Srjiuovpyoi, which can mean either 'magistrates' or 'artisans'.]

A corresponding question concerns the state: does a given action count as its action or not? This arises, for example, when a democracy replaces an oligarchy or tyranny. People then refuse to honour contracts or other obligations, claiming that the tyrant, not the state, undertook them. They argue that certain constitutions rest on force rather than the common good. But the same reasoning applies to democracies, which may also originate in violence. In that case, their actions are no more or less legitimate than those of an oligarchy or tyranny. This leads to a further question: when is a state the same state, and when has it become different? Looking only at its territory and inhabitants would be superficial. A population can be separated from its land, and some inhabitants may settle in one place while others settle elsewhere. This difficulty is not especially serious, however. We need only observe that 'state' has two meanings, referring both to the political community and to the city.

Another question is when people living in the same place form a single city: where should the limit be drawn? Certainly not at the city wall, since a wall could enclose the entire Peloponnesus. A city of such enormous extent would encompass a nation rather than a state. Babylon provides an example: people say it had been captured for three days before some inhabitants learned what had happened. It would be better to postpone this difficulty to another occasion. The statesman must consider the proper size of a state and whether it should contain more than one nation.

Again, if the inhabitants remain of the same stock and occupy the same place, should we call the city the same despite the continual death and birth of citizens? We call rivers and springs the same even though their water constantly departs and is replaced. Or should we say that the successive generations remain the same, like the rivers, while the state changes? A state is a community of citizens sharing a constitution. When that constitution changes into another kind, we may therefore suppose that the state itself changes, just as a tragic chorus differs from a comic chorus even when exactly the same people compose both. We speak similarly of any union or combination whose arrangement changes. A harmony made from the same notes is called different according to whether it uses the Dorian or Phrygian mode. If this is so, a state's identity evidently depends chiefly on its constitution. Its name may stay the same or change, whether its inhabitants remain the same or become entirely different. Whether a state must honour its commitments after a constitutional change is a separate question.

A question closely connected with our preceding discussion is whether the virtue of a good man and that of a good citizen are identical or different. Before we investigate it, however, we must first form a general conception of the virtue belonging to a citizen. A citizen, like a sailor, is a member of a community. Sailors perform different tasks: one serves as a rower, another as a pilot, a third as a lookout, and a fourth has some other similarly designated function. [Compare Nicomachean Ethics, section 11.] A precise account of each sailor's excellence applies specifically to that individual and his work. Yet there is also a common account that applies to every one of them, since they all pursue the same end: safety in navigation. Citizens likewise differ from each other, but preserving their community is the shared concern of them all. That community is the state, so civic virtue must relate to the constitution to which a citizen belongs. Since constitutions take several forms, a good citizen's virtue plainly cannot be one single perfect virtue. But we call a man good when he possesses perfect virtue. A good citizen therefore need not possess the virtue that makes someone a good man.

We can approach the question differently by considering the best state. Suppose a state cannot consist entirely of good men, while each citizen is expected to perform his own task well and therefore needs virtue. Since the citizens cannot all be alike, civic virtue cannot coincide with the virtue of a good man. Everyone must possess the virtue of a good citizen, for only in that way can the state be perfect. They need not all possess the virtue of a good man, unless we assume that every citizen in a good state must himself be good.

We can also compare a state to a living creature. A living creature first divides into soul and body; the soul contains reason and appetite; a household contains husband and wife; and property involves master and slave. These and other unlike elements constitute the state. The virtue of all its citizens therefore cannot be identical, any more than the excellence of a chorus leader is identical to that of the performer beside him. Enough has been said to explain why the two kinds of virtue cannot always and unconditionally be the same.

Will there, then, be no circumstances in which a good citizen's virtue coincides with a good man's? We answer that the good ruler, rather than simply the good citizen, is both a good and a wise man, and anyone intending to be a statesman must be wise. Some people say that even a ruler's education should be different from everyone else's. After all, are the children of kings not taught riding and the exercises of warfare? As Euripides says:

'Not clever accomplishments for me, but the knowledge the state needs.' This suggests that a ruler requires an education of his own. If a good ruler's virtue is the virtue of a good man, while subjects as well as rulers are citizens, civic virtue cannot always be identical with human goodness. In some cases, namely in the best state, the two may coincide; but a ruler's virtue differs from that of a citizen. Jason expressed his awareness of this distinction when he said that 'he went hungry whenever he was not a tyrant', meaning that he could not bear private life. On the other hand, people are praised for knowing both how to command and how to obey. A citizen capable of both is said to possess proven virtue. If we identify the good man's virtue with governing, and the citizen's virtue with both governing and obeying, we cannot praise them equally for the same thing. Some maintain that rulers and subjects must learn different lessons, while citizens must understand and practise both roles. The inference follows plainly. There is indeed a master's authority, concerned with menial tasks. The master need not know how to perform them himself; he can have others perform them. To do otherwise would be degrading. By this I mean the various kinds of menial work undertaken by different classes of slaves, such as handicraftsmen, whose name indicates that they live by the work of their hands. Mechanics fall within this class. In ancient times, and still among certain peoples, working people accordingly had no share in government. They acquired that privilege only under the most extreme democracy. A good man, statesman, or good citizen certainly should not learn the occupations of inferiors except for occasional personal use. If he practises them habitually, the distinction between master and slave disappears.

We are not speaking of that sort of rule. There is another kind, exercised over people who are free and equal by birth: constitutional rule. The ruler must learn it by first being governed himself. A man learns the duties of a cavalry general by serving under a cavalry general, or those of an infantry general by serving under an infantry general. He may also prepare by previously commanding a company or brigade. The saying is therefore sound: 'Someone who has never learned to obey cannot be a good commander.' The

two roles differ, but a good citizen must be capable of both. He should understand how to govern as a free person and how to obey as a free person: these abilities constitute civic virtue. [The earlier inference is that some experience of subjection benefits a ruler; compare below, section 14.] Although a ruler's temperance and justice differ from a subject's, a good man's virtue embraces both. A good man who is free yet subject to rule will not possess merely one virtue, such as justice, in a single form. He will possess distinct forms of virtue, one enabling him to govern and another to obey. They differ as men's and women's temperance and courage differ. A man with only as much courage as a courageous woman would be considered cowardly. A woman who restricted her speech no more than a good man would be considered talkative. Their roles in household management also differ: one acquires, the other preserves. Practical wisdom alone belongs specifically to the ruler; all other virtues seem to belong to ruler and subject alike. A subject's distinctive excellence is not practical wisdom but correct opinion. He resembles the maker of a flute, while the ruler resembles the musician who plays or uses it.

These arguments provide our answer to the question whether the virtue of a good man and that of a good citizen are identical or different. They also show the respects in which the two coincide and those in which they differ.

One further question about citizenship remains. Is a genuine citizen only someone who shares in office, or should a mechanic also count? If people without office are citizens, not every citizen can possess the ability to govern and obey that defines civic virtue. But if no member of the lower class is a citizen, where in the state does that class belong? They are neither resident foreigners nor foreigners. We may answer that excluding them is no more absurd than excluding slaves and freedmen from the categories just mentioned. Not everyone necessary to a state's existence can be counted as a citizen. Children, for example, do not possess citizenship on the same terms as adults. Adults are citizens without qualification; children, because they have not grown up, possess only qualified citizenship. In ancient times, and among some nations, artisans were indeed slaves or foreigners; that is why most are so today. The best state will not admit them to citizenship. If they are admitted, our definition of civic virtue applies only to certain citizens and free people, excluding those compelled to work for their living. Those for whom labour is necessary are either slaves serving individual needs, or mechanics and labourers serving the community. Carrying these reflections a little further will make the position of these people in the state clear; indeed, what we have already said sufficiently explains it.

Because constitutions take many forms, citizenship must have many varieties too, especially the citizenship of those who are governed. Mechanics and labourers will therefore be citizens under some constitutions, but not under others—for example,

in an aristocracy, the so-called government of the best, if such a government exists. There, honours are awarded for virtue and merit, and no one living a mechanic's or labourer's life can practise virtue. [An alternative reading of the earlier passage is: 'for this man', meaning the lower kind of man, 'is a citizen but does not govern'; compare below, section 3. On the interpretation followed in the text, 'this man' means the possessor of the relevant virtue; on the alternative interpretation, it refers to the mechanic.] Oligarchies set a high property qualification for office. No labourer can therefore become a citizen there, though a mechanic can, since many mechanics are wealthy. A Theban law required anyone seeking office to have withdrawn from business for ten years. Many states go so far as to admit foreigners. Some democracies grant citizenship to someone whose mother alone is a citizen and whose father is foreign, and apply a similar rule to illegitimate children. Such restrictions are relaxed when population is scarce. Once citizen numbers increase, they first exclude children of a slave father or mother, then those with only a citizen mother. Eventually citizenship is restricted to people whose father and mother are both citizens.

These considerations make it plain that there are several kinds of citizens. A citizen in the fullest sense is someone who shares in the honours of the state. In Homer's poems, Achilles complains that Agamemnon treats him 'like a stranger without honour'. Anyone excluded from public honours stands no better than a foreigner. If this exclusion is concealed rather than openly acknowledged, its purpose is to deceive one's fellow citizens.

Our earlier arguments settle whether a good man's virtue and a good citizen's are identical: in some states they coincide, while in others they differ. Even where they coincide, this does not apply to every citizen. It concerns the statesman and those who direct public affairs, or are capable of directing them, either alone or together with others. [Compare VI.7, section 4, and Iliad IX, 648.] Having resolved these questions, we must now ask whether there is one form of government or several. If there are several, we must identify them, establish their number, and explain how they differ from one another.

A constitution arranges the offices of a state, particularly its highest office. The governing authority is everywhere sovereign, and that authority is in fact the constitution. In a democracy, for example, sovereignty belongs to the people; in an oligarchy, to the few. We therefore describe these as different constitutions, and apply the same reasoning to other cases.

Let us first consider the purpose of a state and the number of governmental forms that regulate human society. Earlier in this treatise, while distinguishing household management from a master's authority, we said that man is naturally a political animal. People therefore want to live together even when they do not need one another's assistance. Their common interests bring them together, insofar as each thereby gains some measure of well-being. This is certainly the chief aim of states as well as individuals. People also come together and sustain political community simply for the sake of life, which may itself contain something noble, provided life's evils do not greatly outweigh its benefits. We can all see how people cling to life even amid misfortune, apparently finding a natural sweetness and happiness in being alive.

The different kinds of authority are easy to distinguish; works intended for a general audience have often defined them already. Although a natural master and a natural slave genuinely share an interest, a master's authority is exercised primarily for the master's benefit. It benefits the slave only incidentally, since the master's authority would also end if the slave perished. By contrast, governing a wife, children, and household, what we call household management, aims primarily at the good of those governed, or at the common good of both parties. Its essential purpose remains the subjects' good. Medicine, physical training, and the arts generally work in the same way: their practitioners' own benefit is incidental. A trainer may himself exercise, and a ship's pilot is always a member of its crew. Both trainer and pilot attend to the welfare of those entrusted to them. When they are themselves among those receiving that care, they benefit incidentally: the pilot is also a sailor, and the trainer becomes one of the people in training. Politics follows the same principle. Where a state rests on equality and similarity among citizens, they consider it right to take turns in office. Naturally, each would perform his period of service, and later someone else would look after his interests, just as he had looked after theirs while governing. This was the original arrangement. Nowadays, however, because of the advantages to be

obtained from public revenue and office, people want to remain in power continually. One might imagine that they were invalids who could stay healthy only while holding office. If that were true, we can be sure they would be chasing appointments. The conclusion is clear. Governments serving the common interest follow justice in its unqualified sense and are therefore correct constitutions. Those serving only their rulers' interests are defective and distorted, because they treat citizens as a master's subjects, whereas a state is a community of free people. Having settled this, we must identify the forms of government and their number. We should begin with the correct forms, since identifying them will immediately reveal their distortions. 'Constitution' and 'government' mean the same thing, and the government, as the state's supreme authority, must belong to one person, a few, or the many. Each arrangement is correct when the one, few, or many govern for the common interest. Each is distorted when government serves private interests, whether those of one person, a few, or the many. For if people are genuinely citizens, they ought to participate in the advantages that belong to their state. When one person governs for the common good, we call the arrangement kingship or royalty. When several, but not many, govern in this way, we call it aristocracy, the rule of the best. The name means either that the rulers themselves are best or that they seek what is best for the state and its citizens. When the body of citizens governs for the common

interest, it receives the general name 'constitution', or polity. There is a reason for this usage. One man or a few may possess outstanding virtue. But virtue has several forms, and the more people there are, the harder it becomes for all to excel in every form. They may nevertheless excel in military virtue, which the multitude can possess. In a constitutional government, therefore, the fighting men hold supreme authority, and those who possess arms constitute the citizen body.

The corresponding distortions are tyranny in place of kingship, oligarchy in place of aristocracy, and democracy in place of constitutional government. Tyranny is monarchy directed solely towards the monarch's advantage. Oligarchy serves the wealthy, while democracy serves the needy. None of these aims at the common good of everyone.

Difficulties remain concerning these different governments, so we need to describe the nature of each in somewhat greater detail. Someone who studies the sciences philosophically, and does not concern himself with practical results alone, ought to leave nothing unnoticed or omitted, but explain the truth in every particular. Tyranny, as I said, is a monarchy that exercises a master's authority over a political community. Oligarchy exists when owners of property hold the government in their hands. Democracy is its opposite: the rulers are the poor rather than the propertied. The first difficulty arises from these very definitions. Democracy is also called government by the many. Suppose, however, that the majority possess property and that these wealthy people hold power. Similarly, oligarchy is described as government by the few; but

suppose poor people are fewer than rich people, yet possess the governing power because they are stronger. In these circumstances, the distinction we have drawn between the different forms of government would cease to hold.

Suppose we amend the definitions by linking wealth with the few and poverty with the many. We would then call a government oligarchical when its rulers are few and wealthy, and democratic when they are numerous and poor. The difficulty would remain. If these are the only forms available, how should we describe the other governments we have just considered: one where the rich are more numerous and govern, and another where the poor are fewer and govern?

Our argument suggests that the size of the ruling body, whether a majority in democracy or a minority in oligarchy, is incidental. It reflects the fact that everywhere the wealthy are few and the poor numerous. Treating numbers as the cause of the distinction therefore mistakes its basis. Poverty and wealth are the real difference between democracy and oligarchy. Wherever people govern because they are wealthy, whether few or many, the constitution is an oligarchy. Wherever the poor govern, it is a democracy. In practice, however, the rich are few and the poor many: prosperity belongs to few, while freedom belongs to everyone. Wealth and freedom are the respective grounds on which oligarchical and democratic parties claim political authority. Let us now consider the usual accounts of oligarchy and democracy and their respective conceptions of justice. Everyone holds to some kind of justice, but people's conceptions are incomplete and express only part of it. They believe justice means equality, and it does, but equality for equals, not for everyone. Inequality too can be just, but only for those who are unequal, not universally. When people leave out the persons concerned, their judgments go wrong. They are judging their own cases, and most people are poor judges where their own interests are involved. Justice relates to persons as well as things. As I explained in the Ethics, just distribution concerns both. People agree about equality between things but dispute the worth of persons. This happens chiefly because they judge their own affairs badly, and also because both sides express a limited, partial justice while imagining they express absolute justice. Those unequal in one respect, such as wealth, consider themselves unequal in every respect. Those equal in one respect, such as freedom, consider themselves equal in everything. Both overlook the essential issue. If people associated solely to acquire wealth, their share in the state would properly correspond to their property, and the oligarchical argument would seem decisive. It would be unjust for someone contributing one mina to receive the same share of a hundred minae, whether capital or profit, as someone who contributed the other ninety-nine. But a state

exists for living well, not merely for staying alive. [Bernays alternatively interprets the preceding phrase as 'whether in the case of the original contributors or their successors'.] If mere life were its purpose, slaves and animals could form a state. They cannot, because they do not participate in happiness or a life of free choice. Nor does a state exist merely as an alliance for protection against injustice, or for trade and intercourse. Otherwise the Tyrrhenians, Carthaginians, and everyone bound by commercial treaties would be citizens of one state. They certainly have import agreements, promises not to injure each other, and written terms of alliance. But the parties have no common magistracies enforcing these agreements; each state has officials of its own. Neither ensures that the other's citizens have the character they ought to possess. Nor does either require everyone covered by the treaty to refrain from every form of wrongdoing or wickedness. Each requires only that the parties refrain from wronging one another.

Those concerned with good government, by contrast, consider the broader question of virtue and vice within states. A state genuinely deserving its name must therefore make virtue a serious concern. Without this moral purpose, the community is merely an alliance, differing only in location from alliances whose members live apart. Law then becomes no more than a compact, what the sophist Lycophron calls 'a guarantee of justice between one person and another'. It has no effective power to make citizens good and just.
The point is plain. Suppose separate places, for instance,

Corinth and Megara, were enclosed by one wall. Even after that enclosure they would still not constitute one city or political community, even if their inhabitants could intermarry, although that right is especially characteristic of political communities. Conversely, suppose people lived apart, but near enough to have dealings with one another, under laws forbidding them to cheat each other in trade. That too would fall short of a state. Imagine ten thousand people, one a carpenter, another a farmer, another a shoemaker, and the rest similarly employed. If they shared only commerce, an alliance, and similar arrangements, they would not constitute a state. Why not? Surely their physical separation cannot be the reason. Suppose they moved into one place, each occupying a house that served, so to speak, as his own state. Suppose they allied themselves solely for protection against wrongdoers. An exact thinker would still deny that they formed a state if their mutual relations remained the same as before they united. A state, then, is not merely an association occupying a common location to prevent wrongdoing and facilitate exchange. A state cannot exist without these conditions, but together they are still insufficient. It is a community of households and groups of households sharing well-being, aiming at a complete and self-sufficient life. Such a community requires its members to live in the same place and intermarry. Hence cities develop family connections, brotherhoods, common sacrifices, and shared amusements. Friendship creates these ties, since friendship motivates association. Living well is the end, and these are the means to it. A state unites households and villages for a complete, self-sufficient life, by which we mean a happy and honourable life.

We conclude that political community exists for noble action, rather than merely for living together. Those who contribute most to such a community deserve a greater share in it than people equally or more free, or of equally or more noble birth, who possess less political virtue. They also deserve more than those richer than themselves but inferior in virtue.

From our discussion it is clear that the supporters of different constitutions each speak for only a part of justice. Another uncertainty concerns who should possess supreme authority in the state: the multitude, the wealthy, the good, the single best man, or a tyrant? Every one of these possibilities seems to lead to unpleasant consequences. Suppose the poor, relying on their greater numbers, divide the property of wealthy citizens among themselves. Is that not unjust? 'No, by heaven,' someone will reply, 'because the lawful authority, the people, has decided it.' But if this is not injustice, what are we to call injustice? Suppose that after taking everything in the first distribution, a majority again divides the property of the minority. Is it not obvious that continuing in this way will ruin the state? Yet virtue surely does not destroy those who possess it, and justice cannot be destructive of a state. This law of confiscation must therefore be unjust. Otherwise every act of a tyrant would also necessarily be just: his superior power compels others, just as the multitude's power compels the rich. Is it just, then, [compare section 8; Nicomachean Ethics, section 6; Plato, Republic 353]

for a small number of wealthy people to govern? What if they likewise rob the people and plunder their possessions: is that just? If so, the majority's plundering of the minority must be just too. Yet there can be no doubt that all these practices are wrongful and unjust.

Should the good, then, hold supreme authority? But everyone else in the state would then be excluded from power, and that exclusion would deprive them of honour. Public offices are honours, and if one group possesses them permanently, the rest lose their share. Would rule by the single best man be preferable? That is still more oligarchical, since it excludes even more people from honour. Someone may say that it is wrong to entrust supreme authority to a human being, vulnerable to every disturbance of passion, rather than to law. But what if the law itself is democratic or oligarchical? How does that resolve our difficulties? It does not: exactly the same consequences follow.

We can postpone most of these questions. The proposition that the multitude should govern rather than the best few admits a satisfactory explanation. Although difficult, it seems to contain some truth. A collection of ordinary people, each individually unexceptional, may together be better than a small number of good people, when considered as a whole rather than separately. A meal to which many contribute can be better than one paid for by a single person. Each member of the multitude possesses some virtue and practical judgment. When they come together, they

become, in a sense, one person with many feet, hands, and senses. The same image applies to their character and understanding. This explains why a multitude judges music and poetry better than an individual: one understands one part, another another, and together they understand the whole. Good men similarly combine qualities. They differ from ordinary individuals as beautiful people are said to differ from the plain, or works of art from actual objects: scattered excellences are brought together in them. Taken separately, however, one person's eyes or another person's other feature may be more beautiful than the corresponding feature in a picture. It is unclear whether this principle holds for every democracy and every collection of people. Indeed, in some cases, by heaven, it certainly cannot. Otherwise the same argument would apply to beasts, and one might ask how some people differ from beasts. Nevertheless, there may be groups of people for whom it is true. If so, it resolves both our earlier difficulty and a related one: what authority should belong to the body of free citizens who lack wealth and individual distinction?

Allowing them to occupy the highest offices remains dangerous, because foolishness can lead them into mistakes and dishonesty into crimes. Yet excluding them is dangerous too. A state in which large numbers of poor people are

excluded from office necessarily contains a great many enemies. The only escape is to grant them certain deliberative and judicial functions. For this reason Solon and some other legislators allow them to elect officials and call magistrates to account, but do not permit them to occupy offices individually. [Compare II.12, section 5.] Once assembled, their understanding is sufficiently sound, and in combination with the better citizens they are useful to the state. In the same way, impure food mixed with pure sometimes makes the entire mixture more wholesome than a small amount of pure food alone. Each person left on his own, however, reaches an imperfect judgment. This popular constitution nevertheless presents several difficulties. One might first object that the person competent to judge the treatment of a sick man must be someone capable of treating the disease and restoring the patient to health himself: that is, a physician. The same holds in every profession and art. Just as physicians should answer to physicians, practitioners generally should be examined by those who share their expertise.
