But medicine has three kinds of judge: the apothecary, the physician of the higher class, and the intelligent person who has studied the art. Every art has people of this last kind, and we grant them the capacity to judge quite as much as we grant it to professional practitioners. Surely the same principle should govern elections? A correct choice can be made only by someone with knowledge. A geometer chooses correctly in matters of geometry, and a pilot in matters of navigation. Private individuals may be familiar with certain occupations or arts, but they cannot judge better than those who know them professionally. This argument would deny the multitude both the election of magistrates and the examination of their conduct. Yet our earlier answer may meet these objections to a considerable extent. If the people are not entirely degraded, their collective judgment can equal or surpass that of experts, even though each individual judges less well than a specialist. Furthermore, in certain arts the practitioner is not the only or the best judge of what he produces. Understanding a house is not confined to the builder: its user, the householder, will even judge it better. Likewise, a pilot judges a rudder better than the carpenter, and a guest judges a feast better than the cook.

This difficulty seems adequately answered, but a related one remains. It appears strange that inferior people should exercise authority over matters more important than those entrusted to good people. Yet electing magistrates and holding them accountable are the most important matters of all. As I said, some states assign these functions to the people, giving the assembly supreme authority over them.

People of any age and with only a small property qualification can sit in the assembly, deliberate, and judge. Yet major officials, such as controllers and generals, must meet a high qualification. We can solve this difficulty as we solved the previous one, and the existing democratic practice may in fact be defensible.

Authority belongs not to the individual dicast, councillor, or assembly member, but to the court, council, and assembly. Individual officials and participants are merely parts of these bodies. This gives the many a claim to greater authority than the few. The people, council, and courts contain numerous members whose combined property exceeds that of one or a few holders of high office. Let this suffice on that question.

Our discussion of the initial question shows most clearly that good laws should be supreme. Magistrates, whether one or several, should decide only matters the law cannot specify precisely, because a general rule cannot easily cover every particular case. What makes a law good, however, has not yet been clearly established; the original difficulty remains. Laws are necessarily good or bad, just or unjust, in relation to a state's constitution. Correct constitutions must therefore have just laws, while distorted constitutions must have unjust ones.

In every science and art, the end pursued is some good. This is especially and pre-eminently true of the highest of them all, the political science with which we are concerned. Its good is justice, meaning the common interest. Everyone regards justice as a kind of equality, and to some extent accepts the philosophical distinctions we established in the Ethics. People acknowledge that justice concerns persons and that equals should receive equal treatment. But equality or inequality in what? This is the difficulty the political philosopher must resolve. Some will probably argue that public offices should be distributed unequally according to any respect in which a citizen excels, even if he otherwise differs in no way from the community. They suppose that a difference in any one respect establishes different rights and claims. If that is true, a man's complexion, height, or any other advantage would entitle him to more political power. The error is obvious and can be illustrated by other arts and sciences. Among equally skilled flute-players, better birth supplies no reason for receiving better flutes. It does not improve their playing; the best instrument belongs to the best musician. If the meaning of this argument is not yet sufficiently clear, it will become clearer as we carry the discussion further. Suppose an outstanding flute-player is greatly inferior in birth and beauty. Either quality may be a greater good than flute-playing, and others may surpass him in those qualities by a larger proportion than he surpasses them musically. Nevertheless, he should receive the finest flutes, unless wealth and birth improve flute-playing, which they do not. Moreover, the opposing principle would make every good comparable with every other. If a particular height can be compared in this way, height generally could be measured against either height or freedom. Suppose A surpasses B in height more than B surpasses A in virtue, and height generally is superior to virtue. Then every quality becomes commensurable, which is absurd. If some amount of one quality exceeds an amount of another, some other amount must equal it.

Since such comparison is impossible, political claims to office rightly do not rest on every kind of inequality, any more than claims in the arts do. For example, the fact that some people run slowly and others quickly gives no reason to assign the former little political authority and the latter a great deal. Speed receives its reward in athletic contests. Rival claims to office must instead depend on qualities that help constitute a state, such as wealth and virtue. The noble, freeborn, and wealthy therefore have reasonable claims. Officeholders must be free people and taxpayers: a state can no more consist entirely of poor people than entirely of slaves. But if wealth and freedom are necessary, justice and courage are equally necessary. Without the former the state cannot exist; without the latter it cannot exist well.

If we consider only the state's existence, all or at least some of these claims seem just. But if we consider living well, education and virtue have the stronger claim, as I said earlier. Equality in one respect should not mean equality in everything, nor inequality in one respect inequality in everything. Constitutions founded on either assumption are therefore distortions. As we have acknowledged, each group has a claim in a particular sense, but none has an absolute claim. The wealthy ground their claim to political authority on owning a greater share of the land, which is the common element of the state, and because they are generally more reliable in contractual dealings. Free people claim on grounds closely related to those of the nobly born. Nobles are citizens in a fuller sense than those of humble birth, since good birth is always esteemed in one's own country. Moreover, descendants of better ancestors are likely to be better themselves: nobility is excellence of lineage. Virtue also has a genuine claim, since we have recognized justice as a social virtue that embraces the others. The many, in turn, may advance their

claim against the few, since collectively they are stronger, wealthier, and better than the few. But suppose all the groups composing a state live together in one city: the good, the rich, the noble, and the rest. Is there then any doubt about who should govern? Within each constitution already mentioned, the answer is clear. Constitutions are distinguished by their governing bodies: in one the wealthy govern, in another the virtuous, and so forth. But where all these different elements coexist within the same political community, a genuine difficulty arises. By what principle are we to settle their competing claims to govern? Suppose the virtuous are very few. Should we judge their numbers by the tasks they must perform, asking whether they can administer the state, or must they be numerous enough to form a state themselves? Objections can be raised against each of these groups that aspires to the possession of political power. Claims based on wealth or ancestry have no secure basis in justice. On the wealth principle, a single person richer than everyone else together would plainly deserve to govern them all. Similarly, someone whose ancestry was outstanding would deserve superiority over everyone claiming authority as freeborn. Aristocracy, government by the best, faces the same problem concerning virtue. If one citizen is better than all the other rulers, however good they are, the same principle of justice gives him authority over them. And if the people's claim rests on their superior strength, one person or a minority stronger than the multitude should govern instead of the multitude.

Taken together, these considerations suggest that none of the principles by which people claim the right to rule and subject everyone else to their authority is unconditionally correct. Those claiming to master the state because of their virtue or their wealth could fairly be answered by the multitude: the many are often better and richer than the few, not, as I emphasize, as individuals, but as a collective body. We can meet another ingenious objection, sometimes advanced, in much the same way. Suppose all the elements just discussed coexist in one state. Some then ask whether a legislator seeking to enact the most just laws should legislate for the advantage of the higher classes or for that of the multitude. Justice and right must here be understood in the sense of equality. What is right as equality must in turn be considered in relation to the state's advantage and the common good of its citizens. A citizen is someone who participates in both governing and being governed. His character differs with the constitution under which he lives. In the best state, however, he is willing and able both to submit to government and to govern, with the life of virtue as his purpose.

Suppose, however, that one person, or several too few to constitute a whole state, possesses such extraordinary virtue that everyone else's virtue and political capacity cannot be compared with his or theirs. Such people can no longer be regarded as ordinary parts of the state. Treating the superior person as equal to those so far beneath him in virtue and political ability would be unjust. He may truly be called a god among human beings. We can therefore see that legislation necessarily concerns those equal in birth and power. People of outstanding virtue have no law above them: they themselves are law. [Compare section 4.] Trying to legislate for them would be ridiculous. They would probably reply as the lions did in Antisthenes' fable, when the hares addressed the animals' council and demanded equality for everyone: 'Where are your claws?' This is also the reason democratic states introduced the institution of ostracism. Equality is the aim they pursue above everything else. They therefore ostracize and expel from the city for a period those who appear to possess too much preponderance, whether through their wealth, the number of their friends, or some other source of political influence. Myth gives the same reason for the Argonauts leaving Heracles behind: the Argo refused to carry him because she feared he would outweigh the rest of her crew. Those who denounce tyranny and condemn Periander's advice to Thrasybulus are therefore not wholly just in their criticism. The story says that a herald came to Periander seeking advice. Periander said nothing, but cut down the tallest ears of corn until the field was level. The herald did not understand, but reported what he had seen. Thrasybulus understood: he should eliminate the foremost men in the state. This policy is useful not only to tyrants, nor confined to them in practice; oligarchies and democracies need it equally. Ostracism has the same purpose, disabling and banishing the most prominent citizens. Great powers treat entire cities and peoples similarly. The Athenians did so to the Samians, Chians, and Lesbians: once secure in their empire, they humbled their allies in violation of their treaties. The Persian king has repeatedly crushed the Medes, Babylonians, and others whenever memories of former greatness revived their spirit.

This problem affects every constitution, correct as well as distorted. Distorted governments may adopt this policy for their own benefit, but governments pursuing the common good adopt it too. The arts and sciences offer parallels. A painter will not give a figure a disproportionately large foot, however beautiful the foot itself may be. A shipbuilder will not make the stern or any other part excessively large. A chorus-master will not admit a singer whose voice is louder or better than everyone else's. Monarchs can likewise use compulsory measures and still remain in harmony with the cities they govern, provided that their government serves the interest of the state itself. When superiority is acknowledged, therefore, the case for ostracism rests on a certain kind of political justice. It would be better for the legislator to organize the state from the beginning so that no such remedy was needed. If the need arises, the next best course is to correct the problem through ostracism or a similar measure. In practice, states have misapplied the principle, using ostracism for factional purposes rather than the public good. Within distorted constitutions, and from their particular standpoint, it is just and useful; it is not just without qualification. In the best state, serious doubts arise not over applying it to excessive strength, wealth, popularity, or similar advantages, but over applying it to extraordinary virtue. What should be done with such a person? No one would propose expelling and exiling him. Yet he should not be a subject either: that would resemble claiming the right to govern Zeus through rotation of office. The only alternative is for everyone gladly to obey him, in accordance with what appears to be nature's order, and for such people to reign for life. This discussion leads naturally to kingship, which we recognize as a correct constitution. Let us examine whether a state or a country ought to be placed under a king if it is to enjoy good government, or ought instead to receive some other form of government. We must also ask whether monarchy, although advantageous to certain peoples, might prove harmful to others. First, however, is kingship a single kind or does it have several forms? There are several, and their manner of governing is not identical. Of lawful kingships, the Lacedaemonian is regarded as closest to the true pattern. Yet its kings lack absolute authority except on military expeditions, when they command the army. Religious matters also belong to them. In truth the kingly office amounts to a particular kind of military command: a generalship held permanently and without the ordinary obligation to give an account. They cannot impose death except on campaign and in the field, following the ancient practice described in Homer. Agamemnon tolerates attacks in the assembly, but when the army marches into battle he possesses authority over life and death. Does he not say:

'If I discover a man skulking away from battle, nothing will save him from the dogs and vultures, because death lies in my hands.' This is one type of kingship: lifelong military command. Such kingships may be either hereditary or elective.

Another kind of monarchy, common among barbarians, closely resembles tyranny. Nevertheless, it is hereditary and lawful. Barbarians are more servile in character than Hellenes, and Asiatics more so than Europeans, and therefore do not rebel against despotic government. These kingships resemble tyrannies because their peoples are naturally slaves, yet their hereditary and lawful character protects them from overthrow. Consequently, the guards surrounding these rulers are of the kind appropriate to a king, rather than the kind a tyrant would employ: they consist of citizens, while tyrants employ mercenaries. Kings govern willing subjects under law, whereas tyrants govern unwilling subjects. Citizens protect their kings; tyrants require protection against their citizens.

These are two kinds of monarchy. A third existed in ancient Hellas under the name Aesymnetia, or dictatorship. Broadly, it was an elected tyranny. Like barbarian monarchy it was lawful, but unlike it, it was not hereditary. The office might last for life, for a fixed number of years, or until a specified task was completed. For example, the

Mitylenaeans elected Pittacus to lead them against the exiles commanded by Antimenides and the poet Alcaeus. In one of his irregular songs Alcaeus himself says, 'They chose Pittacus as tyrant', reproaching his fellow citizens for 'making low-born Pittacus tyrant of their cowardly, ill-fated city, while unanimously crying out his praises'.

These governments were despotic in possessing tyrannical power, but kingly in being elected and accepted by their subjects. A fourth type is the kingship of heroic times: hereditary, lawful rule over a willing people. The first chiefs benefited their people through practical arts or warfare. They brought them together into a community or obtained land for them, becoming kings with their subjects' consent. Their descendants inherited this authority. They took command of their people whenever they went to war, and presided over religious sacrifices, with the exception of those rites that required the services of a priest. They were also responsible for deciding lawsuits, doing so either after swearing an oath or without taking an oath. When swearing, they extended their sceptre as the form of the oath. Originally, their authority covered everything in city and countryside and in foreign territories. Later they surrendered some privileges, and the people removed others. In some states only their sacrificial duties remained. Where their office retained more substance, their additional power was limited to commanding warfare beyond the frontier.

These, then, are the four different forms of royal government that we have distinguished. First is the heroic form, governing willing subjects but confined to particular tasks: the king commanded armies, judged disputes, and supervised religion. Second is barbarian kingship, a hereditary despotism exercised according to law. Third is the authority of the Aesymnete or Dictator, an elected tyranny. Fourth is the Lacedaemonian form, essentially a hereditary, lifelong generalship. These four kinds differ from one another in the ways I have described.

There is a fifth kind of royal government, in which one person has the disposal and direction of everything, just as a tribe or state collectively controls its common property. It corresponds to household management. As management of a household is kingly rule within a home, so this kingship manages a city, a nation, or several nations as a household.

Only two of these forms require examination: Lacedaemonian kingship and absolute kingship. For the most part, the other kinds occupy an intermediate position between these two. Their rulers possess less power than the absolute king, but more than the Lacedaemonian king. Our inquiry thus reduces to two questions. First, does a permanent military commander benefit the state, and should this office belong to one family or pass among citizens in rotation? Second, is it advantageous for one person to possess supreme authority in everything? The first question concerns laws rather than constitutions. Any constitution could include a lifelong generalship, so this

question can be left aside for the present. The other sort of kingship does constitute a distinct form of government. We must now examine that constitution and briefly go through the difficulties it presents. Our starting question will be whether a state benefits more from being governed by the best individual or from being governed by the best laws.

Supporters of kingship argue that laws state general rules and cannot accommodate particular circumstances. They regard strict adherence to written instructions as absurd in any science. Even in Egypt a doctor may change a treatment after the fourth day; earlier changes are made at his own risk. They infer that government confined to written laws plainly cannot be best. Yet a ruler surely cannot dispense with the general principle embodied in law. A ruler free from passion is better than one moved by it. Law has no passions, while a human heart can never escape their influence.

Someone may reply that an individual nevertheless gives better advice in particular cases. Our answer is that a king must legislate and laws must be enacted. Those laws should lose authority when they fail to fit the case, but retain it otherwise. A further question remains: when law cannot decide a matter at all, or cannot decide it adequately, should the single best man decide, or should everyone? Under present practice, assemblies convene to judge, deliberate, and decide individual cases. Any assembly member considered alone is certainly inferior to the wise man. But the state consists of many individuals. A meal to which all guests contribute is better than a banquet supplied by one person; likewise, a multitude judges many matters better than any individual.

Furthermore, the many are harder to corrupt than the few, just as a large volume of water resists contamination better than a small one. An individual may be overwhelmed by anger or another passion, inevitably distorting his judgment. It is unlikely that a great number would all become angry and mistaken simultaneously. Suppose they are free people who never violate the law but fill the gaps it necessarily leaves. If expecting such virtue from the whole multitude is unrealistic, suppose only that most are good men and good citizens. We can then ask which is less open to corruption: a single good person who governs, or a number of rulers every one of whom is good? Surely the many. You may object that factions can divide them, while one man cannot be divided against himself. We may answer that their characters are as good as his. If we call the government of many good men aristocracy, and that of one man kingship, aristocracy will benefit states more than kingship, whether or not government rests on force, provided several men equal in virtue can be found.

Kingships were probably the earliest governments because ancient cities were small and people of exceptional virtue were few. Such people became kings as benefactors, and only good men can confer benefits. When many people of equal merit emerged, they ceased to tolerate one man's pre-eminence, wanted shared government, and established a constitution. [Compare below, section 15, and section 12.] The governing class soon deteriorated and enriched itself from public funds. Wealth became the route to honour, and oligarchies naturally arose. These became tyrannies, which in turn became democracies. The governing classes' greed continually reduced their numbers and strengthened the multitude, until it attacked its masters and established democracy. Now that cities have grown larger, it seems that no other form of government remains possible.

Even if we accept that kingship is best for states, what should happen to the king's family? Should his children inherit his authority? If they are no better than ordinary people, that would be harmful. A defender of kingship may say that the king, though able to do so, will not pass power to his children. But expecting that is hardly realistic; it asks too much of human nature. His means of force present another difficulty. Should he have guards strong enough to compel those who resist him? If not, how can he govern his kingdom? Even a lawful ruler who never acts arbitrarily or against the law still requires force to uphold it.

Where the monarchy is limited, answering this question presents no great difficulty. The king's force should exceed that of one individual or several individuals, but remain smaller than the people's combined strength. The ancients followed this rule when granting guards to someone appointed dictator or tyrant. Thus when Dionysius asked the Syracusans for permission to keep guards, someone advised granting him only a fixed number.
Rule by one person is considered contrary to nature.

Our argument now leads to the king who governs entirely according to his own will. As I have already said, limited monarchy, or lawful kingship, is not a separate constitution. Any government, whether democracy or aristocracy, may appoint a lifelong general, and often a single person is given supreme control of internal administration. Epidamnus has such an office, and Opus has one with narrower powers. Some consider absolute monarchy, in which a sovereign arbitrarily rules all citizens in a community of equals, wholly unnatural. They argue that natural equals have the same natural rights and worth. Giving equal offices to unequal people, or unequal offices to equals, is as wrong as prescribing identical food and clothing for different bodily constitutions, or different provisions for identical ones. Justice therefore seems to require equals to govern and be governed in turn. This brings us to law, because an established order of succession is a law. The rule of law is preferable to any individual's rule. By the same reasoning, even when particular people should govern, they ought merely to guard and administer the law. Everyone agrees that magistrates are necessary; the objection is that giving one man authority over people who are all equal is unjust. There may indeed be particular cases in which the law seems incapable of arriving at a decision. Yet if the law cannot determine them, can an individual person do so? The answer is that law trains officials for precisely this purpose, assigning them matters it leaves unsettled and requiring their best judgment. [Compare section 2; V.1, sections 10-11; and V.4, section 7.] Law also permits amendments suggested by experience, but the officials remain its servants. To ask law to rule is to ask God and reason alone to rule. To ask a human being to rule introduces something animal as well: desire is a wild beast, and passion distorts rulers' minds even when they are the best men. Law is reason free from desire. We are told that a sick person needs a doctor and will not recover by being treated from a book. But this comparison with the arts misses the point. A doctor does not act irrationally out of friendship: he treats his patient and receives a fee. Magistrates often act from hostility or favouritism. Indeed, a patient who suspected his doctor of accepting a bribe from enemies to kill him would prefer the book. Even doctors consult other doctors when ill, and trainers employ other trainers for their own exercise, recognizing that feelings may prevent them from judging their own cases correctly. It is evident, therefore, that when people search for justice, they search for what stands in the middle, impartial between the parties. The law itself occupies that neutral position. Moreover, customary laws carry greater weight and concern more important matters than written laws. A person may govern more safely than written law, but not more safely than customary law.

Nor is it easy for one person to oversee many affairs. He must appoint numerous assistants. What difference does it make whether they already occupied their positions or were appointed by him because he needed them? [Compare Nicomachean Ethics, section 7.] If, as I said, a good man's superiority entitles him to govern, two good men are better than one. This is expressed in the ancient saying, 'Two travelling together', and in Agamemnon's prayer, 'If only I had ten advisers like these!'

Even today, certain officials, including judges, are empowered to decide matters the law cannot settle. No one doubts that, wherever law can prescribe and decide, it does so best. There are, however, some matters that a general law can encompass and other matters that it cannot encompass in the same way. This gives rise to the disputed question whether the best law or the best man should govern. Legislation cannot cover the particular circumstances over which people deliberate. Everyone accepts that people must decide such cases; the argument is that many judges should do so, rather than only one. Every ruler trained by law judges well. It would be strange to suppose one person could see better with two eyes, hear better with two ears, or act better with two hands or feet than many people with many. Kings themselves already acquire numerous eyes, ears, hands, and feet by making colleagues of people friendly to them and their governments. These colleagues must support both monarch and government, since otherwise they will not do what he wishes. Yet friendship implies similarity and equality. If he therefore thinks his friends should

govern, he must also think that those who resemble him and are his equals ought to take part in government. These are the principal disputed points concerning monarchy. But might the arguments be true in some circumstances and not in others? A master's relationship to his servants can have a natural justice and usefulness, as can a king's relationship to his subjects and the relations of free citizens with one another. Tyranny has no such natural justice or advantage, nor does any other distorted constitution, since these governments come into existence contrary to nature. From our discussion it is clear that, where people are alike and equal, it is neither useful nor just for one person to be master of all the others. This is so whether there are laws, or no laws and the ruler himself takes the place of law. A good man should not be master over other good men, nor a bad man over other bad men. Even if he surpasses them in virtue, that superiority gives no right to rule except in the particular case already mentioned, to which I shall return once more. Before doing so, I must establish what kinds of people are fitted for kingship, what kinds for aristocracy, and what kinds for constitutional government.

A people naturally capable of producing a lineage outstanding in virtue and political ability is suited to kingship. A people willing to be governed as free persons by those whose virtue equips them for political command is suited to aristocracy. Constitutional freedom suits a people containing a naturally warlike multitude capable of governing and obeying in turn, under laws assigning office to the prosperous according to merit. If, however, a family or individual so excels in virtue as to surpass everyone else, it is just for that family to hold royal supremacy or for that citizen to become king of the entire people. As I said, granting them authority agrees with the ground of right commonly invoked by founders of aristocracies, oligarchies, and democracies. All acknowledge the claim of excellence, although they identify different kinds of excellence. It also agrees with our earlier principle. Killing, ostracizing, or exiling such a person would be wrong, as would requiring him to take a turn under others' government. A whole is naturally superior to a part, and someone with this pre-eminence stands to the others as a whole to its part. The only remaining course is therefore to grant him supreme power and obey him continually, rather than in rotation. These are our conclusions about kingship and its several forms, and our answer to whether it benefits states, which states it benefits, and in what way.

We maintain that there are three correct constitutions. The best must be governed by the best, with one man, a family, or several people outstanding in virtue, and with rulers and subjects fitted respectively to govern and be governed so as to attain the most desirable life. At the beginning of our inquiry we showed that a good man's virtue necessarily coincides with a citizen's virtue in the best state. Clearly, then, the same means that make a man truly good will enable him to form a truly good state, whether aristocratic or ruled by a king. The same education and habits produce a good man, a good statesman, and a good king. Having reached these conclusions, we must discuss the best state and explain how it arises and becomes established. [The manuscript text retained in this edition adds only the beginning of a sentence: “Anyone undertaking the appropriate inquiry”. Bekker omits this incomplete transition in his second edition.]

chapters.title: Book 4
paragraphs: Where an art or science covers an entire subject rather than just a part of it, that single art or science must examine everything belonging to its subject. Physical training, for example, investigates which exercises suit different bodies (2), but also which training is absolutely best (1). The absolutely best training must suit the body that is naturally best and has the best material conditions for life. It must also determine what general kind of training suits most people (4). And if someone does not want the finest bodily condition or the greatest athletic skill he could achieve, the trainer or teacher should still know how to provide a lesser degree of either (3). The same principle applies to medicine, shipbuilding, tailoring, and the arts generally.

Clearly, then, government too belongs to a single science. That science must examine which constitution would be best and fulfil our wishes most completely if external circumstances placed no obstacles in its way. It must also consider which constitution suits a particular state. The best is often beyond reach, so a genuine legislator and statesman must understand both what is best without qualification (1) and what is best under particular circumstances. Furthermore, we must explain how to organize a state under any specified conditions (3): how to establish it initially, and how, once established, to preserve it as long as possible. The state in question may fall far short of the best, lacking even the conditions needed for the best. It may also be inferior to the best constitution available in its own circumstances.

The statesman must also understand (4) the constitution most suitable for states generally. Writers on political subjects may have excellent ideas, yet their proposals often turn out to be impractical when someone attempts to put them into effect. We should investigate not only the best government, but also what is possible and what everyone can easily achieve. Some writers accept nothing less than the most perfect constitution, although that requires many natural advantages. Others discuss a more attainable form, rejecting their own state's constitution while praising a particular alternative, such as the Lacedaemonian. Any proposed constitutional change must be something people are willing and able to adopt. Reforming an existing constitution is as difficult as establishing a new one, just as unlearning is as hard as learning. In addition to the abilities already mentioned, therefore, the statesman must know how to remedy defects in existing constitutions. He cannot do that without knowing how many forms of government exist. People often assume there is only one democracy and one oligarchy, but that is mistaken. To avoid such mistakes, we must identify the differences between constitutions and the various ways their elements combine. The same political understanding will reveal both the best laws and the laws appropriate to different constitutions. Laws are, and should be, framed for the constitution, rather than the constitution for the laws. A constitution organizes a state's offices, deciding who governs and what end the community pursues. Laws differ from these constitutional principles: they supply the rules by which magistrates administer the state and act against offenders. Even if our only concern were legislation, we would therefore need to know the number and varieties of constitutions. The same laws cannot suit every oligarchy or every democracy equally, since both democracy and oligarchy certainly have more than one form.

In our initial discussion of government, we distinguished three correct forms: kingship, aristocracy, and constitutional government. Their three corresponding distortions are tyranny, oligarchy, and democracy. We have already considered kingship and aristocracy. Examining the best state amounts to examining these two forms, since both rest on virtue supported by the necessary external resources. We have also established how kingship differs from aristocracy and when kingship should be instituted. We must now describe the so-called constitutional government, which takes the name common to constitutions generally, along with the remaining forms: tyranny, oligarchy, and democracy.

It is plain which distortion is worst and which comes next. The distortion of the first and most divine constitution must necessarily be the worst. Genuine kingship, unless it is merely a name, rests on some exceptional personal superiority in the king. Tyranny, the worst government, is therefore the furthest removed from a well-ordered constitution. Oligarchy is somewhat less bad, although still far removed from aristocracy. Democracy is the most tolerable of the three.

An earlier writer made these distinctions too, but from a different standpoint. He holds that democracy is the worst of the good constitutions, among which he includes a virtuous oligarchy and similar arrangements, but the best of the bad ones. Our position is that all these constitutions are defective. We should not describe one oligarchy as better than another, but only as less bad.

Let us leave that question for now and begin by establishing (1) how many varieties of constitution exist, since both democracy and oligarchy have several. We must then determine (2) which constitution is most generally acceptable, and which deserves preference after the perfect state or any other aristocratic, well-ordered constitution, if there is another that also suits states generally. Third (3), we must establish which peoples are suited to each remaining constitution, because democracy may fit some better than oligarchy, while oligarchy fits others better. Next (4), we should consider how someone seeking to establish one of these different democracies or oligarchies ought to proceed. Finally (5), after discussing these matters briefly and as well as we can, we shall investigate what preserves states and what destroys them, both in general and in particular cases, and identify the causes responsible.

Constitutions have many forms because every state contains many elements. First, all states consist of households. Among their many citizens, some must be rich, some poor, and some between the two. The rich possess heavy arms, while the poor do not. Among the common people, some farm, some trade, and some practise crafts. Notable citizens also differ in wealth and property, for instance in the number of horses they keep: only the wealthy can afford horses. Hence ancient cities that depended on cavalry were oligarchies. They fought their neighbours with cavalry, as the Eretrians and Chalcidians did, and the Magnesians on the river Maeander, along with other Asian peoples. We must also remember that property and wealth are not the only differences: people differ in social rank and in personal merit as well,

and other elements mentioned when we listed the essentials of a state in discussing aristocracy. Of these constituent elements, sometimes all receive a share in government. In other states only some participate, and among these there may be either a smaller number of elements or a greater number. There must therefore be many constitutions differing in kind, because their constituent parts differ in kind. A constitution arranges the offices that citizens distribute among themselves. This distribution follows the power of different classes, such as rich and poor, or some common equality between them, or an authority shared by both. Consequently, there must be as many constitutions as there are ways to arrange offices according to the superior claims and other inequalities of the state's different parts.

People generally recognize two main forms. Just as they say there are only two winds, north and south, with all the others variations of these, they speak of only two governments, democracy and oligarchy. They classify aristocracy as an oligarchy because a few govern, and constitutional government as really a democracy. Similarly, they treat the west wind as a variation of the north and the east wind as a variation of the south. Musical harmonies are also said to fall into two kinds, Dorian and Phrygian, with every other arrangement of the scale included under one of these.

This account is particularly popular in discussions of constitutions. In both fields, however, it is better and more precise to distinguish one or two correct forms, as I have done, and treat the rest as deviations from the most perfectly balanced harmony or the best constitution. [The earlier reference is not to a preceding passage; compare VII.8.] Oligarchical forms may be compared to the stricter, more overpowering musical modes, and democratic forms to the gentler, more relaxed ones.

We should not assume, as some repeatedly claim, that democracy simply means sovereignty of the greater number. In oligarchies too, and indeed in every constitution, a majority governs. Nor does oligarchy simply mean sovereignty of a few. Suppose a city has thirteen hundred inhabitants, of whom one thousand are wealthy. They exclude the remaining three hundred from government, although these are free and equal to them in every respect except wealth. No one would describe the constitution of a city organized in that fashion as a democracy. Similarly, suppose the poor are fewer than the rich but govern them. No one would call that an oligarchy when the wealthy majority have no share in office. It would therefore be more accurate to describe democracy as the form of government in which those who are free hold power, and oligarchy government by the wealthy. The fact that the free are numerous and the wealthy few is incidental. Otherwise, assigning office by height, as reportedly happens in Ethiopia, or by beauty, would count as oligarchy simply because tall or handsome men are uncommon. Yet wealth and freedom alone still do not distinguish oligarchy and democracy adequately. Both include many other elements, so our analysis must go further. [Compare III.8, sections 3–7.] A government is not democratic when a few free men rule many who are not free, as at Apollonia on the Ionian Gulf and at Thera. In both places the nobles, who were the earliest settlers, held the highest honour despite being only a few among many. Nor is a government democratic merely because its wealthy rulers form the majority. Colophon formerly provided an example, since before the Lydian War most inhabitants owned substantial property. Democracy, then, exists when free people who are also poor and a majority govern; oligarchy exists when rich and noble people govern and are also few in number.

I have said that constitutions are numerous and explained the causes of their variety. We must now examine why there are more than the forms already listed, identify them, and trace their origins. Our starting principle, already accepted, is that every state contains many parts rather than one. If we were describing animal species, we would first identify the organs indispensable to every animal: organs of sensation, means of receiving and digesting food such as the mouth and stomach, and organs of movement. Suppose the kinds of organ are limited in number, but each can take different forms: different mouths, stomachs, sensory organs, and organs of movement. The possible combinations of these differences necessarily produce many kinds of animal. Animals with different kinds of mouths or ears cannot be identical in kind. When we have worked through every possible combination, there will be precisely as many distinct kinds of animal as there are different ways of combining the organs that an animal necessarily possesses. Likewise, the constitutions we have discussed consist, as I have repeatedly said, of several elements. One is the class producing food, the farmers. The second constituent part of the state is the class of mechanics, practising arts without which a city cannot exist. Some arts meet absolute necessities; others supply luxury or elegance. Third come traders, by which I mean people who buy and sell, whether wholesale merchants or retailers. A fourth part of the population consists of serfs or labourers. Warriors constitute the fifth part. This military class is as indispensable as any other, provided that the country is to avoid becoming the slave of every enemy who invades it. How could a state worthy of the name have a servile nature? A state is independent and self-sufficient; a slave is the opposite of independent. The Republic treats this subject ingeniously but inadequately. Socrates says a state needs four kinds of people: a weaver, farmer, shoemaker, and builder. Finding them insufficient, he adds a smith, then a herdsman to care for the necessary animals, followed by a merchant and a retailer. Together these complete his first state, as though a state existed simply to provide life's necessities instead of the good life, or needed shoemakers as much as farmers. He introduces warriors only after the territory has grown and begun encroaching on a neighbour's land, causing war. [Republic II, 369.] Yet even his original four citizens, or whatever number he brings together, require someone to administer justice and determine what is just.

The soul can be regarded as more truly part of an animal than its body. Similarly, the higher parts of states—the warriors, those administering justice, and those deliberating, which is the particular task of political judgment—are therefore more essential parts of the political community than those whose work is confined to providing the material necessities that sustain life.

It does not affect our argument whether different citizens perform these functions or the same citizens perform several. The same people, for example, may be both farmers and warriors. Both higher and lower elements must count as parts of the state, so the military element must be included. The wealthy, who serve the state through their property, form a seventh class. An eighth consists of magistrates and public officials, since a state cannot exist without rulers. Some must therefore be capable of holding office and serving the state, either continually or in rotation. There remain the people who deliberate and settle disputes, whom we have just distinguished. If the fair and just arrangement of all these elements is necessary, the state must contain people with a statesman's ability. Many believe that several functions can belong to one person: a warrior may also be a farmer or artisan, and a councillor may also judge. Everyone claims political ability and

considers himself quite capable of holding most offices. But the same person cannot simultaneously be rich and poor. For that reason, rich and poor are regarded as parts of a state in a particularly important sense. Moreover, the rich are usually few and the poor many, making them appear as opposing groups. Whichever group prevails determines the government. This produces the common view that there are two constitutions, democracy and oligarchy.

I have explained the differences between constitutions and the reasons for their variety. Let me now show that democracy and oligarchy themselves have different forms, as our discussion already suggests. Both the common people and the notables contain several classes. Among ordinary people are farmers, artisans, traders who buy and sell, and seafarers. The last work in warfare or commerce, or as ferrymen or fishermen. Any one of these groups can form a substantial population: fishermen at Tarentum and Byzantium, trireme crews at Athens, merchant sailors at Aegina and Chios, and ferrymen at Tenedos. Besides the groups already named, we should include people who work for daily wages, people whose straitened circumstances leave them without any leisure, and people who are not freeborn through both their father and their mother. There may be further classes as well. Notable citizens likewise differ according to wealth, birth, virtue, education, and similar characteristics.

The first democracy is the one said to rest strictly on equality. Its law declares that it is just for no one to be poor and no one rich, and that neither group should dominate the other: both should be equal. [Compare III.]

If freedom and equality belong especially to democracy, as some believe, they are best realized when everyone shares as fully and equally as possible in government. Since the people form the majority and the majority's judgment decides, this government must be democratic. That is one kind. Another form of democracy elects its magistrates subject to a specified property qualification, but sets the required amount at a relatively low level. Anyone possessing the required amount participates in government; losing that property means losing those rights. In another kind, all citizens who are not disqualified take part, while the law remains supreme. In another, citizenship alone admits everyone to government, but the law still governs. A fifth resembles these otherwise, but gives supreme authority to the multitude instead of law, replacing laws with popular decrees. Demagogues bring this situation about. Where democracy obeys law, the best citizens take the leading place and demagogues do not arise. Where law is no longer supreme, demagogues appear. The result is that the people itself becomes a monarch: although composed of many persons, it acts as one single ruler. It holds power collectively rather than as separate individuals. The poet Homer, speaking about the number of those who govern, says that 'rule by many is not

good', though it is unclear whether he means collective rule of this kind or government by many separate individuals. [Victorius reads the earlier sentence as 'the poor should no more govern than the rich'. This amendment is not essential, although VI.2, section 9 supports it by saying that neither poor nor rich should govern more than the other or alone, but all equally according to number.] Now acting as a monarch and no longer restrained by law, the people seeks monarchical power and becomes despotic. Flatterers receive honour. This particular type of democracy has the same relation to other democratic constitutions that tyranny has to the other varieties of monarchy. Both have the same spirit and exercise despotic authority over the better citizens. The demos' decrees correspond to a tyrant's commands; the demagogue plays the same part for the people as the flatterer for the tyrant. Both wield great power, one with the tyrant and the other with democracies of this kind. Demagogues place popular decrees above laws and refer every matter to the assembly. They consequently become powerful: the people controls everything, while they control the people's votes, since the people listens to them too readily. Anyone with a complaint against magistrates likewise says, 'Let the people judge.' The people gladly accepts the invitation, undermining the authority of every office. One may reasonably object that this is no constitution at all. For wherever the laws cease to exercise authority, we cannot properly say that a constitution exists at all. Law should govern everything generally, while magistrates and governing bodies judge particular cases. If democracy is genuinely a constitution, a system deciding everything by decree cannot be democracy in the proper sense, since decrees concern only particular matters.

These, then, are the various different forms of democratic government that we have distinguished. Oligarchy also has several forms. In one, the property qualification for office is high enough to exclude the poor majority, although anyone who acquires the necessary property may enter government. In another, the qualification is high and existing rulers fill vacancies by co-option. Choosing from everyone who meets the qualification gives this constitution an aristocratic tendency; choosing only from a privileged group makes it oligarchical. Another form provides for sons to succeed their fathers. A fourth is hereditary too, but magistrates rather than laws hold supreme authority. This stands to other oligarchies as tyranny does to monarchies, and as the last democracy described does to democracies. Indeed, this oligarchy is called a dynasty, meaning the rule of powerful families.

These, then, are the varieties of oligarchy and democracy. We must remember, however, that in many states a constitution that is not democratic by law can be administered democratically because of the people's character and habits. Conversely, a constitution may formally lean towards democracy yet operate in an oligarchical spirit. This occurs most often after revolution. Government does not change all at once: initially the victorious party is content to make small encroachments on its opponents. The former laws remain in force, but the revolution's authors possess the actual power.

Our earlier argument safely establishes the existence of these several democracies and oligarchies. [Compare V.1, section 8.] Clearly, either all the classes we listed must participate in government, or some participate while others do not. When farmers and people of moderate means are supreme, government follows law. Citizens who must work for a living have little leisure. They therefore establish law's authority and attend assemblies only when necessary. Everyone can participate once he acquires the legally prescribed qualification, so nobody is excluded absolutely. Excluding an entire class outright would move towards oligarchy. But these people cannot have leisure unless public revenues support them. Here, then, we have one definite kind of democracy, together with the conditions and causes that account for its coming into existence. A second follows naturally in the order of electoral arrangements. Anyone whose birth meets the requirements is eligible and may take part if he can find the leisure. In this kind of democracy, the supreme authority continues to belong to law, because the state has no revenues from which to pay its citizens. In a third, every free person is entitled to participate, but does not actually do so, for the reason already given. Here too, therefore, law must govern. A fourth kind of democracy is the one that comes last in the historical development of the constitutions of states. Today cities have expanded far beyond their original size and increased their revenues. The numerical preponderance of the citizens secures everyone a share in government. All participate, including the poor, who receive pay and thus have leisure to exercise their

rights and take part in administration. [Alternative reading of the preceding passage: 'which is proper to it'.] Once paid, ordinary people actually have the most leisure. Managing property does not hinder them as it often hinders the rich, preventing wealthy citizens from attending the assembly or courts. Consequently, the poor majority governs the state rather than law. These are the different democracies, arising from the necessary causes we have described.

The first oligarchy is the one in which most citizens possess some property, though not much, and anyone acquiring the required amount can participate in government. Since the governing body is numerous, law must govern rather than particular individuals. They are far removed from monarchy and own neither enough to live without attending to business nor so little that they need public support. They must therefore accept legal government instead of claiming personal authority. A second oligarchy emerges when property owners are fewer and their holdings larger. As the strength of these property owners increases, they lay claim to a correspondingly greater share of political authority. To secure it, they select for themselves which members of other classes will be admitted to government. Since their strength is still insufficient for them to exercise government independently of the law, they do not yet discard it. Instead, they arrange for the provisions of the law to express their own wishes. When numbers fall further and property grows, their power intensifies and a third stage appears. The governing group reserves offices for itself, and law provides that sons succeed fathers. Finally, when rulers possess immense wealth and numerous friends, this dynastia, or family despotism, approaches monarchy. Individuals govern in place of law. This fourth oligarchy corresponds to the last form of democracy.

Besides democracy and oligarchy there remain two forms. One is universally recognized among the four main constitutions usually listed: monarchy, oligarchy, democracy, and so-called aristocracy, the government of the best. But there is a fifth, called by the general name polity or constitutional government. Because it is uncommon, writers classifying constitutions have overlooked it. Like Plato in his works on the state, they recognize only four. 'Aristocracy' properly describes the constitution examined in the first part of our treatise. Only government by people who are best without qualification, rather than good by some particular standard, truly deserves the name 'government of the best'. In the perfect state, the good man and good citizen coincide without qualification. Elsewhere, a good citizen is good only relative to his constitution. Some states, however, differ both from oligarchy and from polity, and are also called aristocracies. They select magistrates for merit as well as wealth. Such a government is different in character from both of the two constitutions just mentioned. It is neither simply an oligarchy nor simply the so-called polity, and it receives the name of aristocracy. Even states that do not make virtue their purpose contain men of merit and men reputed to be virtuous. Thus a government considering wealth, virtue, and numbers, like Carthage, is aristocratic. So is one considering just virtue and numbers, like Lacedaemon, where democracy and virtue moderate one another. These two aristocracies exist in addition to the first, perfect state. There is, in addition, a third form of this less perfect aristocracy: it consists of constitutional governments whose arrangement inclines in the direction of oligarchy.

Polity and tyranny remain to be discussed. I place them in this order without intending to classify constitutional government as a distortion any more than the aristocracies just mentioned. In truth, all these fall short of the most perfect constitution and are therefore counted as deviations from it. Other constitutions, the genuinely distorted ones, deviate from these in turn, as I explained earlier. I shall discuss tyranny last because our subject is the constitutions of states, and tyranny is the very opposite of a constitution.

Having explained this order, I turn to constitutional government. Its nature should now be clearer from our definitions of oligarchy and democracy. Generally speaking, a polity or constitutional government consists in bringing these two forms, oligarchy and democracy, together within a single constitution. Usually, however, the name is given to mixtures leaning towards democracy, while mixtures leaning towards oligarchy are called aristocracies, because wealth commonly brings birth and education with it. Rich people also already possess the external advantages whose absence tempts others into crime. Hence they are called noblemen and gentlemen.

Since aristocracy aims to place the best citizens in control, people describe oligarchies too as governments of noblemen and gentlemen. It seems impossible that a state governed by its best citizens should be badly governed, or that a badly governed state should have its best citizens as rulers. But good laws that people disobey do not amount to good government. Good government has two elements: citizens actually obey the laws, and the laws they obey are good. Bad laws can be obeyed as readily as good ones. We may make a further distinction: people may obey the best laws attainable in their circumstances, or laws that are best without qualification.

Allocating offices by merit particularly characterizes aristocracy. Virtue is its principle, just as wealth is oligarchy's principle and freedom democracy's. In all these governments, of course, the majority has authority: whatever most participants in government approve becomes binding. A mixed state of the kind under discussion is generally called constitutional government rather than aristocracy, since its combination goes no further than bringing together the poor's freedom and the rich's wealth. The rich generally stand in place of the noble. There are three grounds for claiming an equal share in government: freedom, wealth, and virtue. Good birth, a fourth, results from the latter two, being simply longstanding wealth and virtue. A mixture of rich and poor is therefore a polity or constitutional government, while a union of all three elements is aristocracy. Except for the true and ideal form, no other constitution better deserves the name 'government of the best'. [Textual note: omit the words meaning 'but governed by the wicked'.] We have now described the constitutions besides monarchy, democracy, and oligarchy, explaining their nature, the differences among aristocracies, and the distinction between aristocracies and polities. These last two are clearly close relatives. Next we must examine how polity arises alongside oligarchy and democracy, and how to organize it. Comparing the two will immediately explain its nature. Identify their distinctive arrangements, take a part of each, and fit them together like the matching halves of an indenture. Governments can be combined in three ways. Legislation on justice provides an example. Oligarchies fine rich people for failing to serve as judges but do not pay the poor. Democracies pay poor jurors but impose no fine on wealthy absentees. First, we can unite these two practices in one arrangement, paying the poor for service while also fining the wealthy for absence. This combination is a common or intermediate position between the two systems, and therefore belongs especially to constitutional government. It provides the first method of joining the oligarchical and democratic elements. Second, instead of adopting the complete provisions of both systems, it is possible to establish an intermediate rule lying between the provisions made by each. Democracies require assembly members to possess little or no property, while oligarchies set a high qualification. The common arrangement is neither extreme, but an intermediate qualification. [Compare section 6.] Third, one may take a particular feature from oligarchy and a different one from democracy. Appointment by lot is democratic, election by vote oligarchical. Having no property qualification is democratic, requiring one oligarchical. An aristocratic or constitutional state combines oligarchy's election by vote with democracy's absence of a property qualification. These, then, are the several different ways in which the two constitutional principles can be combined with one another.

Oligarchy and democracy are genuinely united when the same state can be described as either. Anyone using both names evidently senses that the mixture is complete. An intermediate arrangement similarly contains both extremes. Lacedaemon's constitution, for example, is often called democratic because it includes many democratic features. Its education is democratic: poor boys grow up alongside rich boys, and the rich receive an upbringing that poor boys can equally receive. The same sort of equality is observed throughout the next period of their lives. When they finally reach full manhood and take their place as adult citizens, the same principle still applies: no distinction is made between those who are wealthy and those who are poor. Everyone eats the same food at public tables, and the rich wear clothing affordable to any poor man. Furthermore, the people elect holders of one of the two greatest offices and participate directly in the other. They elect the Senators and share in the Ephoralty. [Compare II.9, section 21.] Others, however, describe the

Spartan constitution as oligarchical because it contains many oligarchical elements. Choosing every official by election rather than lot is one; giving a few people authority to impose death or exile is another, and there are more. A well-balanced polity should display both elements while appearing to be neither alone. It should also sustain itself without foreign assistance or the goodwill of most foreign states, since foreigners might equally favour a defective constitution. Instead, its preservation should rest on the general willingness of every class of citizens within the state itself to maintain the established constitution.

We have said enough about the way constitutional government should be established and the way the so-called aristocracies should be formed. The character of tyranny still requires discussion, so that it too receives its proper place in our inquiry. We count even tyranny as a form of government, although there is not very much to say about it. In an earlier part of this treatise I examined kingship in the ordinary sense of the word. I considered whether it benefits states, what kind of royal government should be established, and from what circumstances and through what means it arises.

When discussing kingship, we also considered two tyrannies that operate under law and can therefore readily become kingships. Barbarians have elected monarchs exercising despotic authority. Ancient Hellas also elected despotic rulers called Aesymnetes or dictators. When we compare these forms of monarchy with one another, we find certain differences between their respective arrangements. As I said, they are kingly insofar as their rulers govern lawfully and with their subjects' consent, but tyrannical insofar as they exercise despotic power according to their own wishes. A third kind is tyranny in its fullest sense, the counterpart of perfect monarchy. Here one individual possesses arbitrary authority, answers to no one, and governs everyone, whether equal or superior to himself, for his own advantage rather than theirs. His rule is consequently against their will: no free person will endure it if escape is possible.
These are the several forms of tyranny, and these are the reasons for distinguishing them.

We must now ask which constitution is best for most states and which life is best for most people. We should assume neither a degree of virtue beyond ordinary people, nor an education exceptionally favoured by nature and circumstances, nor an ideal state that remains merely an aspiration. Instead, we must consider a life most people can share and a constitution states generally can achieve. The so-called aristocracies just discussed either exceed the possibilities of most states or approach constitutional government. For that reason, we have no need to undertake a separate discussion of each of them at this point. Indeed, the conclusion that we reach about all these forms of government can be established on one and the same foundation. If the Ethics rightly states that happiness consists in virtue exercised without impediment, and that virtue is a mean, then the life occupying a mean attainable by every [Nicomachean Ethics VII.13, section 2]

person must be best. The same standards of virtue and vice apply to cities and constitutions, since a constitution is, figuratively, the city's life. Every state contains three elements: the very rich, the very poor, and those between them. Moderation and the mean are acknowledged to be best, so possessing fortune's gifts in moderation must also be best. People who live in these moderate circumstances are the ones most disposed to listen to what reason tells them and to act accordingly. Those exceptionally favoured in beauty, strength, ancestry, or wealth find reason difficult to obey, as do those who are desperately poor, weak, or dishonoured. The former become violent offenders committing great crimes; the latter become cheats and petty criminals. Two corresponding classes of offence result from these two dispositions: in one case people commit offences through violence, and in the other they commit them through dishonesty and trickery. Petty rogues also dislike holding military or civil office. Their unwillingness to perform these duties harms the state as much as their inclination towards crime.

People excessively endowed with strength, wealth, friends, and other advantages are neither willing nor able to accept authority. The trouble begins in childhood. Their luxurious upbringing prevents them from acquiring habits of obedience even at school. At the opposite extreme, the very poor are excessively degraded. The first group cannot obey and knows only despotic rule; the second cannot command and must be governed like slaves. The resulting city consists of masters and slaves rather than free people, with contempt on one side and envy on the other. Nothing is more destructive of friendship and fellowship in a state. Fellowship promotes friendship, whereas enemies prefer not even to travel the same road. A city should consist as far as possible of people equal and alike, and these are usually found in the middle class. A city composed of such citizens must therefore be best governed: they are, as we say, the state's natural elements. They are also the safest citizens. Unlike the poor, they do not covet their neighbours' property, and others do not covet theirs as poor people covet the rich people's possessions. Since they neither plot against others nor face plots themselves, they pass their lives securely. Phocylides therefore prayed wisely:

'Many things are best in the middle; I wish to hold a middle position in my city.' It is therefore evident that the political community best constituted for this purpose is one formed from citizens belonging to the middle class. States are likely to be well administered when this class is large, preferably larger than both other classes together, or at least larger than either alone. Adding its strength to one side tips the balance and prevents either extreme from dominating. A state whose citizens have moderate but adequate property is therefore exceptionally fortunate. Where some own a great deal and others nothing, extreme democracy or unmixed oligarchy can arise. Either extreme can also produce tyranny, whether rampant democracy or oligarchy. Tyranny is less likely to develop where conditions are moderate and approximately equal. I shall set out the reason for this more fully later, when our inquiry turns to the revolutions that occur in states and their constitutions. A state's intermediate condition is clearly best, since only it is free from faction. A numerous middle class makes faction and dissension least likely. Larger states are less exposed to faction than small ones for the same reason: their middle class is large. In a small state, the entire citizen body can easily divide into rich and poor, leaving no group in between.

Democracies are also safer and longer-lasting than oligarchies because their middle class is larger and has more participation in government. Where no middle class exists and poor people vastly outnumber the rest, disturbances arise and the state soon collapses. We have evidence of the superiority of the middle class in the social position occupied by the best of the legislators. Solon belonged to it, as his own poems attest, as did Lycurgus, who was not a king, and Charondas and almost every legislator. These considerations explain why most governments are democratic or oligarchical. Their middle class is seldom numerous. Whichever group, rich or common people, passes beyond moderation and becomes dominant draws government into its own hands, producing oligarchy or democracy.

There is another cause. Rich and poor struggle, and the winners treat political supremacy as their prize instead of establishing a just government serving the people. One side sets up democracy, the other oligarchy. The two powers that dominated Hellas likewise promoted their own kinds of constitution, establishing democracies on one side and oligarchies on the other. [Compare Book V; V.1, section 15, and V.7, section 6.] They thought of their own advantage, never of the public good. For these reasons a constitution occupying the middle position has come into existence only very rarely, if indeed at all, and only among a very small number of states. Only one of all those who ruled in Hellas was persuaded to establish it in states. Citizens have now become accustomed to disregarding equality altogether. Everyone seeks domination, or, when defeated, accepts subjection.

It is now clear which form of government is best and what gives it that superiority. Since democracy and oligarchy each have several varieties, it is also easy to rank the other constitutions, deciding which deserves first place, which second, and which any subsequent place, once the best has been established. A constitution nearest to the best must necessarily be better, and one furthest from it worse. This holds when we judge without qualification, rather than in relation to a particular set of conditions. I add this qualification because one government may be preferable for certain people, while another kind is better suited to others.

We must next ask what government suits what kind of people. As a general principle applying to every constitution, let us assume that the part of the state wanting its preservation must be stronger than the part wanting change. Every city must be considered in respect both of the quality of its inhabitants and of their quantity. By quality I mean freedom, wealth, education, and noble birth; by quantity, superiority in numbers. One class within the state may possess quality and another

quantity. The low-born may outnumber the well-born, or the poor the rich, yet their numerical advantage may be smaller than their disadvantage in quality. The decision cannot therefore be made from numbers alone or from quality alone: the quantity on one side must be compared with the quality on the other. Where poor people's numbers outweigh rich people's wealth proportionately, democracy naturally arises. Its form varies with its population. If farmers predominate, the first democracy results; if artisans and labourers predominate, the last; intermediate populations produce intermediate forms. Conversely, when the rich and notable people's superiority in quality exceeds their numerical disadvantage, oligarchy arises. This constitution likewise assumes different forms, depending upon the kind of advantage and superiority that its oligarchical rulers possess in each case.

A legislator should always bring the middle class into government. If his laws are oligarchical, he should look to that class; if democratic, he should equally use them to attach it to the state. Government can be stable only where the middle class exceeds one or both extremes. Then there is no danger of rich and poor joining against the rulers. Neither group will willingly serve the other. If they seek a government satisfactory to both, they will find none better than this. Mutual mistrust prevents them from agreeing to govern alternately. It is always the person acting as arbiter whom the parties are willing to trust, and the group occupying the middle position can perform that arbitrating role. The more completely the political elements are blended, the longer the state will endure. Even many of

those seeking to establish aristocratic government err, both by granting the rich excessive power and by trying to outwit the people. [Alternative construction of the preceding passage: 'to win this class over to his laws'.] Eventually an apparent good produces a real evil, because wealthy people's encroachments do more damage to the state than those of the common people.

The devices employed by oligarchical governments to deceive the common people fall into five distinct kinds. These concern the assembly, magistracies, law courts, possession of arms, and physical training. First, assembly attendance is open to everyone, but only wealthy absentees are fined, or their fines are much larger than everyone else's.

Concerning magistracies, people with the property qualification may not swear an oath excusing themselves from office, while poor people may. In courts, wealthy people alone are fined for failing to serve and poor people escape punishment. Alternatively, as under Charondas' laws, the rich pay a large fine and the poor a smaller one. Some states allow every registered citizen to attend the assembly and hear lawsuits, but impose heavy fines on those who register and then fail to attend either assembly or courts. The purpose is to frighten people out of registering, thereby preventing them from serving in the courts or assembly.

Their laws on weapons and physical training follow the same principle. Poor people need not possess arms, while wealthy people are fined for lacking them. Likewise, the poor face no penalty for failing to attend the gymnasium. Since no penalty threatens them, they have nothing to fear from absence and consequently stay away. The rich, however, risk a fine and therefore take care to attend.

These are oligarchical legislators' devices, and democracies employ corresponding devices of their own. They pay the poor for attending assemblies and courts, while imposing no penalty on wealthy absentees. Someone wishing to blend the two principles properly should clearly combine both practices: pay poor people to attend and fine rich people for absence. Under this arrangement, every part of the citizen body will have a reason to take part. Without this combination, one party alone will hold power. Government should be restricted to people who bear arms. With regard to the property qualification, it is impossible to prescribe a single absolute rule that would apply in every case. We must identify the highest threshold that still admits enough people to make citizens more numerous than those excluded. Even without a share in office, the poor will remain sufficiently peaceful, provided they are neither abused nor deprived of their property.

Securing considerate treatment for the poor is difficult, since governing classes are not always humane. In wartime the poor also hesitate to serve unless supplied with food; once fed, they are quite willing to fight. Some states give political rights both to current soldiers and to veterans. Among the Malians, for example, former soldiers constituted the governing body, while magistrates came from those still serving. After kingship was overthrown among the Hellenes, the earliest governments arose from the warrior class, initially from the cavalry. Military strength and superiority then depended on horses. [Compare IV.3, section 3, and VI.7, section 1.] Infantry is useless without discipline, and ancient peoples lacked military science and tactical organization, so their armies relied on cavalry.
