As cities grew and heavy infantry became stronger, more people entered government. This explains why constitutions we call constitutional governments have hitherto been called democracies. The old constitutions were naturally oligarchical or royal. The total number of inhabitants in these early states was small, so they did not contain a middle class of any considerable size. Weak both in numbers and organization, the people were more content to accept government by others.

We have now explained the reasons why constitutions take several forms, and why there are more such forms than people generally suppose. Democracy, like other constitutions, exists in more than one kind. We have also explained their differences and origins, identified the constitution best in general, and considered the people to whom each different form is most suitable.

This gives us a suitable foundation for the next stage of discussion. We shall consider the subject both generally and in relation to particular states. Every state has three elements, and the good legislator must judge which arrangement of each serves that state best. When these elements are well ordered, the state is well ordered; differences between them account for differences between constitutions. First comes the element deliberating about common affairs. Second comes the element concerned with magistracies: which offices exist, over whom they exercise authority, and how their holders are chosen. Third comes the element exercising judicial authority.

The deliberative element decides war and peace, makes and dissolves alliances, enacts laws, imposes death, exile, and confiscation, and examines magistrates' accounts. All these powers must be assigned either to the entire body of citizens or to a particular portion of it: for example, to the holders of one magistracy or of several magistracies. Alternatively, different matters may go to different offices, or some to all citizens and others only to particular people. Assigning the decision on every matter to all the citizens is characteristic of democracy, since this is precisely the kind of equality that the people desires. Yet universal participation can take several forms. Citizens may deliberate in rotation rather than all together, as in Telecles the Milesian's constitution. Elsewhere, boards of magistrates meet and deliberate, entering office in successive turns. They are chosen from tribes and the smallest divisions until everyone has held office. The citizens themselves assemble only to legislate, discuss the constitution, and hear official announcements. In another democracy, the citizens form one assembly but meet only to elect magistrates, enact laws, discuss war and peace, and conduct scrutinies. Separate officials chosen by vote or lot from the entire population handle other matters. In another arrangement, citizens assemble for appointments and scrutinies and deliberate on warfare or alliances, while magistrates administer the rest. As far as possible, these magistrates are elected by vote, particularly where their duties require special knowledge. A fourth democracy brings all citizens together to deliberate on everything. Magistrates decide nothing and merely conduct preliminary inquiries. This is how the final and worst democracy is currently administered, the form corresponding, as we maintain, to exclusive family oligarchy and tyranny. All these arrangements are democratic.

Having a restricted group deliberate on every matter, by contrast, is oligarchical. This arrangement, like the democratic one that we have just examined, can itself take a number of different forms. The deliberative body may be large, chosen from people with a moderate property qualification, respecting and obeying existing laws without changing them. If everyone reaching the qualification can enter government, the constitution's moderation brings it closer to polity. If only selected individuals, rather than everyone, participate in public deliberation, the government is an unmixed oligarchy even if, like the preceding kind, it obeys law. Where the deliberators select their own successors, sons inherit from fathers, and their authority supersedes law, government is necessarily oligarchical. Another arrangement gives particular powers to particular groups. For example, the people may decide war and peace and scrutinize officials, while magistrates, elected by vote or lot, manage everything else. That constitution is an aristocracy or polity. If some matters go to elected magistrates and others to magistrates chosen by lot, whether from everyone or from selected candidates, or if appointments combine voting and lots, these practices belong partly to an

aristocratic constitution and partly to constitutional government in its proper sense. Such are the different deliberative bodies, corresponding to the different constitutions. Each state is administered according to one of these principles. For democracy as most commonly understood, meaning the extreme form where the people outrank even law, deliberation would improve by adopting the oligarchical practice used in law courts. Oligarchies compel the wealthy judges they need to attend by threatening fines; democracies pay the poor to attend. Democratic assemblies should adopt the oligarchical practice, because deliberation is better when everyone participates together, the people with the notables and the notables with the people. It is also a good plan to select the people who will deliberate either by a vote or by drawing lots, and to take the same number of participants from each of the different classes. If the ordinary people vastly outnumber those with political experience, payment should go only to enough people to balance the notables, rather than to everyone; alternatively, the excess should be excluded by lot. In oligarchies, by contrast, either particular people should be chosen from among the mass of citizens, or a separate class of officials should be established. Some states already have such officials under the names probuli and guardians of the law. The citizens should then occupy themselves exclusively with questions on which these appointed officers have already carried out a preliminary deliberation. The people thereby share in deliberation without being able to unsettle the constitution's foundations. Again, in oligarchies the people should either approve the government's measures or at least enact nothing contrary to them. If everyone shares in discussion, final decisions should belong to magistrates. Oligarchies should follow the opposite practice to constitutional governments: a majority's rejection should be final, but its approval should refer the proposal back to the magistrates. Constitutional governments follow the reverse course. The few possess a veto, but not the power to approve; final approval rests with the multitude.
These are our conclusions about the deliberative element, which holds supreme authority within states.

We turn next to the distribution of offices, another branch of politics raising many questions. How many offices should there be, what should they supervise, and how long should they last? Some terms are six months or less; others a year or longer. Should office last for life or for many years? If terms are short, may the same people serve repeatedly, or only once? We must also ask from whom officials should be chosen, who should choose them, and by what method. Before choosing between these arrangements, we should be able to state all the possible variations in the constitution of offices. Only after doing so can we decide which variations are suitable for the different forms of government. But what exactly counts as an office? This is less easy to answer. A political community needs many officials, yet not everyone chosen by vote or lot is a ruler. Priests, for example, must be distinguished from political officials. Chorus-masters, heralds, and even ambassadors are elected, but are not thereby political officers. Some supervisory duties are political. They may concern all citizens in one field, like a general's supervision of citizens on campaign, or a particular group, like the supervision of women or young people. Other offices have responsibilities belonging to household administration rather than political rule. An example is the office of grain-measurer: in many states there are people elected specifically to perform this task. There are also menial duties that wealthy people assign to slaves. Generally, offices are those positions charged with deliberating on measures, judging, and commanding, especially the last, since issuing commands is a magistrate's particular function. In practice, however, this particular question about what should bear the name of an office has little importance. No one has ever gone to court to litigate the meaning of the word itself. Nevertheless, questions of this kind remain interesting when we consider the subject theoretically.

More important are the kinds and number of offices necessary for a state's existence, and those that, while unnecessary, improve its condition. These questions affect every state, especially small ones. In large states, assigning each office a distinct function is possible and necessary. A large citizen body allows many people to serve. Consequently, some offices become vacant only after long intervals, or a person holds a position only once. It is certainly true that any piece of work is performed better when the person undertaking it can give that task his entire attention, instead of dividing his attention among several tasks. Small states, however, must combine many offices in few hands. Their limited populations cannot supply numerous officeholders: who would succeed them? Yet small states sometimes require the same offices and laws as large ones. Large states need them frequently, small states only at long intervals. There is therefore no reason one person should not oversee several offices, since the duties will not interfere. In a small population, offices should resemble spits that double as lamp-holders. First determine how many magistracies every state needs and how many further offices are useful though not essential. Then deciding which can be combined will be straightforward. We also need to determine under what circumstances a local tribunal should exercise jurisdiction over a number of different matters, and under what circumstances those matters should instead be placed under a single, centralized authority. Should one official maintain order in the market and another elsewhere, or should one person cover every location? Should offices be divided by their subject matter or by the people supervised? For example, should one official supervise good order generally, or should separate officials supervise boys, women, and other groups? Another question is whether different constitutions need the same magistracies or different ones. Should democracy, oligarchy, aristocracy, and monarchy all possess the same magistracies, even though they do not appoint their magistrates from equal or similar classes of citizens, but select different kinds of people under different constitutions? Aristocracies select the educated, oligarchies the wealthy, and democracies the free. Or do constitutions have particular offices suited to them, with the same office appropriate to some but not to others? For it may be useful in one state to give a particular office a broad range of authority, while in another it may be useful to give the very same office a more restricted field of action. Certain offices are peculiar to particular constitutions. The probuli, for example, belong to oligarchy rather than democracy, while a bule or council is democratic. Some body must prepare proposals for the people so that citizens are not diverted from their work. If few undertake this function, the arrangement tends towards oligarchy. Indeed, probuli are necessarily few and therefore oligarchical. Where both institutions exist, the probuli restrain the council: councillors represent democracy and probuli oligarchy. Even the council loses power in extreme democracy, where the people continually assembles and deliberates on everything. This happens when assembly members are wealthy or receive pay. With no other occupation, they constantly meet and decide every matter themselves. Offices supervising boys or women, or similar groups, suit aristocracy more than democracy. How could officials prevent poor men's wives from going outdoors? Nor are such offices oligarchical, since oligarchs' wives consider themselves too grand to be controlled.

Enough on these matters. We should now examine appointments. Three questions, and the combinations of their answers, account for every difference: who appoints, from whom are appointees taken, and how are they chosen? Each allows further variations. First, either all citizens make appointments or only some do;

second, officials are selected either from everyone or from a group distinguished by property, birth, merit, or some special circumstance. At Megara, for example, eligibility belonged only to those who returned from exile and fought together against democracy. Third, appointment may be by vote or by lot. These methods can also be combined: some officers are appointed by a restricted group and others by everyone; some are taken from a restricted group and others from everyone; some are elected and others allotted. Each distinction permits four variations. First, everyone may elect from everyone, or everyone may select by lot from everyone. The selection may draw on the whole body together or pass successively through tribes, wards, and phratries until all citizens have been included. Alternatively, everyone may remain eligible without distinction, with election used for some offices and lot for others. Second, if only some citizens appoint, they may choose from everyone by vote, from everyone by lot, from a restricted group by vote, or from a restricted group by lot. Different offices may follow different procedures. I mean that where all appoint, voting and lot may be combined. [This means selection partly from everyone and partly from a restricted group, and partly by election and partly by lot; compare below, section 6.] Thus there are twelve modes of appointment, apart from the two combinations of electoral method. Two varieties are democratic: everyone chooses from everyone by vote or lot, or by combining the two, electing some and allotting others. Constitutional government includes arrangements where not everyone appoints simultaneously, but some choose from everyone or from a restricted group by vote, lot, or both; or some select from everyone and others from a restricted group, using both voting and lot. Having some appoint from everyone by vote, lot, or both is oligarchical, and more so if some appointees come from everyone and others from a restricted group. Selecting some from everyone and others from a restricted group, or some by vote and others by lot, characterizes constitutional government tending towards aristocracy. Election from a restricted group and allotment from a restricted group are both oligarchical, though not equally. Combining both methods within a restricted group, and having a restricted group select from everyone, are oligarchical too. Having everyone elect from a restricted group, however, is aristocratic.

These, then, are the different ways in which magistracies can be established, and in which their organization corresponds to different kinds of constitution. Which arrangements suit which constitutions, and how to establish them, will become clear when we identify the powers involved. By powers I mean authority over such matters as public revenue or national defence. Powers differ in kind: a general's authority, for example, is different from authority over contracts made in the market.

Of the three constituent elements of government, we still have to examine the judicial element. We shall analyze it on the same principle. Courts differ in three respects: the people from whom judges are drawn, the matters they hear, and the method of appointment. First, do judges come from all citizens or only some? Second, how many kinds of

court exist? Third, are judges selected by vote or lot? [Bekker places the preceding words in brackets in both editions. A further textual note omits 'and', following certain manuscripts and the old translator.]

Let us first determine how many different kinds of law court there are. We can distinguish eight separate kinds. One audits or scrutinizes accounts; a second hears ordinary offences against the state; a third deals with treason against the government. A fourth settles disputes about penalties, whether brought by magistrates or private individuals. A fifth hears the more important civil cases. The sixth concerns homicide, which has several categories: intentional killing, unintentional killing, and cases where the act is admitted but its justice disputed. There may also be a fourth homicide tribunal for murderers who fled justice and are tried after returning, as reportedly happens at Athens' Court of Phreatto. Cases of this last description occur only rarely, even in cities with large populations. The various different classes of homicide may all be tried by a single court, or separate courts may be assigned to hear them. Seventh come courts for foreigners, divided between disputes among foreigners and disputes between foreigners and citizens. Finally, an eighth kind must hear minor claims involving one to five drachmas, or slightly more. Such disputes need decisions but require few judges.
We need say no more about minor claims or courts for homicide and foreigners. I would rather discuss political cases, since their mishandling produces division and unrest within states.

If every citizen can judge the different cases we have listed, judges may be selected by vote, by lot, or sometimes by one and sometimes by the other. Alternatively, within a given class of case, some judges may be elected and others allotted. These, then, give us four different ways of appointing judges when the whole body of citizens is eligible to be chosen. There will likewise be four corresponding ways when the people eligible for selection form only a part of the population. A restricted group may supply elected judges for every case, or allotted judges for every case. Election may be used for some cases and lot for others. Or even within a court hearing the same cases, some members may be elected and others allotted. These, then, are the possible ways of appointing the judges already described.

The methods can also be combined. Some judges may be drawn from the whole population, others from a restricted group, and some from both. For example, a single court may include people selected from everyone alongside people selected from a restricted group, with either voting, lot, or a combination used to choose them.

We have now considered the different ways courts can be established. The first, drawing judges from all citizens to hear every kind of case, is democratic. The second, where only a few judge every case, is oligarchical. The third, with some courts drawn from every class and others from particular classes, is aristocratic and constitutional.

chapters.title: Book 5
paragraphs: The inquiry we set ourselves is now almost complete. We must next examine revolutions in states: how many causes they have and what those causes are; what destroys particular constitutions; and the forms from which, and into which, states most often change. We must also consider what preserves states, both generally and in particular cases, and how each kind of state can best be maintained. These are the questions still before us.

Our starting point must be this: the many constitutions that have arisen have all acknowledged justice and proportional equality, although people fail to achieve them, as I have already explained. Democracy, for instance, begins from the belief that people equal in one respect are equal in every respect. Because all are equally free, they claim equality without qualification. Oligarchy begins from the belief that people unequal in one respect are unequal in every respect. Because their property is unequal, they assume their inequality is absolute. Democrats therefore believe that, since they are equal, they should receive

equality in everything. Oligarchs, believing themselves unequal, demand a greater share, and this too is a kind of inequality. [The translator follows the manuscripts and Bekker's first edition.] Each of these constitutions contains a certain justice, but each is defective when measured against justice without qualification. Both groups therefore start revolutions whenever their share in government fails to match their prior conception of what they deserve. People superior in virtue have the strongest claim of all to rebel, since they alone can reasonably be considered superior without qualification. Yet they are the least inclined to rebellion. People of high birth also claim a superiority of their own: they are regarded as noble because their ancestors possessed wealth and virtue. Here, so to speak, we find the springs from which revolution flows. Two kinds of political change result. One changes the constitution itself: people seek to replace democracy with oligarchy, oligarchy with democracy, either with constitutional government or aristocracy, or the reverse. The other leaves the constitution intact: people want to take control of its administration without altering its form, whether oligarchy, monarchy, or something else. There can also be changes of degree. An oligarchy can become more or less oligarchic, and a democracy more or less democratic. Other constitutions likewise maintain their distinctive features more or less strictly. Or a revolution may target only one part of the constitution, such as creating or abolishing an office. At Sparta, Lysander is said to have tried to abolish the monarchy, and King Pausanias the ephoralty. Epidamnus also underwent a partial change: a council replaced the phylarchs, or tribal heads. Yet even today only the magistrates, among the governing class, must attend the Heliaea when an election takes place; the surviving office of a single archon is another oligarchic feature. Everywhere inequality produces revolution when it lacks proper proportion—for example, permanent monarchy among equals. The desire for equality is always what prompts rebellion.

Equality has two meanings: numerical equality and proportional equality. The first means sameness in number or amount; the second means sameness of ratio. Three exceeds two by the same amount that two exceeds one. But four stands to two in the same ratio that two stands to one: two is half of four, just as one is half of two. As I said earlier, people agree in principle that justice means treating people according to their deserts. They disagree about applying that principle. Some believe equality in any respect establishes equality absolutely; others believe inequality in any respect establishes inequality in everything. This produces the two main constitutions, democracy and oligarchy. Noble birth and virtue are uncommon, whereas wealth and large numbers are more readily found. Where could we find a city with a hundred people both well born and virtuous? Poor people, however, abound everywhere. Organizing a state entirely and exclusively around either kind of equality is unsound. The evidence is that such governments never endure. They rest on an initial mistake; having begun badly, they inevitably end badly. We should therefore employ both kinds of equality, numerical equality in some matters and proportional equality in others.

Nevertheless, democracy seems more secure and less exposed to revolution than oligarchy. Oligarchies face two dangers: conflict among the oligarchs themselves and conflict with the people. Democracies face only conflict with the oligarchs; within the body of the people themselves, no division of any importance develops. We may also observe that government based on the middle class is closer to democracy than to oligarchy, and is the safest of the imperfect constitutions.

To understand the origin of civil conflict and political revolution, we must first identify the beginnings and causes that affect constitutions in general. We can distinguish three, and must outline each: the state of mind of those who rebel, the objects they pursue, and the circumstances that provoke political conflict and quarrels. We have already identified the most general and important source of revolutionary feeling. People desire equality when they believe themselves equal to others who possess more. Or they desire inequality and superiority when, believing themselves superior, they find that they have only as much as, or less than, their inferiors. Such claims may be justified or unjustified. Those in an inferior position rebel to become equal; equals rebel to become superior. This is the disposition from which revolutions arise. The objects sought are profit and honour, or escape from dishonour and loss. Revolutionaries want to avert punishment or disgrace from themselves or their friends. The circumstances that arouse these motives and dispositions concerning the things just mentioned can be counted as seven from one perspective, and more than seven from another. Two have already been mentioned, but they operate here differently. The desire for profit and honour sets people against one another, not because they want these things for themselves, as in the case just described, but because they see others monopolizing them, whether justly or unjustly. Further causes are insolence, fear, excessive superiority, contempt, and disproportionate growth in one part of the state. Causes of a different kind include electoral intrigues, carelessness, disregard of small matters, and differences among the elements composing the state.

The contribution made by insolence and greed to revolution, and the way they operate, are clear enough. When magistrates behave arrogantly and grasp at wealth, they plot against one another and against the constitution that gives them power. They profit at the expense either of private people or of the public. Honour also plainly influences revolution. People rebel when they are denied honour themselves and see it given to others. Honour or dishonour is unjust when undeserved, but just when distributed according to merit. Excessive superiority causes revolution when one person or several acquire power beyond what the state and its government can withstand. Such circumstances produce monarchy or the rule of an oligarchic family. For this reason some cities, including Athens and Argos, use ostracism. It would be far better, however, to prevent people from gaining such overwhelming prominence in the first place than to let them acquire it and only then seek a remedy.

Another of the causes from which political revolution arises is fear. People may have acted wrongly and dread punishment, or expect to suffer wrong and wish to strike before their enemies do. At Rhodes, for example, the notables plotted against the people because they feared the lawsuits brought against them. Contempt also prompts rebellion and political change. In oligarchies, an excluded majority rebels because it considers itself stronger than the rulers. In democracies, wealthy people despise the government's disorder and lack of control. At Thebes, after the battle of Oenophyta, the democracy's poor administration destroyed it. At Megara, a military defeat caused by disorder and anarchy brought democracy down. At Syracuse, democracy was overthrown before Gelo's tyranny arose; at Rhodes, before the insurrection.

Revolution can also follow disproportionate growth in some part of a state. A body contains many members, each of which must grow in proportion if the whole is to remain balanced. If a foot grows four cubits long while the rest of the body measures only two spans, the body loses its proper nature. If the abnormal growth changes quality as well as size, it may even assume the shape of a different animal. A state likewise has many parts, and one may gradually grow without anyone noticing—for instance, the poor in democracies and constitutional governments. An accident can produce this disproportion. At Tarentum, many notables died fighting the Iapygians shortly after the Persian War, and the constitutional government consequently became a democracy. At Argos, losses inflicted by Cleomenes the Lacedaemonian in the 'Battle of the Seventh Day' forced the Argives to give citizenship to some of their Perioeci. At Athens, repeated infantry defeats during the Peloponnesian War reduced the notables' numbers, since soldiers had to be drawn from the citizen roll. Revolutions from this cause occur in democracies as well as under other forms of government, although they do not occur to the same extent. When wealthy people become more numerous or estates increase, government changes into oligarchy or rule by families. Constitutions sometimes change even without revolution. Electoral contests can cause this, as at Heraea, where selection by lot replaced election because voters habitually chose their own partisans. Carelessness can also admit opponents of the constitution to the highest offices. At Oreum, for example, Heracleodorus gained office and overthrew the oligarchy, replacing it with a constitutional and democratic government.

Political change can also happen gradually. Neglect of a small matter may allow a great alteration to enter the constitution unnoticed. At Ambracia, for example, the property requirement for office was originally small and eventually disappeared altogether. The Ambraciots reasoned that a small requirement amounted to much the same thing as having none.

Differences of origin also cause revolution when groups have not yet developed a common spirit. A state does not grow in a day, nor is it simply a crowd assembled by chance. Admitting outsiders to a colony, either at its foundation or later, has therefore generally produced conflict. The Achaeans who helped the Troezenians found Sybaris eventually expelled them because the Achaeans were more numerous; this brought the curse upon Sybaris. At Thurii, the Sybarites quarrelled with the other colonists. Believing the land belonged to them, they demanded too much and were expelled. At Byzantium, newcomers were discovered plotting and driven out by force. The people of Antissa admitted Chian exiles, then fought and expelled them. The Zancleans admitted Samians and were themselves expelled from their city. Apollonia on the Euxine experienced revolution after receiving fresh colonists. After expelling their tyrants, the Syracusans admitted foreigners and mercenaries to citizenship, then quarrelled and fought with them. The people of Amphipolis admitted Chalcidian colonists, who drove out nearly all the original inhabitants.

In oligarchies, the masses revolt because they believe they suffer injustice: as I said, they are equal but receive no equal share. In democracies, the notables revolt because they consider themselves unequal to the rest, yet receive only an equal share.

A city's geographical arrangement can also cause revolution when the territory does not naturally support political unity. At Clazomenae, the Chytrians disagreed with the island inhabitants; the people of Colophon quarrelled with the Notians. At Athens, the residents of Piraeus are more democratic than those of the city itself. In warfare even a small ditch can break up a military formation. Similarly, any difference, however slight, can divide a city. The greatest opposition is admittedly between virtue and vice; next comes the opposition between wealth and poverty. There are also other conflicting elements, greater or smaller in importance, and geographical separation is one of them.

Revolutions may begin over trivial incidents, but the interests at stake are great. Small incidents matter most when they involve rulers. Long ago at Syracuse, for example, a romantic quarrel between two young members of the government changed the constitution. While one was away, his companion won over his beloved. In revenge, the first seduced the other's wife. They drew the entire ruling class into their dispute and brought about a revolution. This teaches us to watch for the beginnings of such troubles and to end quarrels among leaders and powerful people. It is at the very beginning of such an affair that the decisive mistake is made. As the proverb says, a good beginning is half the work; likewise, even a small initial error counts for half of the whole affair. Generally, when notables quarrel, the entire city becomes involved. At Hestiaea after the Persian War, a dispute over an inheritance had this effect. One of two brothers refused to account for their father's property and a treasure he had discovered. The poorer brother quarrelled with him and enlisted the popular party; the other, being very rich, enlisted the wealthy classes.

At Delphi, a marriage dispute likewise began all the subsequent troubles. The bridegroom interpreted an event as a bad omen, visited the bride, and left without marrying her. Her relatives considered this an insult. While he was sacrificing, they planted some sacred treasure among his offerings, then killed him on the pretext that he was robbing the temple. At Mitylene, a dispute over heiresses began many misfortunes and led to the war in which the Athenian Paches captured the city. A wealthy citizen, Timophanes, left two daughters. Doxander wanted them as wives for his sons, but his proposal was rejected. He then stirred up revolution and urged the Athenians, whose proxenus he was, to intervene. At Phocis, another quarrel over an heiress arose between Mnaseas, Mnason's father, and Euthycrates, Onomarchus' father; it began the Sacred War. A marriage quarrel also changed the government at Epidamnus. A man secretly betrothed his daughter to someone whose father later became a magistrate and fined the girl's father. Stung by this insult, the latter conspired with those excluded from citizenship to overthrow the government.

Governments also become oligarchies, democracies, or constitutional governments when magistrates or some other group gain power or prestige. At Athens, the reputation the Areopagus acquired during the Persian War seemed to make government stricter. Conversely, the victory at Salamis, won by ordinary people serving in the fleet, secured Athenian command of the sea and strengthened democracy. At Argos, the notables distinguished themselves against the Lacedaemonians at Mantinea and then tried to suppress democracy. At Syracuse, the people played the chief part in defeating the Athenians and changed constitutional government into democracy. At Chalcis, the people joined the notables in killing the tyrant Phoxus, then took power themselves. At Ambracia, similarly, the people helped the conspirators expel the tyrant Periander and transferred government to themselves. In general, groups that have increased the state's power tend to cause revolutions, whether they are private citizens, magistrates, tribes, or any other section of the community. Either envy of their greatness prompts others to rebel, or pride in their own superiority makes them unwilling to remain on equal terms with everyone else.

Revolutions break out when opposing groups, such as rich and poor, are evenly matched and little or no middle group stands between them. If one side were clearly stronger, the other would not dare attack it. This also explains why people outstanding in virtue do not lead insurrections: they are always a minority. These, then, are the beginnings and causes of the disturbances and revolutions to which every constitution is exposed.

Revolutions are carried out through force or deception. Force may be used when the revolution begins or after it has succeeded. Deception also takes two forms. Sometimes citizens are tricked into changing their government and are afterwards kept in unwilling subjection. The Four Hundred did this: they deceived the people by promising that the king would finance the war against the Lacedaemonians, then tried to retain power after the deception was exposed. In other cases people are initially won over by persuasion, and repeated persuasion afterwards preserves their support and allegiance. The causes already described account for revolutions affecting constitutions in general.

We must now examine each constitution separately and draw the consequences of the principles already established. In democracies, revolution usually results from the excesses of demagogues. Acting privately, they bring accusations against wealthy people until they force them to unite; a shared danger brings even bitter enemies together. Acting publicly, they rouse the people against the rich. The truth of this observation can be established by considering a number of different examples from actual cities. At Cos, corrupt demagogues provoked the notables to combine and overthrow democracy. [Compare the earlier discussion, chapter 2, section 1.] The demagogues provided pay for the masses while preventing repayment to the trierarchs of money they had spent. Lawsuits then forced the trierarchs to unite and suppress democracy. At Heraclea, shortly after the colony's foundation, the demagogues' injustice drove the notables into exile. They returned together and ended the democracy. The overthrow of democracy at Megara followed a course very similar to the one just described. Demagogues expelled many notables in order to confiscate their property. Eventually the exiles became numerous, returned, fought and defeated the people, and established oligarchy. At Cyme, democracy suffered the same fate when Thrasymachus overthrew it. Looking at states more generally, we may observe that most of the political changes they have experienced have had this same character. To win popular favour, demagogues wrong the notables and compel them to join forces. They distribute their property, reduce their incomes by imposing public services, or prosecute wealthy people so that their possessions can be confiscated.

In earlier times a demagogue was also a military commander, and democracies consequently became tyrannies. Most ancient tyrants began as demagogues. This is no longer the usual course, but it was then, because these leaders were generals rather than public speakers: oratory had not yet become fashionable. Today rhetoric has developed greatly, and speakers lead the people. Their ignorance of military affairs prevents them from seizing supreme power, with only a few minor exceptions. Tyrannies were also more common in the past because individuals were often entrusted with great authority. At Miletus, for example, tyranny grew out of the office of Prytanis, whose holder had supreme control over many important matters. Cities were then small, and the people lived in the countryside, occupied with their work. Leaders with military ability could exploit the opportunity, win the masses' confidence by professing hostility to the wealthy, and establish themselves as tyrants. At Athens, Peisistratus led the party opposing the men of the plain. At Megara, Theagenes slaughtered wealthy men's cattle that he found grazing beside the river. Dionysius was likewise considered fit for supreme power because he denounced Daphnaeus and the rich; opposition to the notables earned popular trust. Democracies also change from their older to their most recent form. Where magistrates are popularly elected without a property requirement, candidates gain control of the people and eventually manage to place them above the laws themselves. Having each tribe elect magistrates separately, instead of letting the whole people elect them together, provides a more or less complete remedy.

These are the chief causes of revolution in democracies. Oligarchies have two obvious sources of revolution, one outside the governing group and one within it. First, oligarchs may oppress the people. Almost anyone can then become the people's champion, particularly a member of the oligarchy itself, as Lygdamis did at Naxos before becoming tyrant. The revolutions that begin among people outside the governing class do not all take the same form; we can distinguish further varieties among them. An extremely exclusive government may be challenged by wealthy people whom it excludes. This happened at Massalia, Istros, Heraclea, and other cities. Those denied a share made trouble until first the older brothers, then the younger, were admitted. Some places prohibit fathers and sons from holding office together; others prohibit older and younger brothers. Massalia's oligarchy came to resemble constitutional government, Istros became a democracy, and Heraclea expanded its governing body to six hundred. Cnidos also experienced a substantial change. The notables quarrelled because so few participated in government. They observed the rule just mentioned: father and son could not hold office together, and among several brothers only the eldest was admitted. Taking advantage of their dispute, the people chose a notable as leader, attacked the divided oligarchs, and defeated them. Division always creates weakness. In earlier times the Basilidae governed Erythrae, and governed it well. Yet the people resented the narrow basis of their oligarchy and changed the constitution.

Within oligarchies, personal rivalry among the rulers is one cause of revolution, because it leads them to behave as demagogues. An oligarchic demagogue can operate in two ways. He may appeal to the oligarchs themselves: even a very small ruling group can contain a demagogue. At Athens, Charicles' party dominated the Thirty, and Phrynichus' party the Four Hundred. Alternatively, oligarchs may court the people. At Larissa, the guardians of the citizens sought popular support because the people elected them. The same danger faces every oligarchy whose magistrates are elected, as at Abydos, by the heavy-armed soldiers or the people rather than by the class to which those magistrates belong. A high property requirement or membership in a political club does not prevent it. Again, where courts are independent of the government, oligarchs flatter the people to obtain favourable judgments and thereby alter the constitution. This happened at Heraclea in Pontus. Attempts to narrow an oligarchy also cause change: those seeking equal rights are forced to enlist the people. Another source of change is extravagant living that exhausts the oligarchs' private fortunes. They then seek political innovations, either trying to become tyrants themselves or installing someone else. Hipparinus helped Dionysius in this way at Syracuse. At Amphipolis, Cleotimus brought in Chalcidian colonists and, on their arrival, incited them against the rich. For a similar reason, the man negotiating with Chares at Aegina tried to overturn its constitution. Sometimes a faction within the oligarchy seeks political change; sometimes oligarchs plunder the treasury, and the others quarrel with the thieves, as at Apollonia in Pontus, or the thieves quarrel with them. An oligarchy whose members remain united and agree with one another, however, is not easily brought down by forces arising within the governing body itself. Pharsalus demonstrates this: a small number govern a large city because they maintain agreement among themselves.

Oligarchies also fall when a second oligarchy forms inside the first: the governing body is small already, yet only some of its members can reach the highest offices. At Elis, for example, a small senate governed. Although it had ninety members, very few people ever entered it, since senators were chosen for life from particular families, much like the Lacedaemonian elders. Neither wartime nor peacetime protects an oligarchy from political upheaval: it is exposed to revolution under both sets of circumstances. In war, distrust of the people forces oligarchs to hire mercenaries. Their commander often becomes a tyrant, as Timophanes did at Corinth; several commanders may establish a collective tyranny. Sometimes fear of this danger leads oligarchs to share government with the people, whose services they need. In peace, mutual distrust leads the two parties to entrust the state's defence to an army and to an arbitrator between the factions. He often becomes master of both. This happened at Larissa under Simos and the Aleuadae, and at Abydos in the time of Iphiades and the political clubs. Marriages and lawsuits also cause revolutions by enabling one oligarchic faction to overthrow another. I have already mentioned some marriage quarrels. Another occurred at Eretria, where Diagoras overthrew the oligarchy of the knights after being

wronged in a marriage dispute. At both Heraclea and Thebes, court judgments on accusations of adultery produced revolutions. In each case the punishment was deserved, but partisan hostility determined its execution: at Heraclea the victim was

Eurytion, and at Thebes Archias. Their enemies resented them and therefore arranged for them to be pilloried in the agora. Many oligarchies have fallen because members of the ruling group resented their excessive despotism. The oligarchies of Cnidus and Chios provide examples.

Accidental change often affects both constitutional governments and oligarchies that reserve service as councillor, judge, or other magistrate for people meeting a property requirement. The threshold may originally have suited the circumstances, admitting only a few under oligarchy or the middle class under constitutional government. After a period of prosperity, whether produced by peace or another good fortune, the same property may become worth several times as much. Everyone then qualifies for every office. This can happen gradually and unnoticed, or rapidly. These are the sources of change and revolution in oligarchies.

A general observation applies to democracies and oligarchies alike. They sometimes change into another variety of the same constitution instead of its opposite: a democracy or oligarchy governed by law becomes arbitrary, or the reverse. In aristocracies, revolution arises when only a few people share political honours. We have already seen this cause operating in oligarchies. An aristocracy is a kind of oligarchy, since it too means government by a few, although these few are virtuous rather than wealthy. For this reason people frequently confuse the two kinds of government and fail to distinguish aristocracy from oligarchy. Revolution becomes particularly likely, indeed inevitable, when most of the people are spirited and believe themselves as good as their rulers. At Lacedaemon, the so-called Partheniae, illegitimate sons of the Spartan peers, attempted revolution. When discovered, they were sent to found Tarentum. Revolutions also arise when distinguished people of at least equal merit are dishonoured by those holding higher office, as Lysander was by Sparta's kings; or when a courageous man is excluded from political honours, as Cinadon was when he plotted against the Spartans under Agesilaus. Another cause is extreme poverty alongside great wealth, a condition most often created by war. Lacedaemon during the Messenian War supplies an example. Tyrtaeus' poem Good Order confirms it: he describes citizens ruined by the war who wanted the land redistributed. Finally, a powerful individual who could become still more powerful may seek sole rule, as did Pausanias, Lacedaemon's commander in the Persian War, or Hanno at Carthage.

Constitutional governments and aristocracies usually fall because their constitutions depart from justice. In constitutional government the democratic and oligarchic elements are poorly combined; in aristocracy the mixture of democracy, oligarchy, and virtue is defective, particularly the first two. Combining democracy with oligarchy is the aim of constitutional governments. Most so-called aristocracies seek the same combination, differing from polities by adding virtue. This explains why some endure longer than others. Those leaning towards oligarchy are called aristocracies; those leaning towards democracy are called constitutional governments. Of these two forms, the governments called constitutional are consequently the more secure and less exposed to danger. Greater numbers bring greater strength, and people who enjoy equality remain content. The rich, however, tend to become arrogant and grasping when government empowers them. Generally, a constitution changes in the direction of its existing inclination as the corresponding party gains strength: constitutional government becomes democracy, aristocracy becomes oligarchy. The direction may also reverse. Aristocracy becomes democracy when poor people, believing themselves wronged, force it into the opposite form. Constitutional governments similarly become oligarchies. The only lasting basis for government is equality according to proportion, with each person enjoying what belongs to him.

What I have just described is not merely a possibility: a change of this very kind actually occurred in the city of Thurii. Its initially high qualification for office was lowered, and the number of magistrates increased. Earlier, the notables had illegally taken all the land: the government's oligarchic tendency enabled their encroachments. But military training soon allowed the people to overcome the oligarchs' guards, until those holding too much land surrendered it.

Because every aristocratic government leans towards oligarchy, its notables tend to grasp at advantages. At Lacedaemon, where property has become concentrated in few hands, they enjoy excessive freedom to do as they please, including marrying whomever they choose. [Compare IV; the earlier section 12; and II.9, section 14.] Locri was ruined by a marriage connection with Dionysius. Such a disaster could not have occurred in a democracy or a properly balanced aristocracy.

As I have already observed, revolutions in every state can begin with small matters. In aristocracies especially, the changes are gradual and difficult to notice. Citizens surrender one part of the constitution, making it easier for the government to alter something slightly more important, until the state's entire structure is undermined. Thurii had a law requiring five years between a general's terms. Some spirited young men, popular with the soldiers of the guard, despised the magistrates and expected to get their way easily. They wanted the law abolished so generals could retain command indefinitely, knowing the people would gladly elect them. The magistrates responsible, called councillors, initially resolved to resist. Later they agreed, imagining that changing this single law would bring no further attack on the constitution. Other changes to the constitution followed soon after this first concession. The councillors tried unsuccessfully to resist them, and the state fell into the revolutionaries' hands. They established an oligarchy ruled by powerful families.

Every constitution is overthrown either from within or from outside. External overthrow occurs when a nearby government has opposing interests, or when a more distant government possesses great power. The periods of Athenian and Lacedaemonian supremacy illustrate this. Everywhere, the Athenians

suppressed oligarchies, and the Lacedaemonians suppressed democracies. We have now completed our explanation of the principal causes from which civil divisions and political revolutions arise within states. Our next task is to consider how states can be preserved, both in general and in particular instances. Clearly, knowing what destroys them also tells us what preserves them. Opposite causes produce opposite effects, and preservation is the opposite of destruction.

In every government whose elements are properly balanced, nothing requires more vigilant protection than obedience to law, particularly in small matters. Lawbreaking enters unnoticed and eventually destroys the state, just as repeated small expenses gradually consume a fortune. Because the change does not happen all at once, people fail to notice it. Their minds are deceived by the false argument that if every part is small, the whole must also be small. This is true in one sense but false in another: the total is not small merely because the parts composing it are small.

First, then, we must guard against the beginnings of change. Second, we must not trust the political devices previously described that are intended merely to deceive the people; experience shows them to be useless. Oligarchies and aristocracies can also endure, not because these constitutions are inherently stable, but because their rulers maintain good relations both with the governing class and with those excluded. They avoid mistreating outsiders and admit the leading people among them to government. They must never wrong ambitious people over honours or ordinary people over money. They should deal with one another and their fellow citizens as equals. The equality that supporters of democracy demand for the masses is both just and useful among people who are equals. Thus, where the governing body is large, many democratic arrangements are beneficial. Limiting terms of office to six months, for example, allows everyone of equal standing to participate. Indeed, when people of equal rank or standing form a numerous governing body, that body itself comes to resemble a kind of democracy, and, as already observed, demagogues are likely to arise within it. Short terms prevent oligarchies and aristocracies from coming under family domination. Someone holding office briefly cannot easily do much harm; long possession of office breeds tyranny in democracies and oligarchies alike. Aspiring tyrants are either leading citizens—demagogues in democracies, members of ruling families in oligarchies—or holders of powerful offices who retain them for a long time.

States survive when their destroyers are far away, and sometimes also because they are near. Fear of a nearby threat helps the government keep control of the state. A ruler concerned for its survival should therefore create alarms and bring distant dangers before people's eyes. Citizens will then remain watchful, never relaxing their attention, like sentries on a night watch. Through the laws he should also restrain quarrels and rivalries among the notables, and prevent people previously uninvolved from being drawn into them. The ability to recognize an evil at the very moment when it first begins is not something an ordinary person possesses. Such discernment belongs only to someone who is a statesman in the true sense.

In oligarchies and constitutional governments, changes in the effective property qualification may arise from an increase in monetary wealth rather than an alteration of the census rules. The total valuation should then be compared with earlier years. Cities conducting an annual census should compare it yearly; larger cities should do so every three or five years. If the total is several times greater or smaller than when the qualification was fixed at the previous census, the law should authorize a corresponding increase or reduction in the requirement.

Without such a provision, a rising effective threshold turns constitutional government into oligarchy and narrows oligarchy into family rule. A falling threshold turns constitutional government into democracy, and oligarchy into either constitutional government or democracy.

Democracy, oligarchy, and every other constitution share one principle: no citizen should be allowed to grow disproportionately powerful. It is better to confer honours of moderate size over a long period than to concentrate great honours upon someone within a short time. People are easily corrupted, and not everyone can bear prosperity. If this rule has been ignored, honours conferred all at once should at least be withdrawn gradually. Above all, the laws should prevent anyone from gaining excessive power through friends or money. If someone does acquire it, he and his followers should be sent abroad. Since innovations enter through private ways of life, an office should supervise people whose conduct conflicts with the constitution, whether democratic, oligarchic, or otherwise. For the same reason, any growth in the prosperity of a particular section of the state needs close attention. The remedy is always to entrust administration and public offices to opposing elements—for example, the virtuous and the many, or rich and poor. Another remedy is to bring rich and poor into a single body, or to enlarge the middle class. These measures put an end to revolutions arising from inequality.

Above all, administration and law should make it impossible for magistrates to profit from office. Oligarchies must take particular precautions against this abuse. Exclusion from government does not greatly anger the people; indeed, they generally welcome the time it leaves for their own business. What angers them is the belief that their rulers are stealing public funds. Then they suffer a double grievance, losing both honour and profit. Only when office offers no financial gain can democracy and aristocracy be combined. Both notables and people can then obtain what they want. Everyone is eligible for office, fulfilling democracy's aim, while the notables actually serve as magistrates, fulfilling aristocracy's aim. This arrangement becomes possible when there is no opportunity to make money

from public office. Poor people will not want to take on public office when they cannot gain anything from it. They would prefer to spend that time attending to their own work and private concerns. Wealthy people, who need no money from the public treasury, can undertake the duties. Thus the poor continue their work and become wealthier, while the notables avoid being governed by the lower class.

To prevent the theft of public money, revenue should be handed over before a general assembly of the citizens, and copies of the accounts deposited with the various brotherhoods, companies, and tribes. The law should also reward magistrates known for incorruptibility with honours. In democracies, wealthy people should receive protection. Their property must not be redistributed, and their incomes, which some states gradually take away, should also be secured. It is useful to prevent wealthy citizens from undertaking costly, pointless public services, even voluntarily, such as providing choruses, torch races, and similar spectacles. In oligarchies, by contrast, the poor require particular care and should receive offices that bring financial benefits. A wealthy person who insults them should be punished more severely than someone of their own class committing the same offence. Estates should pass by inheritance rather than gift, and no one should receive more than one inheritance. This will make property holdings more equal and allow more poor people to reach a comfortable condition. Both democracies and oligarchies should also give those with less political power an equal or preferential share in every office except the most important. This means the rich in a democracy and the poor in an oligarchy. The highest offices should be entrusted mainly, or entirely, to the governing class.

Holders of the highest offices need three qualifications. First comes loyalty to the existing constitution; second, the greatest possible administrative ability; third, the virtue and justice appropriate to that constitution. Since justice does not mean the same thing under every government, the relevant quality of justice must differ too. A difficulty arises, however, when no single candidate possesses all these qualities together. We must then decide how to choose between people whose qualifications differ. Suppose an able general is a bad man and hostile to the constitution, while another candidate is loyal and just. Which should we select? Should we not distinguish qualities commonly found from those that are rare? In choosing a general, military skill should count for more than virtue, because few possess military skill while many possess virtue. In an office involving custody or management of property, the opposite rule applies. Such a position requires more than ordinary virtue, while the knowledge it needs is something everyone possesses.

One might ask why a person needs virtue if he already possesses political ability and loyalty. Should those qualities not be enough to make him act for the public benefit? Yet he might possess both and still lack self-control. People know and care about their own interests without always attending to them. Why could they not be equally neglectful of the public interest?

Generally, every legal measure regarded as beneficial to a state also helps preserve it. The great principle of preservation is the one repeatedly mentioned: ensure that loyal citizens outnumber disloyal ones. We must also keep the mean firmly in mind, a principle that is currently being overlooked in the defective forms of government. Many measures that look democratic actually destroy democracies, and many that look oligarchic destroy oligarchies. Their apparent conformity to a party's principles does not make them beneficial.

People who locate all virtue in their own party's principles carry those principles to extremes. They fail to see that a lack of proportion destroys a state. A nose that departs from ideal straightness by being hooked or snub can still have a pleasing shape. But an extreme departure destroys its balance, until excessive length in one direction or deficiency in another makes it cease to be a nose at all. The example of the nose is not exceptional: this principle holds equally for every other member or part of the human body. The rule requiring proportion among parts operates in precisely the same way when we turn from bodies to states. Democracy or oligarchy, although departing from the best constitution, may still provide reasonably good government. Pushing either principle to its extreme first damages government and ultimately eliminates it. Legislators and statesmen must therefore know which democratic measures preserve democracy and which destroy it, and which oligarchic measures preserve or destroy oligarchy. Neither constitution can arise or survive unless it includes both rich and poor. Introducing complete equality of property necessarily changes the state's form. Laws carried to excess destroy one of its constituent elements and thereby destroy the constitution itself. Democracies and oligarchies share a further error. In democracies, when the mass of the people stands above the law,

demagogues continually split the city by quarrelling with the rich. Instead, they should always profess to defend the rich, just as oligarchs should profess to defend the people. The oath taken by oligarchs should likewise express the exact opposite of what they swear at present in some of the cities where they rule. In some cities their oath is: 'I shall oppose the people and devise whatever harm against them I can.' They should express and sincerely hold exactly the contrary intention. Their oath should contain an explicit promise: 'I shall do the people no wrong.'

Of all the measures discussed, the most effective in making constitutions last is education suited to the form of government. Yet this principle is universally neglected today. Even the finest laws, approved by every citizen, are useless unless the young are educated and habituated in the constitution's spirit: democratically where laws are democratic, oligarchically where they are oligarchic. A failure of self-discipline is not confined to individual people. The same failing can belong to states as a whole and affect their public conduct. Education in a constitution's spirit does not mean learning to do whatever oligarchs or democrats enjoy. It means learning the conduct that enables oligarchy or democracy to survive. In our oligarchies, however, the ruling class's sons live luxuriously while the poor's sons are hardened by work and exercise. As a result, the sons of the poor acquire both a stronger inclination towards revolution and a greater capacity to carry it out successfully. Extreme democracies develop a mistaken conception of freedom that conflicts with the state's real interests. Democracy has two defining principles, majority government and freedom. People identify justice with equality, equality with the supremacy of the people's will, and freedom and equality with doing whatever one wants. Everyone in such democracies lives as he pleases, or, in Euripides' phrase, 'as his fancy takes him'. This is entirely mistaken. Living under the constitution's rules should not be regarded as slavery. It is what keeps people safe.

We have now considered generally why states undergo revolution and destruction, and how they can be preserved. We still need to discuss monarchy, examining the causes that bring about its destruction and those that keep it secure. Much of our account of other constitutions applies equally to kingship and tyranny. Kingship resembles aristocracy. Tyranny combines the most extreme forms of oligarchy and democracy, and is therefore especially harmful to its subjects: it joins two bad constitutions and inherits the distortions and errors of both. These two kinds of monarchy differ from their beginnings. The better classes establish a king to protect themselves against the people. They choose him from among themselves because he or his family excels in virtue and virtuous action. A tyrant, by contrast, comes from the people and is chosen to protect them against the notables and prevent their mistreatment.

History shows that nearly every tyrant began as a demagogue, winning popular support by accusing the notables. At least, this was how tyrannies arose once cities had grown powerful. Other tyrannies, dating from an earlier period, began with ambitious kings who wanted to go beyond the limits of their hereditary authority and turn themselves into despotic rulers. Others developed from the chief magistracies: in ancient times, those elected to civil or religious office were given long terms. Others arose because oligarchies placed one person above the highest offices. In any of these situations an ambitious man could easily establish tyranny if he wished, since authority was already in his hands, either as king or as a public official. Pheidon at Argos and several others began as kings and became tyrants. Phalaris and the Ionian tyrants, on the other hand, gained supreme power through high office. Panaetius at Leontini, Cypselus at Corinth, Peisistratus at Athens, Dionysius at Syracuse, and several others who later became tyrants began as leaders of the people.

Thus, as I said, kingship belongs alongside aristocracy. It rests on the merit of the individual or his family, on benefits conferred, or on these claims reinforced by power. Everyone awarded this honour has benefited, or been capable of benefiting, a state or people. Some, such as Codrus, prevented wartime enslavement; others, such as Cyrus, secured their country's freedom. Others settled or acquired territory, as did the Lacedaemonian, Macedonian, and Molossian kings. A king's purpose is to protect the wealthy against unjust

treatment and the people against insult and oppression. A tyrant, as we have often said, cares only about his private purposes, not the public interest. He seeks pleasure, while a king seeks honour. Their desires consequently differ: a tyrant wants wealth; a king wants what brings honour. A king's guards are citizens, whereas a tyrant employs mercenaries.

Tyranny plainly combines all the faults of democracy and oligarchy. Like oligarchy, it aims at wealth, since only wealth can support a tyrant's guards and luxurious living. Both distrust the people and therefore disarm them. Both also mistreat them, drive them out of the city, and scatter them. From democracy, tyrants borrow the practice of attacking notables, destroying them secretly or openly, or exiling them. They are rivals and obstacles to the tyrant's power. They also organize plots, either because they want to rule themselves or because they want to escape subjection. Hence Periander's advice to Thrasybulus to cut off the tallest ears of grain: he meant that citizens who rise above the rest must always be removed. As already indicated, political change therefore begins in monarchies just as in other constitutions. Subjects attack their rulers through fear, contempt, or resentment of unjust treatment. Of the injustices involved, personal insult is the most common; confiscating property is another.

Conspiracies against monarchies, whether kingships or tyrannies, have the same objects in view as those pursued by people who conspire against other forms of government. [Compare III.14, section 7, and III.13, section 16.]

Monarchs possess great wealth and honour, things everyone desires. Attacks sometimes target their lives and sometimes their office. When insult is the motive, the attack targets their lives. Any of the many forms of insult can provoke anger, and angry people generally act from revenge rather than ambition. The attack on the Peisistratidae, for instance, arose from public dishonour to Harmodius' sister and an insult to Harmodius himself. He attacked the tyrant for his sister's sake; Aristogeiton joined him for Harmodius' sake. Periander, tyrant of Ambracia, also faced a conspiracy after he asked a favourite youth, while drinking with him, whether he was not yet pregnant by him. Pausanias attacked Philip because Philip allowed Attalus and his friends to insult him. Derdas attacked Amyntas the Little because Amyntas boasted of having enjoyed his youth. Evagoras of Cyprus was killed by a eunuch avenging an insult: Evagoras' son had carried off his wife. Many conspiracies have begun with rulers' shameful sexual treatment of their subjects. Crataeus' attack on Archelaus was one. He had always hated their relationship. Archelaus promised him one of his two daughters, but gave him neither. Hard pressed in his war with Sirrhas and Arrhibaeus, he married the elder to the king of Elymaea. He married the younger to his own son Amyntas, hoping this would prevent Amyntas from quarrelling with Cleopatra's son. Crataeus used the broken promise as his reason for attacking Archelaus. Even a smaller grievance would have sufficed, since the real source of his hostility

was disgust at his relationship with the king. Hellanocrates of Larissa joined the conspiracy from a similar motive. Archelaus, his lover, had promised to restore him to his country but failed to do so. Hellanocrates concluded that the relationship rested on the abuse of power rather than affection. Parrhon and Heracleides of Aenos killed Cotys to avenge their father. Adamas also rebelled against Cotys, seeking revenge for the outrageous injury of being mutilated by him as a child.

Many people, angered by blows they considered insulting, have killed or tried to kill the officials and royal princes who struck them. At Mitylene, for example, Megacles and his companions attacked and killed the Penthalidae, who were going around

hitting people with clubs. Later, Smerdis killed Penthilus after Penthilus had beaten him and dragged him away from his wife. In the plot against Archelaus, Decamnichus inflamed the assassins' anger and led the attack. He was furious because Archelaus had handed him over to Euripides for a flogging. The poet had taken offence when Decamnichus commented on his bad breath. Many other murders and conspiracies could be cited as examples of the same causes.

Fear has also prompted conspiracies in monarchies, just as in more popular constitutions. Artapanes plotted against Xerxes and killed him, fearing prosecution for hanging Darius without orders. He had acted under the impression that Xerxes would

forget what he had said during a meal and pardon the offence. [An alternative reading of the earlier sentence is: 'Many people, even among those connected with the government or royal family.' It attaches the relevant phrase to the subject.] Contempt is another motive, as in the case of Sardanapalus, who was reportedly seen carding wool among his women. If the storytellers are right, the story concerns him; if not, it may concern someone else. Dion attacked the younger Dionysius because he despised him, saw his subjects held him in equal contempt, and knew he was constantly drunk. Even a tyrant's friends sometimes attack from contempt. His trust makes them despise him and believe they can escape detection. Confidence of success is itself a kind of contempt: attackers discount the danger and prepare to strike because they believe power is already in their hands. Army commanders attack monarchs in this way. Cyrus attacked Astyages because he despised his effeminate life and thought his power exhausted. Seuthes the Thracian likewise plotted against Amadocus, whose general he was.

Several motives sometimes operate together. Mithridates plotted against Ariobarzanes partly from contempt and partly from desire for gain. Bold men whom their rulers have placed in high military commands are particularly likely to attack in the expectation of success. Power gives courage greater confidence, and the combination makes them hope for an easy victory.

Conspiracies inspired by ambition have a different origin. Some people would not risk their lives for any profit or reward, however large, but regard killing a tyrant as an exceptional deed that will bring worldwide fame and honour. They want a name, not a kingdom. People moved by this kind of ambition are nevertheless rarely to be found. Anyone intending to kill a tyrant must be ready to lose his life if he fails. He needs Dion's resolution. When Dion made war on Dionysius, he brought very few soldiers, saying that any degree of success would satisfy him: even death immediately on landing would be welcome. The determination shown in that statement is, however, a state of mind that very few people are capable of attaining. [Compare I.11, section 8.]

Like other constitutions, tyrannies can also be destroyed from outside by a stronger government of the opposite kind. Such a government will clearly want to attack, since their principles conflict, and people do what they want when able. Democracy too is hostile to tyranny, on Hesiod's principle that one potter hates another. They are close relatives, since extreme democracy is tyranny. Both kingship and aristocracy are opposed to tyranny for a different reason: the kind of constitution they embody is fundamentally unlike that of a tyranny. The Lacedaemonians therefore suppressed most tyrannies, as did the Syracusans during their period of good government.

Tyrannies also collapse from internal divisions in the ruling family. Gelo's family provides one example, and Dionysius' a more recent one. In Gelo's case, Hiero's brother Thrasybulus flattered Gelo's son and encouraged his excesses so that he could govern in the young man's name. The family plotted to remove Thrasybulus and preserve the tyranny. But those who joined their conspiracy used the opportunity to expel the entire family. Dionysius was attacked and driven out by his relative Dion with the people's assistance; Dion himself subsequently perished.

Hatred and contempt are the two chief motives for attacking tyrannies. Tyrants inevitably attract hatred, and contempt frequently brings about their destruction as well. Most men who win power manage to keep it; those who inherit it generally lose it almost immediately. A life of luxurious ease makes them contemptible and gives attackers many opportunities. Anger belongs under hatred and has similar effects. Often it is even quicker to strike: angry people attack more impulsively because they refuse to listen to reason. Insult particularly inclines people to surrender to their passions. This brought down the Peisistratidae and many others. Hatred, in comparison with anger, leaves a person more capable of following the guidance of reason and calculation. Anger involves pain, which obstructs reason, whereas hatred does not involve pain.

All the causes described as destroying the final, purest form of oligarchy and the most extreme democracy can therefore be expected to affect tyranny. Indeed, those extreme constitutions are simply tyrannies shared among several people. The rule of a king is affected relatively little by causes operating from outside the state, and for that reason it generally lasts longer; its destruction usually comes from within. This happens in two ways: members of the royal family quarrel, or kings try to govern too much like tyrants, extending their authority beyond the law. Kingships no longer exist today; where monarchy survives, it is tyranny. A king rules willing subjects and possesses supreme authority in all important matters. Today, however, people are more nearly equal, and no one so vastly surpasses the rest as to embody adequately the office's greatness and dignity. People therefore refuse such rule when they can, and immediately regard anyone who gains power by force or deception as a tyrant. Hereditary monarchies face another danger: kings often become objects of contempt, yet mistreat people even though their authority is merely royal, not tyrannical. They are then easily overthrown. A king ceases to be king when his subjects no longer want him; a tyrant remains whether they want him or not.

These and similar causes destroy monarchies. If we ask what preserves monarchies, the general answer is that their preservation results from causes opposite to those responsible for destroying them. Considering each kind separately, kingship survives by limiting its authority. The narrower a king's functions, the longer his power remains intact. Restricted kings behave more moderately and less despotically, and their subjects envy them less. This explains the long survival of kingship among the Molossians. A similar explanation applies to Lacedaemon: kingship there was always divided between two men, and Theopompus later restricted it further in several ways, especially by establishing the ephoralty. Although he reduced the amount of power exercised by the kings, he established the kingly office itself on a foundation that was more likely to endure. In a sense he therefore made it greater, not smaller. The story goes that his wife asked whether he was ashamed to leave his sons less royal authority than he had inherited from his father. He answered, 'Certainly not: the authority I leave them will last longer.' [The translator omits a conjunction, following Bekker's second edition.]

Tyrannies survive by two entirely opposite methods. The first is the traditional approach followed by most tyrants. Periander of Corinth is said to have mastered these practices, and Persian government supplies many similar devices. The old prescriptions for preserving tyranny, so far as it can be preserved, run as follows. The tyrant must cut down those who stand too high and kill spirited men. He must prohibit common meals, clubs, education, and similar institutions, watching everything that might give subjects courage or confidence. Literary gatherings and other meetings for discussion must be forbidden. Every effort must prevent people from becoming acquainted, because familiarity produces mutual trust.
