He must also require inhabitants to appear publicly and spend their time at his gates, so that he knows what they are doing. Constant subjection will teach them humility. [An alternative reading is 'at their doors'.] He should, in brief, follow these practices and others like them that are used by Persians and other barbarian peoples. They differ in their details, but the object at which they all aim is the same. A tyrant must try to learn everything his subjects say and do. He should use spies, like the female informers at Syracuse or the listeners Hiero used to send to gatherings and meeting places. Fear of informers keeps people from speaking freely; if they do speak, they are more easily detected. Another part of the tyrant's method is deliberately to provoke quarrels and stir up disputes: friends against friends, the people against the notables, and wealthy people against one another. Impoverishing subjects supplies money for his guards and keeps people working too hard to conspire. Egypt's pyramids exemplify this policy, as do the Cypselid family's offerings, the Peisistratidae's temple of Olympian Zeus, and Polycrates' great monuments at Samos. All aimed to keep people occupied and poor. Another device habitually employed by tyrants is to impose taxes repeatedly and increase the number of payments required from their subjects. Dionysius at Syracuse arranged matters so that within five years his subjects had paid their entire property into the treasury. The tyrant likes making war, keeping subjects busy and continually in need of a leader. Whereas friends preserve a king's power, a tyrant characteristically distrusts his friends. He knows everyone wishes to overthrow him, and his friends above all have the ability to do it.

Tyrannies also adopt every harmful practice of the latest and worst democracies. They give women power within their households in the hope that they will inform against their husbands, and allow slaves freedom of conduct so that they will betray their masters. For women and slaves do not organize conspiracies to overthrow the rule of tyrants. They naturally favour both tyranny and democracy because they fare well under them. The people themselves wish to act as a monarch, and honour flatterers just as a tyrant does. In democracy the flatterer is the demagogue; the tyrant has his own deferential companions who flatter him.

This explains tyrants' fondness for bad people: they enjoy flattery, and no one with a free person's spirit will stoop to it. Good people love others but flatter no one. Moreover, people of bad character are useful to a ruler who has bad purposes to carry out. As the proverb says, one nail drives out another. A tyrant characteristically dislikes anyone possessing dignity or independence. He wants glory exclusively for himself. Anyone claiming similar dignity or asserting independence intrudes upon his privilege and is hated as a threat to his power. Another characteristic is his preference for foreigners over citizens. He lives with foreigners and invites them to dine, since citizens are his enemies whereas foreigners do not compete with him.

These are the tyrant's characteristics and the devices that preserve his power; no wickedness is beyond him. Everything said can be grouped under three headings corresponding to his three aims. First, he humiliates his subjects, knowing that a person with a crushed spirit will plot against no one. Second, he creates distrust among them. A tyrant cannot be overthrown until people begin trusting one another. This explains his hostility to good people: he regards them as dangerous not only because they reject despotic rule, but because they remain loyal to one another and to others, and refuse to inform against either. Third, he makes his subjects incapable of action. For no one undertakes an action that he believes it is impossible for him to accomplish, and powerless people will not try to overthrow tyranny. The tyrant's policy as a whole can be brought together under these three headings. Everything he plans, and every device he uses to keep his position secure, can be referred to one or another of these aims. He sets his subjects against one another through mistrust, deprives them of the power to act, and breaks their spirit.

That is one way to preserve tyranny. The other follows a different principle, which we can understand by comparing the causes that destroy kingship. Just as making kingship more tyrannical destroys it, making tyranny more like kingship preserves it. The tyrant must nevertheless retain enough power to rule his subjects whether they consent or not. Surrendering that power would mean surrendering his tyranny. With power secured as his foundation, however, he should act, or appear to act, like a king in every other respect. First, he should appear careful with public revenues. He should avoid lavish gifts that anger ordinary people when they see their meagre earnings taken away and squandered on courtesans, foreigners, and performers. He should give a public account of the money that comes into his hands and of the purposes for which he spends it. Some tyrants have already adopted this practice in the conduct of their government. This makes him look like a household manager instead of a tyrant. While he remains master of the city, he need not fear running short of money. When he travels abroad, this policy is far safer than leaving a treasure hoard behind: the garrison remaining in the city will have less reason to attack his authority. An absent tyrant has more to fear from the keepers of his treasure than from the citizens, since the citizens accompany him while the keepers stay behind. Second, he should appear to levy taxes and require public services solely for public purposes. In building a war reserve, he should present himself as custodian and treasurer of money belonging to the public rather than to himself. His manner should be dignified rather than harsh, inspiring respect in those who meet him instead of fear. Yet respect is hard to secure without deserving any. Whatever other virtues he neglects, he should at least maintain the character of a statesman and make people believe he possesses it. Neither he nor his associates should commit even the slightest sexual impropriety towards young subjects of either sex. The women of his household should exercise similar restraint towards other women; women's insolence has destroyed many tyrannies. In pleasure he should behave unlike modern tyrants, who begin their indulgences at dawn, continue all day, and want spectators to admire their supposedly blessed happiness. Here particularly he should practise moderation, or at least avoid displaying his vices publicly. A drunken, sleepy tyrant quickly attracts contempt and attack; a temperate, alert one does not. In nearly every respect, the way he conducts himself should therefore be the very reverse of the behaviour we described earlier when setting out the characteristic practices of tyrants. He should beautify and improve the city as its guardian would. He should also appear especially devoted to worship of the gods. When people consider a ruler religious and reverent, they are less afraid of injustice from him and less willing to plot, believing the gods themselves fight on his side. At the same time, his religious observance must not give the impression of foolishness. The reverence he shows should inspire confidence in his character without appearing irrational to those who see it. He should honour people of merit and convince them that free government would honour them no more highly. When honours are to be awarded, he should distribute them in person, so that they are received directly from him. When punishments are required, however, he should leave their imposition to the appropriate officials and the courts of law. Every monarch takes care not to make one person overwhelmingly great. If one must be elevated, two or more should be raised together so they watch one another closely. Anyone who nevertheless must receive exceptional power should lack a bold spirit, since bold dispositions are the readiest to strike. If someone must lose power, it should be reduced by degrees instead of removed all at once. The tyrant should avoid every outrage, particularly physical violence and sexual misconduct towards the young. He must take special care with people who value honour. Just as lovers of money resent interference with their property, honour-loving and virtuous people resent injury to their honour. He should therefore avoid force altogether, or make it appear paternal correction rather than an attempt to trample on others. His relationships with the young should appear grounded in affection instead of arrogant power. In general, whenever his conduct seems dishonouring, he should offset that appearance by conferring greater honour.

The most dangerous would-be assassins, requiring the closest watch, are those willing to die provided they achieve their purpose. Particular precautions are therefore needed against anyone who believes that he or his relatives have been insulted. People carried away by anger to attack others disregard their own safety. As Heracleitus says, anger is difficult to fight, because a person will pay for revenge with his life.

The inhabitants of a state fall into two classes, those who are poor and those who are wealthy. The tyrant should persuade both that his rule protects them and prevents either from harming the other. He should attach the stronger class to his government. With that advantage, he need neither free slaves nor disarm citizens. Either class, added to his existing force, will make him stronger than those attacking him.

We have now said enough about the particular details of these arrangements. The tyrant's general course is clear: he should appear to his subjects as a household manager and king. Instead of taking their possessions, he should protect them. His way of life should be moderate rather than extravagant. He should associate with the notables and stand as the people's champion. His rule will then necessarily be nobler and happier, because his subjects will be better people whose spirits remain intact. They will not hate him, and he will not fear them. By following this course he will also make his own power more secure and more likely to last. He should be virtuous, or at least partly virtuous; if he must be wicked, let him be only partly so. [The preceding Heracleitus reference is fragment 69 in Mullach's edition.] Nevertheless, oligarchy and tyranny are the shortest-lived constitutions. The longest tyranny was that of Orthagoras and his sons at Sicyon, lasting a hundred years. They treated their subjects moderately, largely respected the laws, and won popular favour through the care they took of the people. Cleisthenes in particular earned respect through military skill. According to the story, he crowned the judge who ruled against him in the games. Some say the seated statue in Sicyon's agora represents that judge. Peisistratus is the subject of a similar account: on one occasion he reportedly allowed himself to be summoned before the Areopagus and tried.

After Orthagoras' dynasty, the longest tyranny was the Cypselidae's at Corinth, lasting seventy-three years and six months. Cypselus ruled for thirty years, Periander for forty-four, and Gordius' son Psammetichus for three.

The continued existence of their rule is explained by causes similar to those already mentioned. Cypselus enjoyed popular support and never maintained a bodyguard throughout his rule. Periander, though a tyrant, was an outstanding soldier. Third in duration was the Peisistratidae's government at Athens, though it was interrupted. Peisistratus was expelled twice, ruling only seventeen of a thirty-three-year period; his sons ruled eighteen, giving thirty-five years altogether. Among other tyrannies, Hiero and Gelo's at Syracuse lasted longest. Even that was brief, no more than eighteen years in all. Gelo ruled seven years and died in his eighth; Hiero ruled ten; Thrasybulus was expelled in his eleventh month. Tyrannies have generally lasted only a short time.
We have now completed our examination of all the causes through which constitutional governments and monarchies are either brought to ruin or preserved in existence.

In Plato's Republic, Socrates discusses revolutions inadequately. He identifies no cause of change peculiar to the first, perfect state. He merely says that nothing endures and that everything changes in a certain cycle. He traces the change to a numerical base in the ratio four to three which, combined with a figure of five, produces two harmonies—meaning when the number belonging to this figure becomes solid. Nature will then, he thinks, produce bad people who resist education. On this last point he may well be right: some people may indeed be incapable of education and virtue. But why should this cause affect his ideal state particularly, rather than every state and indeed everything that comes into being? How does time specifically alter a state, when, as he says, it alters everything? Things that did not begin together also change together. Something created only a day before the cycle ends would change along with it. Further, why should the perfect state become the Spartan constitution? Governments more often change into opposites than into related forms. The objection we have just made does not concern this first transition alone. It applies equally to the other changes of constitution that he describes. He says the Spartan constitution becomes oligarchy, oligarchy democracy, and democracy tyranny. Yet the reverse happens just as often. Democracy is actually more likely to become oligarchy than monarchy. Nor does he say whether tyranny undergoes revolution, what causes such a revolution, or what constitution follows it. He could hardly supply an answer, because no fixed rule exists. His account requires a return to the original, best state to complete the cycle. In fact, tyranny often becomes another tyranny: at Sicyon, Myron's tyranny became Cleisthenes'. It becomes oligarchy, as Antileon's did at Chalcis; democracy, as Gelo's did at Syracuse; or aristocracy, as at Carthage and in the case of Charilaus' tyranny at Lacedaemon. Oligarchy often becomes tyranny, as happened to most ancient Sicilian oligarchies: Leontini's became Panaetius' tyranny, Gela's Cleander's, and Rhegium's Anaxilaus'. These cities are only examples; the same change from oligarchy into tyranny has also taken place in a great many other states. It is also absurd to suppose that a state becomes oligarchic merely because, as Plato says, [An alternative rendering of the earlier question is: 'During the period which, he says, changes everything, things that did not begin together change together.']

[In his second edition, Bekker changes the manuscripts' wording concerning time. The translation in the main text is compatible with either reading; the alternative translation given in the note is compatible only with the manuscript reading.]

the governing class love and make money, rather than because the very rich regard it as unjust for the very poor to share government equally with them. Many oligarchies, moreover, prohibit earning money through trade. Carthage, which is a democracy, imposes no such prohibition, yet its people have never experienced revolution to this day. His description of oligarchy as two cities, one rich and one poor, is also absurd. Why does this description not apply just as much to the Spartan constitution? Or indeed to any other constitution in which all the citizens do not possess equal amounts of property, or in which they are not all equally good people? An oligarchy can become a democracy without anyone growing poorer, provided the poor constitute a majority. A democracy can become an oligarchy if the wealthy are stronger than the people, energetic while the people are indifferent. Again, although revolution has many causes, he mentions only one: citizens become poor through extravagance and debt. This seems to assume that everyone, or most people, was originally wealthy. That is false. Leaders who lose their property certainly become disposed to revolution, but similar losses among other people matter little. Oligarchy does not change into democracy more frequently than into other constitutions. Furthermore, deprivation of political honours, injustice, and insults cause people to revolt and change their government even if they have not squandered their possessions through being allowed to

do whatever they pleased—the extravagance he attributes to excessive freedom. Finally, there is not just one form of oligarchy or one form of democracy: each of them exists in a number of different varieties, yet Socrates describes their revolutions as though each existed in only one form.

chapters.title: Book 6
paragraphs: We have examined the different forms of deliberative, or supreme, authority in states, the various ways of arranging law courts and public offices, and which arrangements suit each kind of government. We have also discussed how states are destroyed or preserved, and the causes that bring about each result.

Democracy, like all other forms of government, exists in several different kinds. It will be useful to assign to each the arrangements that are proper to it and advantageous for it, adding whatever remains to be said about these governments. We must also examine combinations of the arrangements themselves. Such combinations make constitutions overlap, giving aristocracies an oligarchical character and causing constitutional governments to incline towards democracies.

By the combinations still awaiting examination, I mean arrangements such as these: a state may organize its deliberative authority and its election of officials on oligarchical principles, but its courts on aristocratic principles. Alternatively, the courts and deliberative body may be oligarchical while appointments to office are aristocratic. The state's components may also fail to agree in some other way. We have considered which form of democracy suits particular cities, which form of oligarchy suits particular peoples, and which groups are suited to each of the other kinds of government.

We must not merely identify the government best suited to each state. We must also briefly consider how these and other governments can be established. Let us begin with democracy. Doing so will also clarify the opposite form, generally called oligarchy. This inquiry requires us to identify every element and characteristic of democracy, since its different forms arise from combinations of these. There are several varieties, and two causes explain their differences. The first, already mentioned, is variation in population. The common people may consist of farmers, artisans, or labourers. Adding farmers to artisans, or labourers to both, does not simply make a democracy better or worse; it changes its actual character. The second cause remains to be stated. Democracy's various features produce differences according to how they are combined. One democracy has fewer of these features, another more, and another all of them. Knowing them all is useful whether someone wants to establish a new kind of democracy or reform one already in existence. Founders of states try to assemble every element that fits their particular conception of a constitution. As I remarked when discussing how states are destroyed and preserved, this is a mistake. Let us now explain the conditions these states require, their character, and their aims. Freedom is the foundation of a democratic state. People commonly believe that only in such a state can freedom be enjoyed, and they declare it the great purpose of every democracy. One principle of freedom is that everyone should take turns governing and being governed. Democratic justice means numerical equality rather than proportionate equality. Consequently, the majority must be supreme, and whatever it approves must be the final decision and count as just. Every citizen, they say, must have equality. The poor therefore possess more power than the rich in a democracy: there are more of them, and the majority's will is sovereign. This is one feature of freedom that every democrat regards as fundamental to the state. Another is living as one pleases. They call this a free person's privilege, while having to live contrary to one's wishes marks a slave. From this second feature comes the demand that no one should be ruled by anyone, if possible; if that is impossible, people should govern and be governed in turn. It thus converges with the freedom grounded in equality that we identified first.

[An alternative interpretation takes the word for 'rule' in the sense of 'beginning': 'With this as our foundation and starting principle, democracy has the following characteristics.'] Appointments not requiring specialized skill should be made by lot. Offices should require no property qualification, or only a very low one. No one should occupy the same office twice, or at least not often, except in military commands. Every office, or as many as possible, should have a short term. Everyone should participate in judging, or judges chosen from everyone should hear every kind of case, most cases, or at least the greatest and most important: the examination of accounts, constitutional questions, and private contracts. The assembly should have final authority in every matter, or at least in the most important ones; magistrates should have final authority in none, or in very few. A council is the most democratic institution when there is not enough money to pay every citizen. Once citizens are paid, even the council loses its power, because the people draw all business to themselves, as I explained earlier. Another democratic characteristic is payment for public service. When funds permit, everyone receives pay: assembly members, jurors, and magistrates. If there is not enough for everyone, payment goes to courts and regular assemblies, the council, and magistrates, or at least to those magistrates obliged to dine together. Oligarchy is marked by birth, wealth, and education. Democracy seems marked by their opposites: low birth, poverty, and humble occupations. A further characteristic is the absence of permanent magistracies. If any survive from an earlier constitutional change, they should be deprived of power, and their holders selected by lot instead of elected by vote. These features occur in all democracies. But democracy and the demos in their fullest form rest on the accepted democratic conception of justice: every person counts equally. Equality means that the rich should have no greater share in government than the poor, nor govern alone. Instead, everyone should exercise an equal share of rule according to their numbers. This is how people expect to secure equality and freedom in their state.

The next question we must answer is how this equality is to be brought about in practice. Should the property qualification be apportioned so that five hundred wealthy people balance one thousand poor people, and should we give the thousand poor people as much power as the five hundred rich people? Or, keeping this ratio, should we select equal numbers from each group and give them control of elections and courts? Which constitution is more just by democratic standards: this arrangement or one based solely on numbers? Democrats identify justice with the majority's agreement, oligarchs with the agreement of the wealthy. For oligarchs, the amount of property should determine the decision. Both principles contain inequality and injustice. If justice is the will of the few, then one person possessing more wealth than all the other members of his class combined should, by oligarchical reasoning, have sole authority. But that would be tyranny. If justice is the majority's will, on the other hand, the majority will, as I said earlier, unjustly seize the property of the wealthy minority. To

find a principle of equality acceptable to both, we must investigate what each means by justice. Both agree that whatever a majority of citizens decides should count as law. Let us grant that, but with a qualification. Since the state contains two classes, rich and poor, the law should be what both classes, or the greater part of each, approve. If they disagree, the decision should follow the majority understood in terms of the larger property qualification. Suppose there are ten rich people and twenty poor people. Six of the rich favour a proposal and fifteen of the poor oppose it; the remaining four rich people join the poor opponents, and the remaining five poor people join the rich supporters. In that case, add together the property qualifications on each side, and let the side with the greater total prevail. If the totals are equal, the difficulty is no worse than when an assembly or court is evenly divided today and resorts to drawing lots or some similar device. However hard it may be in theory to determine justice and equality, it is far harder in practice to persuade those capable of taking more than their share to restrain themselves. The weak continually ask for justice and equality, while the strong disregard both. As we said in the earlier discussion, the first of the four types of democracy is the best and also the oldest. Here I classify them according to the natural divisions among their inhabitants. An agricultural population provides democracy's best material. It is easy to establish democracy where most people live by farming or raising livestock. Their poverty leaves them little leisure, so they seldom attend the assembly. Because they lack life's necessities, they work continually and do not covet others' property. Indeed, they prefer their work to the responsibilities of government or office, where those positions offer no large financial rewards. Most people desire profit more than honour. This is proved by their patient endurance of ancient tyrannies, as they still endure oligarchies, provided they can work and keep their property. Some quickly become rich, and the others are comfortably enough situated. They also have the power to elect magistrates and demand an account of their conduct, which satisfies whatever ambition they possess. In some democracies they do not even participate directly in every appointment, but act through representatives selected in rotation from the whole population, as at Mantinea. Even there, the many remain satisfied if they retain deliberative authority. This arrangement, too, can be considered democratic, as it was at Mantinea. It is therefore both useful and customary in such a democracy for everyone to elect officeholders, scrutinize their conduct, and serve in the courts. The major offices, however, should be filled by election from people with a property qualification, with higher offices requiring greater qualifications. Alternatively, if no offices require property, those with exceptional ability should be appointed. Citizens are certain to be well governed under this arrangement: the best people will always occupy the offices, since the people are willing to elect them and do not resent [compare IV.13, section 8, and II.12, section 5]

the good. Good men and notable citizens will then be satisfied, because they will not be governed by their inferiors. Those elected will govern justly because others can hold them accountable. Everyone should answer to someone else, and no one should be permitted to act entirely as he pleases. Complete freedom leaves nothing to restrain the evil present in every person. Accountability secures the greatest benefit a state can have: the right people govern, they are prevented from acting wrongly, and the people receive their due. Clearly this is the best kind of democracy, precisely because its people belong to a particular class. Many states had excellent ancient laws designed to make their people farmers. They either limited the amount of land any person could own, or required holdings above that amount to lie beyond a specified distance from the town or acropolis.

In earlier times, many states had a law forbidding anyone to sell the allotment of land originally assigned to him. A similar law attributed to Oxylus required a certain portion of every person's property to remain free from loans secured against it. The Aphytaeans' law would be a useful corrective to the evil we are discussing. Although their population is large and their land limited, they are all farmers. Their property is assessed in the census not as entire estates, but in units small enough to allow even poor people to possess more than the amount required for qualification.

A pastoral population living from its flocks is the next best after a farming population, and resembles it in many respects. [Alternative reading of the preceding passage: 'so that the poor people's qualification may exceed the rich people's'.] Such people are better prepared for war than any others, physically sturdy and accustomed to sleeping outdoors. The populations of other democracies are far inferior because their lives are inferior. Their occupations, whether as artisans, traders, or labourers, leave no room for moral excellence. They can also attend the assembly easily, since they are constantly moving around the city and the agora. Farmers, by contrast, live scattered across the countryside; they do not meet one another or feel the same need to assemble. Where a state's territory reaches far beyond the city, establishing an excellent democracy or constitutional government is easy, since people must settle in the country. Even where there is an urban population, the assembly should not meet when country people cannot attend. We have thus explained the organization of the first and best democracy. The inferior forms plainly depart from it in a regular sequence, with the population excluded at each stage belonging to a lower kind.

The final kind of democracy is the one in which everyone participates on equal terms. Not every state can sustain this form, and it will not last long unless it is properly regulated by laws and established customs. We have already examined fairly fully the general causes that destroy this and other governments. To establish such a democracy and strengthen the people, its leaders habitually admit as many as possible to citizenship. They include not only legitimate children, but illegitimate ones and people with just one citizen parent, whether father or mother. A democracy of this kind welcomes all such additions. Demagogues follow this course. The proper course, however, is to stop adding citizens once the common people outnumber the notables or the middle class, and go no further. [Compare III.5, section 7.] Beyond that point the state becomes disorderly, and notable citizens become agitated and impatient with democracy, as happened in the revolt at Cyrene. A small evil passes unnoticed; once it grows, it becomes conspicuous.

The extreme form of democracy benefits from measures like those Cleisthenes enacted when he wanted to enlarge democratic power at Athens, or those introduced by the founders of popular government at Cyrene. New tribes and brotherhoods should be established. The private religious rites of families should be restricted and transformed into public observances. In short, every available device should be adopted to mingle citizens with one another and break down their old connections.

The policies of tyrants also all seem democratic. Examples include the freedom allowed to slaves, which may be advantageous up to a point; similar freedom for women and children; and permission for everyone to live as he pleases. Such a government will attract many supporters, because most people prefer a disorderly life to a disciplined one.

For a legislator, or anyone seeking to create a democracy, establishing it is neither the sole nor the chief task. Any state, however badly constituted, can survive for one, two, or three days. Preserving it is far more difficult. The legislator should therefore lay secure foundations, following the principles already stated concerning the preservation and destruction of states. He must guard against destructive forces and make written or unwritten laws embodying every means of preservation. He should regard as truly democratic or oligarchical not the measure that maximizes democracy or oligarchy, but the one that enables it to last longest. Today's demagogues frequently arrange confiscations through the courts to gratify the people. Those concerned for the state's welfare should oppose them. They should require confiscated property paid into the treasury to become sacred property rather than public property. Wrongdoers would remain equally afraid, since punishment would be unchanged. But the people would gain nothing and would be less eager to convict defendants. Public prosecutions should also be kept as few as possible, and those bringing unfounded charges should face severe penalties. Such accusations are usually directed against notable citizens, not members of the popular party. Yet all citizens ought to feel equally attached to the state, or at least ought not to regard their governors as enemies.

In the final and worst democracy, citizens are so numerous that assembling them without payment is difficult. Where there is no revenue, paying them burdens the notables severely. The money must come from property taxes, confiscations, and corruption in the courts—practices that have already destroyed many democracies. Where revenue is lacking, therefore, the government should hold few assemblies. Courts should contain many jurors but sit for only a few days. This has two advantages. First, the rich will not fear the cost, even if they receive nothing while poor jurors are paid. Second, cases will be judged better. Wealthy people dislike prolonged absence from their affairs but are willing to spend a few days in court. [Compare V.11, sections 2–3, and section 5.] Where revenue exists, demagogues should not be allowed to distribute every surplus as they habitually do. The poor are continually receiving such payments and are continually in need of still more. Assistance given in this fashion is like water poured into a barrel that leaks. A genuine friend of the people must nevertheless prevent them from becoming excessively poor, because extreme poverty degrades democracy. Measures should also be taken that give them prosperity which will endure, rather than merely momentary relief. Since every class benefits from this, public revenues should be saved up and distributed to the poor in amounts sufficient, if possible, to buy a small farm, or at least to begin trading or farming. If everyone cannot receive this assistance at once, distribute it in rotation by tribes or other divisions. Meanwhile, the rich should pay for poor citizens to attend necessary assemblies and, in return, be excused unnecessary public services. Governing in this spirit, the Carthaginians retain popular affection. Periodically they send some of the people to dependent towns, where they become wealthy. A generous and sensible nobility could also divide the poor among themselves and supply them with the means to work. Tarentum offers another example worth following: by sharing the use of their property with the poor, its people earn their goodwill. They also divide their offices into two groups, choosing half by vote and half by lot. Selection by lot gives the people participation; election by vote improves administration. Dividing the same offices between two sets of magistrates, one elected and the other selected by lot, could produce a similar result.

We have said enough about how democracies should be organized. These arguments also make it easy to see how oligarchies should be constituted. We must work out each oligarchy by reasoning from its opposite, considering its structure in relation to the corresponding form of democracy.

The first and most balanced oligarchy approaches constitutional government. It should have two property qualifications, one high and one low. The lower should admit people to lesser but necessary offices, and the higher to the more important offices. Anyone who attains the required qualification should receive citizenship. Those admitted must be of such a character that the governing body as a whole is stronger than those excluded, and new citizens should always come from the better part of the people. Restricting this principle somewhat produces another oligarchy. Continuing the restriction brings us finally to the most exclusive and tyrannical form, corresponding to extreme democracy. As the worst oligarchy, it demands care proportionate to its badness. Healthy bodies and ships with adequate crews can survive many accidents. Sickly bodies and rotten, poorly crewed ships are destroyed by the slightest mistake. So too the worst governments require the greatest vigilance. Large populations generally preserve democracies, since numbers serve democracy in place of justice based on proportion. Oligarchy's preservation clearly rests on the opposite principle, good order. [Textual note: reading 'of the same office' with Bekker's second edition.] Just as the common people fall into four chief groups—farmers, artisans, retailers, and labourers—military forces have four branches: cavalry, heavy infantry, light troops, and the navy. Where the land suits cavalry, a powerful oligarchy is likely to arise. The inhabitants' safety depends on that force, and only wealthy people can afford horses. The second oligarchical form prevails where heavy infantry is important, because this service is more suitable for the rich than the poor. Light troops and naval forces, however, are wholly democratic. Nowadays their numbers are so great that, when the parties clash, they often defeat the oligarchs. Generals' practice suggests a remedy: they combine an appropriate contingent of light troops with cavalry and heavy infantry. Light arms explain how the poor defeat the rich in civil struggles; they give an advantage against cavalry and heavily armed soldiers. An oligarchy recruiting such troops from the lower classes raises a force against itself. Citizens differ in age, however, so fathers should have their sons trained while young in the quick movements of light troops. Some should then be selected when grown to serve as actual light-armed soldiers. Oligarchy must also grant the people a share in government. As already suggested, it can admit those with the required property; or, following Thebes, those who have avoided lowly occupations for a prescribed number of years; or, following Massalia, men chosen for their merit, whether previously citizens or not. The highest magistracies, properly reserved for the governing body, should carry expensive obligations. The people will then have no wish to occupy them and will not resent their rulers' privileges when they see the heavy price paid for that dignity. On entering office, magistrates should also make splendid sacrifices or erect a public building. The people, who share in the feasts and enjoy seeing their city adorned with votive offerings and buildings, will then have no wish to change the government. The notables, meanwhile, will possess lasting monuments to their generosity. Our modern oligarchs behave quite differently. They desire profit as eagerly as honour, and their oligarchies could aptly be called petty democracies. Let this suffice on the organization of democracies and oligarchies.

We turn next to the proper distribution of offices: how many there should be, what kind they should be, and what duties they should perform. We have already touched on these questions. No state can exist without necessary offices, or be well governed without offices that maintain harmony and order. As we have said, a small state does not need many, whereas a larger state needs more. We must consider carefully which functions can properly be combined and which should remain separate. The market requires a magistrate to oversee contracts and preserve order. Every state necessarily has buyers and sellers supplying one another's needs. This is the most direct means of making a state self-sufficient and fulfilling the purpose for which people unite in a state. A second, similar office supervises and improves public and private buildings, maintains and repairs houses and roads, prevents boundary disputes, and deals with related matters.

This office is usually called that of City-warden. It has several branches, divided among different people in larger towns. One might oversee the walls, another the fountains, and another the harbours. Another equally necessary, similar office manages the same matters outside the walls and in the countryside. Its holders are called Wardens of the country or Inspectors of the woods. Beyond these three comes a fourth office, the tax receivers. They administer the revenue and allocate it among the different departments. They are called Receivers or

Treasurers. Another official records private contracts, court decisions, public accusations, and all preliminary proceedings. This office too is sometimes divided into branches, with one official supervising all the others. Its holders have names such as Recorders, Sacred Recorders, and Presidents.

Next comes an office with duties that are at once among the most necessary and the most difficult. It is responsible for carrying out punishments, collecting fines from those whose names are publicly displayed in the registers, and keeping prisoners in custody. The difficulty arises from the hatred attached to these duties. No one will accept the office unless there is a prospect of considerable profit, and even someone who accepts it is reluctant to carry out the law. Yet the office is indispensable. Judicial decisions serve no purpose unless they take effect. If society cannot exist without such decisions, it cannot exist without their enforcement either. Since this task is so unpopular, it should be divided among several people drawn from different courts, rather than given to one person alone. Similarly, the work of displaying the names of people registered as debtors to the state should be spread among different officials. Some sentences should be carried out by officers whose duties also include other functions. New officials should exact penalties for new offences. In cases that are not new, the authority that imposes the sentence should differ from the authority that collects the penalty. City-wardens, for instance, should collect fines imposed by the wardens of the agora, while other officials should collect the fines imposed by city-wardens. Penalties are more likely to be collected when collecting them attracts less resentment. Those who both pronounce judgment and enforce it incur double hatred. If the same judges always execute the sentences they pronounce, they become enemies of everyone.

In many places, keeping prisoners and enforcing sentences are assigned to different magistracies; Athens provides the example of 'the Eleven'. It is advisable to separate prison custody and devise some means of reducing its unpopularity. The task of keeping prisoners in custody is quite as necessary as the task of carrying out sentences. Yet good men do everything possible to avoid it, while worthless men cannot safely be trusted with it: they need guarding themselves and are unfit to guard others. The duty should therefore not belong to one specially appointed or permanent official. Where young men are organized into a corps or guard, they should undertake it, with different magistrates taking responsibility in rotation.

These are the indispensable offices and must be placed first in our account. Next are others equally necessary but higher in rank, demanding considerable experience and trustworthiness. Among them are the offices entrusted with the protection of the city and with the performance of other military duties. In peace as well as war, their holders must defend walls and gates, muster citizens, and arrange them in formation. Some states have many such offices, others only a few; small states manage with one. Their holders are called generals or commanders. Where a state has cavalry, light infantry, archers, or a navy, each branch sometimes has its own officers, called admirals, cavalry generals, or infantry generals. Below them are naval captains, military captains, and cavalry captains, with further officers under their command. All these fall within the military department. Let this be enough about military command.

Since many, if not all, of these officials deal with public money, another office must examine and audit their work, without undertaking any other duties. Its holders bear various titles: Scrutineers, Auditors,

Accountants, and Controllers. Beyond all these stands an office with supreme authority over them. It is often responsible both for introducing measures and for confirming them; in a democracy it presides over the assembly. The authority that summons the people must necessarily stand at the head of the state. In some places its members are called 'probuli', because they deliberate beforehand; in democracies they are more commonly called 'councillors'. These are the principal political offices.

A further group of officials maintains religion. Priests and guardians oversee the preservation and repair of the gods' temples and attend to other religious matters. Small communities may need only one such office. Larger ones have many in addition to priests, including supervisors of sacrifices, keepers of shrines, and treasurers of sacred revenues. Closely related are officials appointed to perform public sacrifices, except those the law assigns specifically to priests. These officials take their dignity from the city's public hearth. Their titles vary: sometimes archons, sometimes kings, and sometimes prytanes.

These, then, are the necessary offices of a state, and we may summarize their responsibilities in the following way. They concern religion, warfare, public income and expenditure, the market, the city, harbours, and the countryside; the law courts, records of contracts, enforcement of sentences, prison custody, and the auditing and examination of magistrates' accounts. Finally, some preside over the state's public deliberations. Other offices characterize states that are peaceful and prosperous while attentive to good order. These include guardians of women, guardians of laws, guardians of children, and directors of physical training, as well as supervisors of athletic and Dionysiac competitions and similar public spectacles. Some are plainly undemocratic. Guardians of women and children are examples, since poor people have no slaves and must use their wives and children as servants. [Compare IV.15, section 11, and III.14, section 14.] Lastly, the highest elective offices in states take three forms: guardians of the law, probuli, and councillors. Guardians of the law belong to aristocracy, probuli to oligarchy, and a council to democracy. Let this be enough of our discussion of the several different kinds of public office.

chapters.title: Book 7
paragraphs: To investigate the best state properly, we must first determine which kind of life is most desirable for human beings to lead. While that remains unsettled, the best constitution remains uncertain too. In the natural course of things, people governed as well as their circumstances permit should be expected to live best. We must therefore establish, first, which life is most desirable in general, and then whether the same life is best for a whole state and for an individual.

Let us assume that our discussions intended for a general audience have sufficiently considered the best life, and simply repeat their conclusions here. No one will dispute dividing goods into three classes: external goods, goods of the body, and goods of the soul. Nor will anyone deny that happiness requires all three. No one would call a man happy if he possessed no courage, temperance, justice, or practical wisdom; if every insect fluttering past frightened him; if he would commit any crime, however great, to satisfy his appetite for food or drink; if he would betray his dearest friend for half a farthing; and if his understanding were as weak and mistaken as a child's or a madman's. Everyone accepts these propositions as soon as they are stated, but people

disagree about how much of each good we should desire and how their values compare. Some regard a very modest amount of virtue as sufficient, while placing no limit on their appetite for wealth, possessions, political power, reputation, and similar advantages.

Our reply to those who hold this opinion is to appeal to the facts that experience places before us. These readily show that people acquire and preserve external goods through virtue, rather than acquiring and preserving virtue through external goods. Happiness, whether it consists in pleasure, virtue, or both, is more often found among those whose minds and characters are highly developed and whose external possessions are moderate than among those with uselessly abundant possessions but deficient higher qualities. This conclusion is not merely a report of what we observe in experience. Anyone who reflects on the matter will readily see that it also agrees with the argument of reason. The quantity of external goods that can serve a purpose has a limit, just as the usefulness of any other instrument has a limit. Anything useful becomes harmful, or at least useless to its owner, when possessed in excess. Goods of the soul, however, become more beneficial the greater they are, if we may properly call them useful as well as noble. No proof is needed that the relative value of the best conditions of two things corresponds to the difference in excellence between their natures. If the soul is nobler than property or body, both absolutely and for us, its best condition must be correspondingly superior to theirs. Moreover, bodily and external goods are desirable for the soul's sake. A wise person chooses them to serve the soul, rather than choosing the soul to serve them.

Let us therefore agree that each person's happiness corresponds to his virtue and wisdom and to his virtuous and wise activity. God bears witness to this: his happiness and blessedness come not from external possessions but from himself and his own nature. This necessarily distinguishes good fortune from happiness. External advantages may arrive on their own, through chance; but no one becomes a just or temperate person by chance, or acquires either quality through an accidental turn of fortune. A similar argument shows that the happy state is the morally best state, acting rightly. A state cannot act rightly without performing right actions, and neither states nor individuals can do that without virtue and wisdom. The courage, justice, and wisdom of a state consequently have the same nature and form as the qualities that make their individual possessor just, wise, or temperate.

This will suffice as an introduction. I could not avoid touching on these questions, but neither could I examine here every argument bearing on them. A fuller treatment must be reserved for another discussion.

We may therefore assume that the best life, for individuals and states alike, is a virtuous life supplied with enough external goods to perform good actions. We shall pass over anyone disputing this claim for the purposes of the present treatise and examine their objections later.

We must still ask whether the happiness of a person differs from that of a state. Once again, this question admits of no doubt. No one maintains that happiness has one character for the individual and another character for the state. People who identify personal well-being with wealth also think riches make an entire state happy. Those who admire a tyrant's life most consider the happiest city the one ruling the greatest number of others. Those who praise individual virtue likewise say that a city's happiness grows with its virtue. At this point two distinct questions present themselves for our consideration, and we need to keep both of them in view. First, is the more desirable life that of a citizen participating in a state, or that of someone living outside political ties? Second, what constitution or condition of a state is best, whether political rights belong to everyone or only a majority? Political thought properly concerns the state's good rather than the individual's, and our inquiry is political. The second question will therefore be our main concern; the first has a secondary place.

The best constitution is plainly the one in which every person, whoever he is, can act as well as possible and live happily. Yet even people agreeing that virtue offers the most desirable life dispute whether practical and political activity is preferable to a life independent of external goods. I mean contemplation, which some call the only life worthy of a philosopher. Both the philosopher's life and the statesman's have attracted those most devoted to virtue, in our time and in earlier ages. It is no small matter to decide which of these two lives is better and more worthy of choice. A person who exercises wisdom, just like a state that exercises wisdom, must necessarily arrange the whole course of life with reference to the best end that can be pursued. Some consider despotic authority over others the greatest injustice, and constitutional authority, even if just, a serious obstacle to personal well-being. Others take a position directly opposed to this. They maintain that a life of practical action and participation in politics is the true life for a human being. In their view there is no virtue whose exercise is less open to statesmen and to those who govern than it is to people living as private individuals. Still others identify happiness solely with arbitrary, tyrannical power. In some states, indeed, the entire purpose of legislation is to secure despotic authority over neighbouring peoples. Although the laws in most cities are generally disordered, whatever purpose they possess tends towards maintaining power. At Lacedaemon and Crete, for example, education and most legislation aim at warfare. Every people capable of pursuing its ambition honours military strength, including Scythians, Persians, Thracians, and Celts. Some even have laws encouraging martial virtues. At Carthage, we are told, a man may wear as many armlets as the campaigns he has served. Macedonia once required anyone who had never killed an enemy to wear a halter. Among the Scythians, a man who had killed no enemy could not drink from the cup passed around at a certain feast. Among the warlike Iberians, spits planted around a tomb record the number of enemies its occupant killed. Other nations have numerous

similar practices, some established by law and others by custom. [An alternative reading, inserting 'and' before the relevant word, apparently as in the old translation, makes the preceding statement refer to the entire purpose of both constitution and laws.] Yet reflection makes it seem very strange that a statesman should continually seek ways to dominate others and rule them tyrannically, willing or unwilling. How could something unlawful belong to the legislator's or statesman's proper task? Governing without regard for justice is certainly unlawful: possessing power need not mean possessing right. Other arts and sciences offer no parallel. A physician is not expected to persuade or coerce his patients, nor a pilot his passengers. Nevertheless, many treat despotism as a genuine political constitution. They unashamedly do to others what they call unjust and harmful when done to themselves. They demand justice for themselves but disregard it for others. This is unreasonable, unless one group is naturally fitted to command and the other to serve. Even then, the right extends only over those intended for subjection, not over every fellow human being. Similarly, we should not hunt human beings for food or sacrifice, but only creatures suited to those purposes, namely edible wild animals. Moreover, an isolated city could surely be happy. Let us suppose it well governed, as an isolated city quite possibly could be, with sound administration and good laws. Such a city would not be organized for war or conquering enemies; those purposes must be excluded. Clearly, then, warfare, though generally honourable, is a means rather than the supreme end. A good lawgiver should ask how states, peoples, and communities can share in the good life and in the happiness attainable to them. The laws he establishes will not be identical in every case; the circumstances of different communities call for different provisions. Where neighbours exist, he must consider their character and the duties owed to each. The question of the precise end towards which the best constitution should be directed can appropriately be reserved for further consideration later in our inquiry.

Let us address those who agree that virtue offers the best life but disagree about how to practise it. Some renounce political authority and distinguish the free person's life from the statesman's, calling the former best. Others prefer the statesman's life, reasoning that someone who does nothing cannot do well and that virtuous activity constitutes happiness. To the supporters of each of these views we must give the same answer: part of what you say is correct, but another part of it is mistaken. Those in the first group are right to maintain that the life of a free person is better than the life of a despot. Using a slave simply as a slave, or issuing orders concerning necessities, contains nothing grand or noble. But not every kind of government resembles a master's despotic authority over slaves. Governing free people differs from governing slaves as natural freedom differs from natural slavery, a distinction sufficiently discussed at this treatise's beginning. It is equally mistaken to prefer inactivity to action. Happiness is activity, and the actions of just and wise people bring many noble things into being.

Someone accepting these premises might still argue that supreme authority is best because it permits the greatest number of actions that are noble and worthy of choice. A capable ruler should then surrender nothing to his neighbour, but instead remove the neighbour's power. A father should take no account of his son, a son no account of his father, and a friend no account of his friend. None should give a thought to the claims of another when weighed against this supposedly higher aim. What is best is most desirable, and doing well is best. That argument would have some force if robbers and plunderers could attain the highest good. They cannot, so the conclusion is false. A ruler's actions cannot be truly honourable unless his superiority over others resembles a husband's over his wife, a father's over his children, or a master's over his slaves. Someone violating law therefore cannot recover through any subsequent success, however great, what he has lost by abandoning virtue. Equals justly receive equal shares in what is honourable and just. Giving unequal treatment to equals, or unlike treatment to those alike, contradicts nature, and nothing contrary to nature is good. We should therefore follow and obey someone superior in virtue and in the capacity for the best actions. But virtue alone is insufficient: he must also possess the capacity to act.

If our account is correct and happiness consists in virtuous activity, an active life is best both for individuals and for the city as a whole. Activity need not, however, involve relations with other people, as some assume. Nor should we call only thinking directed towards practical results active. Independent thinking and contemplation, complete in themselves, have an even stronger claim, since virtuous activity, and therefore action, is itself an end. Even when action does produce an outward result, it is the intelligence directing and organizing it that most truly deserves to be called active. Similarly, states isolated from others and choosing to live alone need not be inactive. Activity can occur among their constituent parts, with citizens acting upon one another in many ways. The same principle holds for each individual. Otherwise God and the universe, whose activities extend no further than their own energies, would fall far short of perfection. Thus the same life is best for each person, for states, and for humanity collectively.

So much for our introduction. Having examined other constitutions, we must now first establish the conditions required by the ideal or perfect state. It cannot exist without adequate means of life. We must therefore assume many conditions that are imaginary, but none that is impossible. Among the things we must assume are a body of citizens of a particular size, a country in which that body of citizens can live, and the other resources of the same kind. A weaver, shipbuilder, or other craftsman needs material suited to his work, and the better prepared that material is, the better his achievement. The statesman and legislator likewise require material appropriate to their task.

The first material the statesman needs is population. [Compare section 10 and II.6, section 7.] He must ask how many citizens the state should contain and what sort of people they should be. After this he must consider the extent of the country they will inhabit and the character of that country. Most people think a happy state must be large, yet even if they are right, they misunderstand what makes a state large or small. They judge a city's size by counting inhabitants rather than assessing its capacity. Like an individual, a city has a task, and the greatest city is the one best equipped to perform it. In the same sense Hippocrates may be greater as a physician, though not as a man in physical size, than someone taller. Even if we measure greatness numerically, we should not count everyone. Cities necessarily contain many slaves, temporary residents, and foreigners. We should count only actual members of the state, its essential parts. Their numbers indicate its greatness. A city with many artisans but few soldiers cannot be great: greatness and mere populousness are different. Experience also shows that an excessively populous city is seldom, if ever, well governed. Every city renowned for good government limits its population. We need not rely upon observation alone to reach this conclusion. If we approach the matter through an argument grounded in reason, we shall arrive at just the same result. Law is order, and good law is good order. An immense multitude cannot readily be orderly. Ordering the unlimited requires divine power, like the power that holds the universe together. Beauty is realized through number and magnitude, so a state combining magnitude with order must be the most beautiful. A state therefore has a limit to its proper size. The same is true of other things: a plant, an animal, or an implement cannot be increased or diminished without regard to its nature. If too large or too small, they cannot retain their natural capacity: they lose their nature altogether or become defective. A ship a span long is no ship, nor is one a quarter of a mile long. Between these extremes a vessel may still be a ship yet be too large or small to sail well. Likewise, a state with too few members cannot achieve proper self-sufficiency. One with too many may supply every material necessity but is a nation rather than a state, almost incapable of constitutional government. Who could command such a multitude, or serve as its herald without Stentor's voice?

A state first exists when its population is sufficient for a good life in political community. It may exceed that number somewhat, but, as I said, a limit remains necessary. We can readily discover what that limit should be by considering the experience of political life. Governors and governed each have duties, and the ruler's particular tasks are commanding and judging. To judge cases and distribute offices according to merit, citizens must know one another's characters. Without that knowledge, both appointments and judicial decisions go wrong. Where the population is extremely large, it is plain that appointments to office and the settlement of legal disputes are made at random. Yet that is clearly not the way either kind of decision ought to be made. Foreigners and metics also easily acquire citizenship unnoticed in an overcrowded state: who could identify them? The best population limit is therefore the greatest number sufficient for life's purposes that can still be surveyed as a whole. [Compare section 7.] Let this suffice concerning a city's size.

The same general principle applies to territory. Everyone would praise the state that is most completely self-sufficient. Such a state produces everything it needs, since sufficiency means possessing everything necessary and lacking nothing. Its area and extent should let its inhabitants enjoy leisure while living temperately and generously. We shall examine this proposed limit more closely later, when considering the proper use of wealth and property. The right use of property and wealth is a subject on which there is considerable disagreement. People have a tendency to rush headlong towards one of two opposite extremes, some falling into meanness and others into an extravagant and luxurious way of life.

The general character of the territory that a state requires is not difficult to establish, although certain points call for military expertise. Military authorities advise that enemies should find access difficult, and that the location should be advantageous in relation to both land and sea. One principle, then, is that it should provide a convenient centre from which to defend the entire country. Another is that it should facilitate receiving agricultural produce and bringing in timber and other necessary products.

The question whether communication with the sea helps or harms a state that is otherwise well organized has often been raised and discussed. One argument against it is that admitting strangers who have grown up under a different set of laws, together with the resulting increase in population, will work against the maintenance of good order. Maritime communities always attract merchants coming and going, and intercourse by sea, they say, harms government. Apart from these objections, a city and its territory clearly benefit from sea access for both security and necessary supplies. Defenders resisting an enemy should be able to receive assistance easily by land and sea. Even if they cannot attack on both at once, possessing both routes makes it easier to harm their attackers through one. Furthermore, they must import what their own country lacks and export what it produces in excess. The purpose of a city in serving as a market should be to supply its own needs. It should not undertake this role simply to provide a marketplace for other communities.

States that turn themselves into markets for the world do so for revenue. If a state should not pursue that sort of profit, it should not maintain such an emporium. Today, many cities and countries have conveniently located dockyards and harbours outside the city but not too far away. Walls and similar fortifications keep them under the city's control. Such cities plainly enjoy the benefits of their ports. Laws can readily guard against the possible harms by specifying who may have dealings with whom, and who may not.

There is no room for doubt that a city benefits from possessing a naval force of moderate size. Citizens need one for their own purposes, and should also be able, in certain circumstances, to inspire fear in neighbouring states. When necessary, they should be capable of assisting their neighbours by sea as well as by land. [Compare Plato, Laws IV, 704 and following.]

How numerous the ships of this fleet should be, and how great its overall strength, must be determined in relation to the particular character of the state. If the state is intended to lead in political affairs, its naval strength should match the scale of its undertakings. Its citizen population need not increase greatly, since sailors need not be citizens. The marines exercising command and control will be free men belonging also to the infantry. Where Perioeci and farmers form a dense population, sailors will always be more than plentiful. Present examples confirm this. Heraclea, though small compared with many cities, can crew a substantial fleet. These are our conclusions about territory, harbours, towns, connection with the sea, and naval power.

We have now considered the number of citizens required. The next step is to examine what their character ought to be and what natural qualities they should possess. Anyone looking at the more distinguished Hellenic states and at the distribution of peoples throughout the inhabited world can readily understand this subject. Peoples of cold regions and northern Europe have abundant spirit but insufficient intelligence and skill. They retain freedom, yet lack political organization and cannot govern others. Asian peoples are intelligent and inventive but deficient in spirit, and consequently remain in subjection and slavery. The Hellenic people occupies the geographical middle and has an intermediate character, combining spirit with intelligence. It therefore remains free, possesses the best government, and could rule the world if united into one state. Differences of the same kind are also found within Hellas itself when we compare the several tribes that make up the Hellenic people. Some of these tribes have a one-sided character: they possess intelligence without courage, or courage without intelligence. In others, by contrast, the two qualities come together in a fortunate combination. Clearly, the people a legislator can most readily guide towards virtue should be both intelligent and courageous. Some, like Plato, say guardians should treat acquaintances kindly and strangers fiercely. Spirit is the part of the soul that produces friendship and affection. When we think ourselves despised, our spirit is particularly stirred against friends and acquaintances rather than strangers. Archilochus therefore naturally addresses his soul while complaining of his friends:

'Were you not tormented because of your friends?' Everyone's capacity to command and love of freedom rests on this quality, for spirit is commanding and unconquerable. Nor is it right to say guardians should treat strangers fiercely. We should not be angry with anyone simply as such, and a noble spirit is not

naturally fierce, becoming so only when provoked by wrongdoers. [Alternative reading: 'Surely you are not tormented because of your friends?' The line is probably corrupt. Bergk's preferable reading means 'for you indeed were tormented by friends'.] As I was saying earlier, it is towards their own friends that people display this feeling with the greatest force, whenever they believe they have suffered an injury at those friends' hands. This is reasonable: besides the injury itself, they feel deprived of a benefit by people who owed them one. Hence the saying,

'Bitter is the quarrel between brothers'; and again, 'Those who love excessively also hate excessively.' We have now approximately established the number and character of our state's citizens, together with the size and nature of their territory. I say approximately because theoretical discussion should not be expected to match the precision required in actual practice.

In natural compounds, something necessary for a whole's existence is not necessarily one of its organic parts. The same holds for a state or any other unified association: not every necessary condition is a constituent part. An association's members must share something in common, equally or unequally, such as food, land, or another possession. But when one thing is a means and another its end, they share nothing beyond the fact that one receives what the other produces. Workers and tools stand in this relation to their work. A house and its builder share nothing in themselves; the builder's art exists for the house's sake. Likewise, states require property, but property is not part of the state, even when it includes living beings. A state is not simply a community of living creatures: it is a community of equals pursuing the best possible life. Happiness is the highest good and consists in the complete realization and practice of virtue. Some attain it, while others possess little or none. Differences in people's qualities therefore account for different states and constitutions. People seek happiness in different ways and through different means, establishing corresponding ways of life and governments. We must also identify everything indispensable to a state's existence, since its actual constituent parts will be found among these necessities. Let us therefore set out the several functions that a state must perform. By doing so we shall readily discover the answer we are looking for.

First, the state requires food. Second, it needs arts and crafts, because life depends on many instruments. Third, it requires weapons to maintain authority over disobedient subjects and defend the community against outside attackers. Fourth, it needs revenue for domestic requirements and warfare. Fifth, or rather first in importance, there must be provision for religion, commonly called worship. Sixth, and most necessary of all, there must be authority to decide the public interest and what is just in people's dealings with one another.

These are the requirements we may attribute to every state. A state is not merely an aggregate or collection of separate people, but a union sufficient for life's purposes. If any of these requirements is absent, the community cannot possibly be self-sufficient. A state therefore

must be organized to perform these functions. Farmers must supply food; artisans must practise their crafts; there must be military and wealthy classes, priests, and judges deciding questions of justice and advantage. Having established this, we must ask whether everyone should perform every occupation. Should every individual perform all these tasks at once, acting as a farmer and an artisan as well as serving as a councillor and a judge? Should these functions belong to different people? Or should some occupations be assigned to particular individuals while others are shared by all? The answer is not the same in every state. As we said, everyone may share in every function, or only particular people may share particular functions. These differences produce different constitutions: democracies share everything among everyone, while oligarchies follow the opposite practice. Our subject, however, is the best government, under which the state will be happiest. Since happiness requires virtue, as already established, citizens who are just without qualification, rather than merely relative to their constitution, cannot live as mechanics or traders. Such lives are ignoble and hostile to virtue. Nor should they farm, since leisure is necessary both to cultivate virtue and to carry out political duties.

A state also contains warriors and councillors, the latter advising on expediency and deciding legal matters. These two classes, more particularly than any of the others we have mentioned, appear to be the constituent parts of the state itself. Should the two classes be separate, or should the same people perform both functions? The answer is readily apparent: in one sense the people should be the same, in another different. The occupations suit different ages, because one requires wisdom and the other strength; in that respect their holders differ. Yet those able to exercise or resist force cannot be expected to accept permanent subjection. From this perspective the same people must hold both roles, since the armed can always determine the constitution's fate. Both governing functions should therefore be assigned to the same people at different times, following nature's order: strength belongs to the young, wisdom to the old. Distributing the duties of government in this way will serve the state's advantage, and it will also be just. For this arrangement gives people functions in accordance with what they deserve. The governing class should also own property. They are citizens, and citizens should be prosperous. Mechanics and anyone whose occupation prevents the practice of virtue have no share in the state. This follows from our initial principle: happiness cannot exist without virtue, and a city is called happy with regard to all its citizens, not merely some. Property must clearly belong to these citizens, since the farmers will necessarily be slaves, barbarians, or Perioeci. Only the priests remain from our list, and arranging their office is straightforward. No farmer or mechanic should be appointed: the gods should receive honour from citizens alone. The citizen body has two divisions, warriors and councillors. Religious worship should be properly performed, and service to the gods should also provide

rest for people whose age has ended their active careers. The priestly duties should therefore be assigned to elderly men from these two classes. We have now distinguished the conditions necessary for a state to exist from the parts that actually constitute that state. Farmers, craftspeople, and labourers of every kind are indispensable to its existence, but warriors and councillors are its constituent parts. These groups are distinct from one another, in some cases permanently and in others only temporarily.

Political philosophers did not recently discover that a state should be divided into classes and its warriors separated from its farmers. Egypt and Crete still maintain this arrangement. According to tradition, it was established by the legislation of Sesostris in

Egypt and of Minos in Crete. The practice of gathering together at common dining tables also appears to be of great antiquity: in Crete they date to Minos, and in Italy they are older still. Italian historians describe Italus, a king of Oenotria, after whom the Oenotrians became known as Italians. He gave the name Italy to Europe's promontory between the Scylletic and Lametic Gulfs, separated by only half a day's journey. They say Italus changed the Oenotrians from shepherds into farmers and, among his other laws, instituted common meals. Some of his descendants preserve that institution and certain other laws of his even today.
On Italy's side facing Tyrrhenia lived the Opici, still called Ausones as in earlier times. On the side towards Iapygia and the Ionian Gulf, in the district named Syrtis, lived the

Chones, themselves of Oenotrian stock. Common dining tables originated in this region, while the much older division into castes came from Egypt: Sesostris reigned long before Minos. These and many other institutions have certainly been invented repeatedly through the ages, indeed an incalculable number of times. Necessity presumably taught people the absolutely essential inventions first. Once those needs were met, things that embellished and enriched life naturally developed little by little. We may reasonably infer that political institutions developed by following the same course over time.
