The example of Egypt provides evidence of how far back into antiquity arrangements of all these kinds extend. The Egyptians seem the oldest people, with laws and an orderly constitution extending beyond memory. We should therefore use existing discoveries as well as possible and try to remedy what remains defective.

I have already said that land should belong to those who bear arms and participate in government, while farmers should form a separate class. I have also specified how extensive the territory should be and what character it should have. Let us now discuss the distribution of land and the nature of the agricultural population. I do not believe property should be held in common, as some

argue. Instead, its use should be shared by friendly agreement, and no citizen should lack the means of subsistence. There is general agreement among those considering this subject that a city which is well organized ought to provide meals taken in common. We shall explain our own reasons for this view later. These meals should be accessible to every citizen. Yet poor people cannot easily contribute the required amount from their own resources while also supporting their households. The expenses of religious worship should likewise fall on the public.

Land must therefore be divided into public and private portions, each subdivided again. One half of the public portion should be set aside to provide for worship of the gods. The other half should supply the funds required to meet the cost of the common meals. Of private land, half should lie near the frontier and half near the city. Every citizen should receive two allotments, so that everyone owns land in both areas. This division is fair and just and encourages agreement when frontier wars arise. Without it, some citizens rush too readily into conflict with neighbours, while others become so cautious that they abandon honour altogether. Some places therefore prohibit frontier residents from deliberating about wars against neighbouring states, on the ground that personal interests distort their judgment. For the reasons that have now been stated, the land should therefore be apportioned between public and private use, and between the two locations, in the way I have described.

[Compare Plato's Laws, which contains the same proposal. In II.6, section 15, Aristotle criticizes the division into allotments that he accepts here.] Ideally, the farmers should be slaves of different peoples and lacking spirit. Their lack of spirit will fit them better for their labour and remove the danger of rebellion. The next best arrangement uses foreign Perioeci of a similarly subordinate character. Some of these agricultural workers should be privately owned slaves, employed to cultivate the estates of individual property holders. The rest should belong to the state itself and be employed in working the land that is held in common. Later I shall explain the proper treatment of slaves and why it is advantageous always to offer freedom as the reward for their services.

We have said that the city should have access to land and sea and, as far as possible, the entire territory. As for the site itself, we would wish it to be fortunate in four respects. First comes health, an indispensable requirement. Cities facing east and exposed to easterly winds are healthiest. Next are those sheltered from the north wind, which consequently enjoy milder winters. The location chosen for the city must also be convenient for carrying on the work of political administration, as well as appropriate to the requirements of warfare. For warfare, citizens should be able to leave easily, while enemies should find entry and capture difficult. Springs and fountains should naturally abound within the town. Where they are insufficient, large reservoirs should collect rainwater, providing supplies that will not fail when war cuts the inhabitants

off from the countryside. Particular attention must be given to their health. The health of the inhabitants depends first and foremost on the healthiness of the site itself and the direction in which it faces. A second factor is the purity of the water they use. Calling this second in order certainly does not make it a matter of minor importance. The things used most frequently and extensively to maintain the body have the greatest influence on health, and these include air and water. A wisely governed state whose water is not all equally pure should therefore separate drinking water from supplies intended for other purposes.

When we consider fortified positions, the kind of stronghold that is suitable varies according to the form of government that the city possesses. An acropolis suits oligarchy or monarchy, while level ground suits democracy. Aristocracy suits neither, but instead several fortified positions. Regular streets in the modern arrangement introduced by Hippodamus make private housing more pleasant and generally more convenient. For wartime security, however, the older irregular arrangement is better: strangers find it hard to leave, and attackers struggle to find their way in. A city should therefore combine both plans. Houses can be grouped irregularly, as farmers plant vines in so-called clumps. Only certain districts, rather than the whole city, should follow straight lines. By using this combination of arrangements, the city will secure the advantages of beauty together with those of protection against attack.

Those who say a city claiming military virtue should have no walls hold thoroughly outdated views. Anyone can see the error by looking at the experience of those cities that once took pride in this belief: events themselves have disproved their claim. [Compare II.8, section 1; Plato, Laws VI, 778–779.] Seeking shelter behind walls against an enemy similar in character and only slightly superior in number certainly shows little courage. But besiegers often possess overwhelming strength that human resistance and the bravery of a few cannot overcome. If warriors are to escape defeat and outrage, the strongest possible wall is their best protection, especially now that catapults and siege engines have reached such perfection. Refusing walls would be as foolish as placing a town in exposed country and levelling its heights, or leaving a private house without enclosing walls lest its inhabitants become cowards. We should also remember that people whose city is surrounded by walls retain the option of taking advantage of their protection or declining to do so. A city without walls has no such choice available.

If our conclusions are sound, cities should not only have walls but make them attractive as well as militarily useful and capable of resisting modern inventions. Those attacking a city make every effort they can and use every available means to gain an advantage over its defenders. Defenders must therefore employ every defence already discovered and devise new ones besides. When preparations are thorough, an enemy will not even contemplate an attack.

Walls require guardhouses and towers at suitable intervals, and citizens require organized common meals. When we put these two requirements together, the suggestion naturally presents itself that some of the groups eating together should be assigned their common tables in the guardhouses. The arrangement could be as follows. The magistrates' principal common tables should occupy an appropriate site, alongside buildings for religious worship, except where law or the Pythian oracle assigns particular rites to a special location. This site should be visible from far away, standing above its surroundings and giving virtue its proper elevation. Nearby should lie an agora like the Thessalians' 'freemen's agora'. All commerce should be excluded, and no mechanic, farmer, or similar person admitted unless magistrates summon him. The space would be attractively used for older men's physical exercises. Different ages should be separated in this noble activity. Some magistrates should remain with the boys, while adult men exercise near the magistrates in the freemen's agora. There is no better way to encourage true modesty and the respectful fear appropriate to free people than to have the magistrates present among them. A separate traders' agora should occupy a location convenient for goods arriving by both land and sea.

In discussing magistrates, we must remember the priests, another part of the citizen body. They too should have public dining tables appropriately situated near the temples. Officials handling contracts, charges, summonses, and similar business, together with those supervising the agora and city, should occupy a public meeting place near the agora. The area around the traders' agora would be a suitable place in which to establish these officials and accommodate their public business. We reserve the upper agora for

leisure, while the other meets commercial necessities. [Alternative reading: 'this institution should be divided according to ages'.] The countryside should follow the same arrangement. Its magistrates, variously called Inspectors of Forests or Wardens of the Country, need guardhouses and common dining tables while on duty. Temples should also be distributed throughout the territory, some dedicated to gods and others to heroes.

To spend any more time dwelling on arrangements of this detailed kind would be a waste of our time. The difficulty lies in carrying them out rather than imagining them. We can describe them as fully as we please, but their realization depends on fortune. Let us therefore leave these matters for the present.

Returning to the constitution, let us determine which elements, and elements of what character, should compose a happy, well-governed state. Well-being depends on two things: selecting the right end for action and finding the actions that lead to it. The means chosen and the end pursued can correspond with one another, but they can also be at odds with one another. Sometimes people choose the right goal but fail in practice to achieve it. Sometimes they carry out every means successfully but pursue a bad goal. Sometimes they fail in both respects. Medicine illustrates this: doctors do not always understand health correctly, and their treatments may also fail to produce the intended result. In every art and science, we must command both the end and the means to it.

Everyone plainly wants happiness and well-being. Some people have the ability to achieve them; others are prevented from doing so by an accident or a deficiency in their nature. A good life needs a supply of external goods: fewer of them when people are in a good condition, and more when their condition is worse. Still others possess the conditions needed for happiness but take an entirely mistaken course in seeking it from the beginning. Our task, however, is to discover the best constitution, the one under which a city will be governed best. And the best-governed city is the one with the greatest opportunity to achieve happiness. We must therefore establish clearly what happiness is. [The translator follows the reading in Bekker's first edition.]

In the Ethics we argued, if those arguments carry any weight, that happiness is the actual and complete exercise of virtue, understood absolutely rather than conditionally. By 'conditionally' I meant something that necessity requires; by 'absolutely', something good in itself. Consider just actions. Just punishments and corrections come from a good principle, yet they are good because we cannot dispense with them. It would be better if neither individuals nor states needed anything of this kind. Actions directed towards honour and benefit, on the other hand, are the best without qualification. In the former case we merely choose the lesser evil; in the latter we establish and produce something good. A good person can make the best of poverty, illness, and the other misfortunes of life, but can achieve happiness only under the opposite conditions. As the Ethics also explains, a good person is someone for whom what is good absolutely is also personally good, because of that person's virtue. Clearly, the use such a person makes of other goods must itself be virtuous and good without qualification. This leads people to imagine that external possessions cause happiness. They might just as reasonably attribute a brilliant performance on the lyre to the instrument instead of the player's skill.

Our argument therefore implies that the legislator must find some things already available in the state and must supply others. We can only wish that our state may be so constituted as to receive the goods that fortune controls, acknowledging her power over them. Virtue and goodness in the state, however, come from knowledge and deliberate purpose, not chance. A city becomes virtuous only if the citizens who participate in its government are virtuous; and in our state every citizen participates. We must therefore examine how a human being becomes virtuous. Even if we could imagine all the citizens being virtuous collectively without each being virtuous individually, individual virtue would still be preferable. For when each possesses virtue, all necessarily possess it too.

Three things make human beings good and virtuous: nature, habit, and reason. First, one must be born a human being rather than another kind of animal. Next, one must have a particular bodily and mental character. Yet some qualities are of no advantage at birth because habit changes them, and some natural gifts can be directed by habit towards either good or evil. Most animals live by nature alone, though habit also influences some of them in minor respects. Human beings alone have reason as well. Nature, habit, and reason must therefore agree with one another, although they do not always do so. People often act against both nature and habit when reason convinces them that they should. We have already identified the natural characters most readily shaped by a legislator. Education must accomplish the rest: we learn some things through habituation and others through instruction. [Compare Nicomachean Ethics X.9, section 6.]

Every political community contains rulers and subjects. We must therefore ask whether these positions should alternate or remain permanently assigned. The answer necessarily determines the education that citizens receive. Suppose some people surpassed others as much as gods and heroes are believed to surpass ordinary human beings. Suppose their bodily advantages were great, and their mental advantages likewise, so that the rulers' superiority over their subjects was obvious and beyond dispute. In that case it would clearly be best to settle the matter permanently: one class should govern, and the other should serve.

But that condition cannot be achieved. Our kings have no obvious superiority over their subjects of the kind Scylax describes among the Indians. Many considerations therefore make it necessary for all citizens alike to take turns ruling and being ruled. Equality requires similar treatment for similar people, and a government without justice as its foundation cannot last. Under an unjust government, everyone in the country joins the subjects in wanting revolution. Those who hold power cannot possibly be numerous enough to overcome all their opponents combined. Nevertheless, rulers must unquestionably excel those they govern. The legislator must work out how to reconcile these requirements and how the different people will participate in government. We have already touched on this question. Nature herself supplies a basis for choosing by distinguishing young from old, although both belong to the same kind: she equips the older to govern and the younger to be governed. Being governed in youth causes no resentment; young people do not consider themselves superior to their rulers, particularly when they will receive the same privilege on reaching the appropriate age.

We conclude that rulers and subjects are the same in one respect and different in another. Their education must accordingly be both the same and different. As the saying goes, someone who wants to command well must first learn to obey. At the beginning of this inquiry I distinguished government exercised for the rulers' benefit from government exercised for the subjects' benefit. The former is despotic; the latter is government of free people. Some commands differ in their purpose rather than in what they require. Thus a free young person may perform apparently servile tasks with honour. Whether an action is honourable or shameful depends less on the action itself than on its purpose and intention. But we maintain that the virtue of a citizen and ruler is the virtue of a good person,

and that the same person must be a subject before becoming a ruler. The legislator must therefore consider how citizens can become good people, the means of making them so, and the end towards which a complete life is directed. The human soul has two parts: one possesses reason in itself, while the other lacks reason of its own but can listen to it. We call someone good through possessing the virtues of these two parts. Anyone who accepts this division can have no doubt about which part is more likely to contain the end. In nature as in craft, the inferior exists for the sake of the better and superior; here the superior is the part that possesses reason. Reason itself, as we ordinarily describe it, also has two parts, practical and speculative. Actions must be divided correspondingly. Whoever can achieve both kinds, or all kinds, should prefer the activities of the principle that is naturally superior. What is most desirable for each person is always the highest thing within that person's reach. Life as a whole also divides into work and leisure, war and peace; actions divide into those that are necessary and useful and those that are honourable. Our preference between these kinds of action must follow our preference between the soul's parts and their activities. We must wage war for the sake of peace, work for the sake of leisure, and pursue necessary and useful things for the sake of honourable ones. When making laws, the statesman must keep all these distinctions in view: the parts of the soul and their activities, above all the superior part and the end, and the different kinds of human life and conduct. People must work and fight, but peace and leisure are better. They must do what necessity and usefulness require, but honourable action is better. These principles should guide the education of children and everyone else of an age to need it. Yet even the Hellenic cities now regarded as best governed, and the legislators who established their constitutions, seem not to have organized government around the highest end. Their laws and education do not aim at every virtue. Instead, with a common and narrow outlook, they concentrate on virtues that promise usefulness and profit. Many recent writers take the same position. They commend the Lacedaemonian constitution and praise its legislator for directing everything towards war and conquest. Argument can refute this doctrine, and events refuted it long ago. Most people desire empire because they hope to accumulate the goods bestowed by fortune. On precisely this ground Thibron and the other writers on the Lacedaemonian constitution praise its legislator: training in hardship enabled the Lacedaemonians to become powerful. But now that their empire has disappeared, surely they are not happy, nor was their legislator right. What an absurd result, if they continue to observe his laws without interference and yet have lost the better part of life! These writers are also mistaken about the kind of government a legislator should favour. Governing free people is noble and requires more virtue than despotic rule. A city does not deserve to be called happy, nor its legislator praised, merely because its citizens are trained to conquer and dominate their neighbours. This involves a great evil. Apply the same principle within the city, and any citizen able to do so will naturally try to seize supreme power. That is exactly the offence the Lacedaemonians accused King Pausanias of attempting, despite the great honours he already enjoyed. Neither this principle nor any law directed towards such an end is statesmanlike, useful, or right. The same things are best for individuals and states, and these are what the legislator should impress upon the citizens' minds. Military training should not aim at enslaving people who do not deserve enslavement. Its first aim should be to prevent our own enslavement; its second, to acquire an empire for the benefit of those governed, rather than to impose despotism everywhere; its third, to obtain mastery only over those who deserve to be slaves. Events support the argument that military arrangements, like all the legislator's other measures, should aim to secure leisure and establish peace. Most military states remain safe only while fighting. Once they have gained an empire they collapse, losing their edge in peacetime like iron left unused. Their legislator bears the blame, because he never taught them how to live at peace.

Individuals and states have the same end; consequently the best person and the best state must have the same end too. It follows that both the best individual and the best state must possess the virtues appropriate to the proper enjoyment of leisure. As we have repeatedly said, peace is the purpose of war, and leisure the purpose of work. Leisure and cultivation depend not only on virtues exercised during leisure but also on some that serve practical activity. Many necessities must be supplied before leisure becomes possible. A city must accordingly possess temperance, courage, and endurance. The proverb rightly says that slaves have no leisure, and people who cannot meet danger bravely become slaves to any invader. Work requires courage and endurance; leisure requires intellectual virtue. Both require justice and temperance, especially peace and leisure. War compels people to act justly and temperately, whereas prosperity and peaceful leisure tend to make them insolent. Those apparently most fortunate, who possess every good, therefore particularly need justice and temperance. Consider the inhabitants of the Islands of the Blest, if such people exist as the poets say. They above all need philosophy, temperance, and justice, and need them all the more because they enjoy greater leisure amid abundance. It is easy to see why a state that seeks goodness and happiness must possess these virtues. Inability to use life's goods is disgraceful in anyone; inability to use them in peace is especially so. What could be more shameful than displaying excellent qualities in action and warfare, then proving no better than slaves when peace brings leisure?

We should therefore avoid the Lacedaemonian approach to virtue. They agree with other people about what the highest goods are, but differ in believing that the exercise of a single virtue secures them. These goods, and the enjoyment of them, plainly surpass the enjoyment derived from the virtues that serve as means to them. We must now examine how these higher goods can be reached, and by what means we can acquire them and enjoy them.

We have already established that nature, habit, and reason are necessary, and defined the character our citizens should possess. It remains to decide whether early training should begin with reason or with habit. The two must agree; when they do, they produce the finest harmony. Reason can go astray and fail to reach the highest ideal of life, and habit can exert an equally harmful influence. One point is clear at the outset. Here, as everywhere, development begins from a starting point, and the ends reached from some starting points serve a further end. In human beings, reason and intelligence are the end towards which nature works. The citizens' procreation and moral training should therefore be organized with these in view. A second point follows. Just as soul and body are distinct, the soul itself contains a rational and an irrational part, with two corresponding conditions, reason and appetite. In the order of development, the body precedes the soul; similarly, the irrational part develops before the rational.

We see the proof in children. Anger, will, and desire are present from birth, whereas the powers of reason and understanding emerge later, as the children grow older. Care for the body should therefore come before care for the soul, followed by training of the appetites. Nevertheless, training the appetites must always serve reason, just as caring for the body must serve the soul.

The legislator must begin by considering how the children being brought up can have the best possible bodies. His first concern will therefore be marriage: at what age should citizens marry, and which people are suited to marry one another? His laws must take account of the partners and their relative ages, so that their ages and bodily powers are not mismatched. A man may still be able to father children when the woman can no longer bear them, or the woman may remain capable of bearing them after the man has lost his power to father them. Such differences produce quarrels and disagreements between spouses. Second, the legislator must consider when children will succeed their parents. If the gap between generations is too great, parents will be too old to enjoy their children's affection or help them. But their ages should not be too close either. Very early marriage has many disadvantages: children show insufficient respect to parents whom they regard as contemporaries, and disputes arise over running the household. Third, returning to the point from which we departed, the legislator must shape the bodies of newborn children as he intends. Nearly all the aims just set out can be secured if the legislator pays careful attention to a single point: the ages at which the reproductive capacities of men and women normally come to an end. Men's reproductive period generally ends at seventy, women's at fifty; the beginning of their union should be timed accordingly. A union when both are very young produces poor offspring. Among other animals, the young of immature parents are small, underdeveloped, and usually female. The same holds for human beings, as the small and weak inhabitants of cities where early marriage is customary demonstrate. Younger women also suffer more during childbirth and die more frequently. Some say this explains the oracle once given to the Troezenians, 'Do not harvest the young field.' It referred to the many deaths caused by marrying too early, not to gathering crops. Delaying marriage also encourages temperance, since women who marry early are liable to sexual misconduct. Men who marry while still growing likewise stunt their bodies; bodily growth has a definite time at which it ends. Women should marry at about eighteen and men at thirty-seven. They will then be in their prime, and their reproductive powers will decline together. Moreover, if children arrive at the reasonably expected time, they will reach their prime and take their parents' place when their fathers are declining and approaching the end of their seventy years.

That settles the appropriate ages for marriage. The time of year must also be considered. Our present custom generally confines marriage to winter, and rightly so. The teachings of doctors and natural philosophers about reproduction should also be studied by the

parents themselves. Doctors offer sound advice concerning the age at which the body is suitably prepared, while natural philosophers advise about the winds, preferring winds from the north to those from the south.

We shall later examine which parental bodily condition benefits offspring most, when we discuss children's education. For the present occasion, however, it will be enough to set down a few observations of a general kind. An athlete's condition is no more appropriate to a citizen's life, good health, or producing children than a sickly or exhausted condition. The right condition lies between these extremes. The body should be accustomed to exertion, but neither excessive exertion nor the single kind practised by athletes. A person should be capable of every activity belonging to a free citizen. This applies equally to both parents. Pregnant women should care for themselves, exercise, and eat nourishing food. The legislator can easily secure the exercise by requiring a daily walk to a temple where they can worship the gods who oversee childbirth. Their minds, however, should be kept at rest, unlike their bodies. For children draw their nature from their mothers as plants draw theirs from the soil.

Concerning the exposure and upbringing of infants, the law should forbid a child born deformed to be allowed to live. Where there are too many children, however—for our state sets a population limit—and couples exceed the permitted number, if public feeling opposes exposing infants, an abortion should take place before sensation and life have begun. Whether such an act is lawful in these circumstances depends on the presence of life and sensation.

Having established the ages at which men and women should marry, we must also establish how long they should continue producing children for the state. Parents who are too old, like those who are too young, produce children deficient in body and mind; the children of very old men are frail. The limit for producing children should therefore be determined by the time when a person's intellectual powers are at their highest and most fully developed. For most people this is about fifty, according to certain poets who divide life into seven-year periods. Four or five years after that point, they should stop having children. From then on they should have intercourse only for health or some comparable purpose.

Marital unfaithfulness should be considered disgraceful for either a man or a woman who is married and bears the name of husband or wife. If it occurs during the period assigned to childbearing, the offender should lose privileges in proportion to the seriousness of the offence.

Once children are born, the way they are reared can be expected to affect their bodily strength greatly. The example of animals, and of peoples intent on developing a military character, suggests that a diet richest in milk best suits human beings. As for wine, the less they receive, the better they can avoid disease.

Every movement suitable for children at this early age is highly beneficial. Some peoples use devices to keep their bodies straight and prevent their delicate limbs from becoming misshapen. Another excellent practice is to accustom children to cold from their earliest years: this greatly benefits health and toughens them for military service. Many barbarians therefore plunge newborn children into a cold stream; others, including the Celts, dress them in only a light covering. Human beings should become accustomed early to enduring whatever habit can teach them to endure, though the training must be gradual. Children's natural warmth makes it easy to train them to withstand cold. These are the provisions appropriate to the first stage of life.

The next stage lasts until the age of five. During it, children should not be required to study or work, since this might obstruct their growth. They should move enough to keep their limbs active. Play is one means of securing this, but it must not be coarse, exhausting, or disorderly. The officials called Directors of Education must carefully supervise the tales and stories children hear. Children's games should prepare them for adult activities, and should generally imitate occupations they will later pursue seriously. Those who try to suppress children's loud cries and screams, as Plato does in the Laws, are mistaken. Crying helps children grow and in a sense exercises their bodies. Straining the voice has an effect like holding the breath during vigorous exertion. Among their other duties, the Directors of Education must oversee children's upbringing and ensure that they spend as little time as possible with slaves. Children must remain at home until seven. Even at this young age, therefore, everything mean and debasing should be kept from their eyes and ears. Indeed, nothing deserves more careful attention from the legislator than the exclusion of

indecent speech. Readily speaking shameful words brings people close to shameful acts. Young people especially must never be allowed to say or hear such things. If a free person is caught saying or doing something forbidden, and is still too young to have a place at the common meals, the punishment should be public disgrace and a beating. An older offender should suffer degradation appropriate to such slavish behaviour. Since we prohibit improper language, we must clearly also exclude indecent pictures and stories. Rulers should ensure that no image or painting depicts indecent acts, except in temples of gods whose festivals legally permit ribaldry. The law also allows mature people to worship these gods for themselves, their children, and their wives. The legislator should forbid young people to hear satirical iambic poetry or watch comedy until they are old enough to join the common meals and drink strong wine. By then education will have equipped them to resist the harmful influence of such performances.

These brief observations suffice for our present purpose. Later we shall return to the subject, discuss it more fully, and determine whether such freedom should be allowed and, if so, on what terms. The tragic actor Theodorus rightly said that he would not let any other actor appear before him, even a second-rate one, because audiences become attached to the first voices they hear. This principle of association applies everywhere, to things as well as people: what comes first generally wins our strongest affection. Young people should therefore be kept unfamiliar with everything bad, especially anything that encourages vice or hatred. After their fifth year, they should spend the next two years watching the activities they will later learn. Education itself must be divided into two periods: from seven to puberty, and from puberty to twenty-one. The poets who divide ages into periods of seven years are not always correct. We should follow nature's actual divisions instead, since craft and education aim to supply what nature leaves deficient.

First, then, let us ask whether rules concerning children should be established at all. Second, should their care belong to the state or to private individuals, as is generally customary today? Third, once those questions have been answered, we must consider what the regulations themselves ought to be and what they should prescribe.

chapters.title: Book 8
paragraphs: No one will dispute that a legislator's first concern should be the education of the young, or that neglecting education damages states. Citizens must be formed to fit the government under which they live. Every constitution has a distinctive character that first brings it into existence and then keeps it in being. A democratic character produces democracy, and an oligarchical character produces oligarchy. In every case, the better the character, the better the government.

Exercising any ability or art requires prior training and the formation of habits; clearly, the practice of virtue does too. Since the entire city pursues one end, everyone should plainly receive the same education, provided publicly rather than privately. At present, each person looks after his own children independently and arranges whatever separate instruction he considers best. But training in matters of common concern should be shared by all. Nor should we think that a citizen belongs to himself alone. All citizens belong to the state; each is a part of it, and caring for a part cannot be separated from caring for the whole. On this point the Lacedaemonians deserve praise: they devote the greatest attention to their children and make education a public responsibility.

We cannot deny that education should be governed by law and undertaken by the state. What this public education should be like, however, and how the young should be educated, remain open questions. [Compare sections 11–16, and Nicomachean Ethics X.9, section 13.] People disagree profoundly about what should be taught, whether the aim is virtue or the best life. Nor is it clear whether education should concern itself more with intellectual or moral virtue. Present practice leaves us perplexed. No one knows which principle should guide us: should training pursue practical usefulness, virtue, or higher knowledge? Each of these aims has its advocates. There is no agreement about the means either. People begin with different conceptions of virtue and naturally disagree about how to practise it. Children must certainly learn useful things that are necessary, but they need not learn everything useful. Occupations divide into those worthy of free people and those that are not. Young children should acquire only the kinds of useful knowledge that do not debase them. Any occupation, art, or science that makes a free person's body, soul, or mind less capable of practising virtue is debasing. Hence we call trades that deform the body vulgar, and the same applies to paid employment, which engrosses and degrades the mind. Some liberal arts are suitable for a free person to learn, but only to a certain extent. Pursuing them too closely in the effort to attain perfection produces the same harmful effects. The purpose for which someone acts also makes a considerable difference. Learning or doing something for oneself, for one's friends, or for the sake of excellence does not appear servile. Doing exactly the same thing for other people may be regarded as menial and fit for a slave. [Compare III.4, section 13.] As I have already remarked, the established subjects of instruction are partly liberal and partly illiberal. There are four customary branches of education: reading and writing, physical training, music, and, sometimes, drawing. Reading, writing, and drawing are considered useful in various aspects of life, while physical training is thought to cultivate courage. Music presents a difficulty. Today most people practise it for pleasure. It was originally included in education, however, because nature herself, as we have often said, requires us to use leisure well as well as to work well. I must repeat that leisure is the first principle of all activity. Both work and leisure are necessary, but leisure is better than work. We must therefore ask in earnest what activities we ought to pursue during the time we have at leisure. Plainly, we should not simply amuse ourselves, since that would make amusement life's purpose. Such a conclusion is inconceivable. Yet amusement is particularly necessary during serious work: someone working hard needs relaxation, and amusement supplies it, whereas work always involves effort and exertion. We should therefore introduce amusements at suitable times, using them as remedies. The feeling they create relaxes the soul, and their pleasure brings rest. Leisure itself supplies pleasure, happiness, and the enjoyment of life. These belong to those at leisure, not to those occupied with work. A busy person is pursuing an end he has not yet reached, whereas happiness is itself an end, which everyone associates with pleasure rather than pain. People understand this pleasure differently, according to their individual habits. The best person's pleasure is best and comes from the noblest sources. Clearly, then, some kinds of learning and education should be pursued so that we can enjoy leisure, and valued for their own sake. Knowledge useful for business, by contrast, is necessary and serves other ends. Our forefathers therefore included music in education neither because it was necessary nor because it was useful. It is not necessary, and it is not useful in the way reading and writing are useful for earning money, managing a household, acquiring knowledge, or participating in politics. Nor does it serve drawing's purpose of helping us judge artists' work more accurately, or physical training's purpose of providing health and strength. Music provides neither of these advantages. Its remaining purpose is intellectual enjoyment during leisure. This apparently explains its introduction into education: it was thought to be one way a free person should spend leisure. As Homer says—

'How fine it is to invite people to a delightful feast!' Later he describes others inviting 'the singer who would bring pleasure to them all'. [An alternative interpretation, perhaps intended by Aristotle though not the passage's original meaning, is 'to invite Thalia to the feast'. Odyssey XVII, 385.]

Elsewhere Odysseus says that there is no better way to live than when 'people's hearts are joyful, and the guests seated in order in the hall listen to the singer's voice'. Clearly, then, parents should give their sons a kind of education pursued for its nobility and its fitness for free people, rather than for necessity or usefulness. Whether there is just one such subject or several, what these subjects are, and how to teach them must be decided later. For now, we can say that the ancients support our position. Their view is evident from music's place among the accepted, traditional branches of education. Children should also clearly learn certain useful skills, such as reading and writing, not merely for their practical value but because these open the way to many other kinds of knowledge. Drawing can be taught with a similar purpose. Its aim should not be to prevent mistakes in one's purchases, or to protect against deception when buying and selling goods, but to develop judgment of beauty in the human form. Constantly pursuing utility is unworthy of free and noble souls. In education, moreover, habits plainly must precede reasoning, and the body must be trained before the mind. Boys should therefore be entrusted to the trainer, who develops the proper bodily condition, and to the wrestling-master, who teaches them the exercises.

Among states that now seem most attentive to children's upbringing, some seek to produce the physique of an athlete. In doing so, however, they damage children's bodily form and restrict their growth. [Odyssey IX, 7; compare Plato, Republic VII, 535 and following.]

The Lacedaemonians avoid this particular mistake, but make their children brutal through exhausting exercises that they believe will produce courage. In truth, as we have repeatedly said, education must not pursue this or any other single aim exclusively. Even supposing their chosen aim to be correct, they fail to reach it. Among both barbarians and animals, courage accompanies a gentle, lion-like disposition rather than the greatest ferocity. Many peoples are perfectly willing to kill and eat human beings, including the

Achaeans and Heniochi who live around the Black Sea. Other tribes farther inland are equally bad or worse. All live by plundering, yet lack courage. It is well known that the Lacedaemonians surpassed others while diligently maintaining their arduous drill, but now suffer defeat both in warfare and in athletic contests. Their former superiority came not from the particular method of training their young, but from training them at a time when others did not. We should conclude that nobility, rather than brutality, deserves first place. No wolf or other wild creature will confront a truly noble danger; that belongs to the courageous man. Parents who devote their children to gymnastics while neglecting the education they need actually debase them. They make them useful to the state in only one capacity, and our argument shows that even in that capacity they fall below others. We should judge the Lacedaemonians by their present condition, not their past. Their educational system now has competitors, whereas formerly it did not.

We agree that physical exercises belong in education, and that children's exercises should be gentle. Strict regimens and painful exertion must be avoided so that bodily growth is not damaged. Olympic victors provide striking evidence of the harm caused by excessive training in childhood. No more than two or three have won prizes both as boys and as adults, because early training and strenuous exercises wore out their constitutions. After boyhood, three years should be given to other studies; the period after that can be devoted to demanding exercise and a strict regimen. People should not work their minds and bodies strenuously at the same time. The two kinds of effort interfere with each other: bodily exertion hinders mental work, and mental exertion hinders the body.

We have already raised some questions about music. Let us return to them and pursue them further, using our remarks as an introduction to this or any other inquiry into the subject. It is difficult to determine what music is or why anyone should study it. Is it for amusement and relaxation, like sleep or drinking? These are pleasant rather than good in themselves, and, as Euripides says, they 'put an end to care'. People therefore place them alongside music and use all three—sleep, drinking, and music—with some adding dance. Or should we say that music contributes to virtue because it shapes our minds and trains us to enjoy the right pleasures, just as our bodies acquire their character through

physical training? [Compare Plato, Republic VII, 537 B; Euripides, Bacchae, 380.] Or does it serve the enjoyment of leisure and the cultivation of the mind, a third possibility? Plainly, education for the young cannot aim at amusement, since learning is painful rather than pleasant. Nor is intellectual enjoyment appropriate to boys of that age. It is the final end, and what is still incomplete cannot attain completeness or the end. Perhaps, however, boys learn music so they can enjoy amusement as adults. If that is the purpose, why must they learn to perform themselves? Why not follow the Persian and Median kings, who gain pleasure and instruction from listening to others? Surely musicians who have devoted their lives to the art as their profession perform better than those who practise merely as part of their education. If personal study is necessary, the same reasoning would require them to learn cookery, which is absurd. Even if we grant that music shapes character, the objection remains. Why learn to perform ourselves? Why not acquire sound judgment and the right pleasures by listening to others, as the Lacedaemonians do? They claim to judge good and bad melodies correctly without studying music. Again, suppose music promotes cheerfulness and cultivated intellectual enjoyment. The same objection persists: why learn it ourselves instead of enjoying others' performances? Our conception of the gods illustrates the point. In the poets, Zeus neither sings nor plays the lyre himself. Indeed, we call professional performers vulgar; a free man would not sing or play unless drunk or joking. Let us leave these matters for the moment.

The first question is whether music belongs in education at all. Of the three distinct purposes mentioned in our discussion, which should we assign to it: education, amusement, or intellectual enjoyment? It can be placed under all three and seems to partake of each. Amusement provides relaxation, and relaxation must be pleasant, since it remedies the pain produced by work. Everyone also acknowledges that intellectual enjoyment includes pleasure as well as nobility, for happiness consists of both. Everyone agrees, too, that music, with or without singing, is among the most pleasurable things. As Musaeus says,

'For mortals, song is the sweetest thing of all.' We therefore rightly bring music into gatherings and celebrations, because it gladdens people's hearts. This alone would give us grounds for training the young in it. Harmless pleasures accord with life's complete purpose and also offer relaxation. People seldom reach that ultimate end, but often pause along the way to rest and amuse themselves. They do so not only for some further good, but also for pleasure itself. It may therefore be good for them sometimes to find refreshment in music.

People sometimes make amusement their final aim. The true end probably includes pleasure, though not pleasure of an ordinary or inferior kind. They confuse the inferior pleasure with the higher one, and while pursuing the latter encounter the former, because every pleasure resembles the end of action. The final end is not chosen for the sake of some future good. Likewise, the pleasures just described do not look towards a future benefit, but back towards what has already happened: they relieve previous exertion and pain. This may explain why people look for happiness in ordinary pleasures.

Music is pursued not only to relieve past exertion, but also as recreation. Who can say that, alongside this use, it has no higher purpose? Its pleasure is natural and therefore suits every age and character; everyone feels and shares in it. But beyond this common pleasure, may music not also influence character and the soul? It must do so if it affects our dispositions. The songs of Olympus and many other composers demonstrate that it does. They unquestionably inspire enthusiasm, and enthusiasm is a feeling belonging to the soul's ethical part. Moreover, hearing imitations moves our feelings in sympathy even without melody or rhythm. Music gives pleasure, while virtue consists in taking pleasure, loving, and hating in the right way. Clearly, then, we should chiefly cultivate the ability to judge correctly and to delight in good dispositions and noble actions. Rhythm and melody imitate anger, gentleness, courage, temperance, and virtues and vices generally, with a force scarcely less than the feelings themselves. We know this from our own experience: when we listen to music of this kind, our souls themselves undergo a change. Feeling in this way about an imitation is close to feeling the same way about reality. For example, if someone enjoys looking at a statue solely for its beauty, he must also enjoy seeing

the original. Other senses, such as taste and touch, offer nothing resembling moral qualities. Sight offers a little, since visible forms have some moral character and everyone responds to them to that extent. Yet shapes and colours are signs of moral dispositions rather than imitations of them. These signs appear only when emotion affects the body. Their connection with morals is slight; nevertheless, insofar as it exists, young people should look at the works of Polygnotus or another painter or sculptor who expresses moral character, rather than those of Pauson. Mere melodies, by contrast, already imitate character. Musical modes differ fundamentally, and each affects its listeners differently. Some, such as the so-called Mixolydian, make people solemn and sad. Relaxed harmonies weaken the mind. Others produce a measured, steady disposition, which seems to be the distinctive effect of the Dorian. The Phrygian arouses enthusiasm. Philosophical writers on this branch of education have examined the subject well, supporting their reasoning with observed facts. Rhythms follow the same principles. Some express rest, others movement; among those expressing movement, some are more vulgar, others nobler. We have said enough to establish that music can form character and therefore belongs in the education of the young. It suits their age, because young people avoid anything that is not made pleasant if they can, and music is naturally sweet. [Compare Poetics 2, section 2, and 6, section 15; Plato, Republic III, 398–399.] There seems to be something within us that has a natural affinity with musical harmonies and rhythms. This leads some philosophers to call the soul a harmony, while others say it possesses harmony.

We must now settle the question already raised: should children themselves learn to sing and play? Actually practising the art clearly makes a considerable difference to character. Judging other people's performance well is difficult, perhaps impossible, for someone who has never performed. Besides, children need something to occupy them. Archytas' rattle was an excellent invention: people give it to children to keep them amused and stop them breaking things in the house, since a young child cannot remain still. A rattle is a toy suited to an infant's mind; musical education is a rattle or toy for older children. We conclude that children should learn music in a way that makes them performers as well as judges.

It is easy to answer the question of what is or is not appropriate to different ages. We can also readily answer those who object that studying music is vulgar. First, those who will judge performances must themselves have experience of performing. They should begin practising while young, though when older they can be excused from actual performance. Through the knowledge acquired in youth, they should have learned to recognize what is good and to take pleasure in it. Second, music's allegedly degrading influence is a question of degree. We shall have no difficulty settling it once we consider how far free people being trained for political virtue should pursue this art, what kinds of melodies and rhythms they should be allowed to use, and which instruments should be employed in teaching them to play. The instrument itself, as well as the manner of teaching, makes a difference. [Compare sections 5–8 and, above, section 7.] Our answer to the objection depends on these distinctions, since certain ways of teaching and learning music may indeed have a degrading effect. Clearly, musical study must neither interfere with the work of mature life nor degrade the body or make it unfit for civic or military duties, whether for the early practice of those duties or for their later study.

Students will reach the right level if they stop before acquiring the techniques used in professional competitions. They should not pursue the astonishing displays of execution now fashionable in those contests, which have spread from competitions into education. Let young people continue their studies until they can enjoy noble melodies and rhythms, rather than merely the ordinary pleasures in music that appeal to every slave and child, and even to some animals.

These principles also tell us which instruments to use. The flute, and other instruments demanding great technical skill, such as the harp, should be excluded from education. We should admit only instruments that develop intelligent understanding of music or other educational subjects. Besides, the flute does not have a beneficial moral influence; it is excessively exciting. Its appropriate use is in performances meant to relieve the passions rather than instruct. A further objection is that playing it prevents use of the voice, reducing its educational value. [Compare section 3.] The ancients were therefore right to forbid the flute to young people and free men, although they had previously allowed it. As wealth brought them more leisure, their ideas of excellence grew loftier. Elated by their successes before and after the Persian War, they pursued every branch of knowledge with more enthusiasm than judgment, and introduced the flute into education. A Choragus at Lacedaemon directed the Chorus with a flute. At Athens the instrument became so popular that most free men could play it. The tablet dedicated by Thrasippus when he supplied the Chorus for Ecphantides illustrates its popularity. Later experience taught people to distinguish what genuinely contributes to virtue from what does not. They rejected the flute and several other old instruments: the Lydian harp, the many-stringed lyre, the 'heptagon', 'triangle', 'sambuca', and similar instruments, intended merely to entertain listeners and requiring exceptional manual skill. The ancient story of Athene inventing the flute and then throwing it away also has meaning. The explanation that the goddess disliked it because it distorted her face was not a bad one. But there is a better reason for saying she rejected it: learning to play the flute contributes nothing to the mind, whereas we associate Athene with knowledge and art.

We therefore reject instruments designed for professionals, as well as the professional manner of teaching music. By 'professional' I mean the training adopted for competitions. Here a performer practises the art not to improve himself, but to give pleasure to his listeners, and pleasure of a vulgar kind at that. This is why the performance of such [compare Plato, Republic III, 399 D]

music is the work of a paid performer, rather than a free person. The performers are debased by it because the goal they pursue is low. The spectator's vulgarity lowers the character of the music and consequently of the musicians. They direct their attention towards him: he makes them what they are, and even moulds their bodies through the movements he expects them to display. We must also consider the question of rhythms and harmonies. Should we use every kind in education, or distinguish between them? If we make a distinction, should we adopt the one used by people engaged in education, or should we choose another? We can see that melody and rhythm together produce music. We therefore need to know the influence each has on education, and whether to prefer excellence in melody or excellence in rhythm. Many contemporary musicians have discussed these questions very well, as have philosophers with considerable practical experience of musical education. To them we refer anyone seeking a more exact study of the subject. Here we shall discuss it only from the legislator's standpoint, with attention to its general principles.

We accept certain philosophers' division of melodies into ethical melodies, melodies of action, and melodies that stir passion or enthusiasm. Each, they say, has a corresponding mode or harmony. But we also maintain that music should be studied for several benefits, not just one. It serves, first, education; second, purgation—we leave that word unexplained for now, but shall discuss it more precisely when we examine poetry; and third, intellectual enjoyment, relaxation, and recovery after exertion. We must therefore use every harmony, though not all in the same way. Education should favour ethical melodies, while melodies of action and passion may be enjoyed by listening to others perform them. Feelings such as pity, fear, and enthusiasm are exceptionally strong in some souls and influence everyone to some degree. Some people fall into religious frenzy; we see sacred melodies release them from it, bringing healing and purgation to their souls. Those subject to pity or fear, and emotional temperaments generally, experience something similar. Other people likewise experience these feelings in their own degree, each being moved by something that has a particular influence on him. Everyone is in some sense purged by the experience, and their souls are left lighter and filled with pleasure. Melodies of purgation likewise give people harmless pleasure. These are the harmonies and melodies in which theatre musicians should be invited to compete. But there are two kinds of spectators: free, educated people, and a vulgar crowd of artisans, labourers, and similar people. Competitions and performances should provide relaxation for the second group too. Their music will correspond to their minds. Just as their minds depart from the natural condition, so exaggerated and corrupted harmonies represent a comparable departure. People enjoy what is natural to them, so professional musicians may perform this inferior music for an inferior audience. For education, however, as I have already said, we should employ ethical modes and melodies, such as the Dorian, together with any others approved by philosophers who possess musical training. Socrates in the

Republic wrongly keeps the Phrygian alongside the Dorian as the only modes. His rejection of the flute makes this all the more mistaken, since the Phrygian is among modes what the flute is among instruments: both excite and stir the emotions.

Poetry confirms this. The flute most appropriately expresses Bacchic frenzy and similar feelings, which suit the Phrygian harmony better than any other. The dithyramb, for example, is acknowledged to be Phrygian. Musical experts offer many proofs, including the story that Philoxenus tried to compose his Tales as a Dorian dithyramb, found it impossible, and reverted to the more suitable Phrygian. Everyone agrees that Dorian music is the most solemn and manly. We hold that one should avoid extremes and follow the mean. Since the Dorian stands between the other harmonies, the Phrygian and Lydian, it plainly follows that the young should be taught Dorian music.

We must keep two principles in view: what is possible and what is fitting. Everyone should aim at these, but both depend on age. Older people, whose powers have declined, cannot readily sing demanding melodies. Nature herself seems to indicate that their songs should be more relaxed. Musicians are therefore right to criticize Socrates for excluding relaxed harmonies from education on the ground that they intoxicate. He does not mean intoxication in the usual sense, since wine tends to excite people, but rather that these harmonies lack vigour. Looking ahead to the time when they begin to age, people should therefore practise gentler harmonies and melodies alongside the others. If any harmony suits very young children and combines order with educational value, we should clearly use it. The Lydian seems above all to have this quality. Education should thus rest on three principles: the mean, the possible, and the fitting.
